AI.method: The authors characterize the minimax risk of KV cache compression as a function of intrinsic cache compressibility, deriving design principles under causal masking that achieve minimax-optimal risk and map efficiently to prefill and autoregressive decoding phases.
AI.result: The proposed principles yield a practical algorithm with promising performance on LongBench, demonstrating that theoretically grounded compression can be both principled and effective in practice.
AI.conclusion: The results bridge the gap between theory and practice for KV cache compression, offering a principled framework with theoretical guarantees that guides practical algorithm design.

title: Epic-Organized vs. Requirement-Aligned Gherkin: An Empirical Evaluation of LLM-Based Acceptance Criteria Generation
comment: Accepted for publication at the International Conference on Software Engineering of Emerging Technologies (SEET 2026)
summary: Automated authoring of Gherkin Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) acceptance criteria remains a manual bottleneck in requirements engineering. This study investigates whether epic-organized LLM-generated Gherkin produces higher quality and coverage than requirement-aligned generation. We compare our Timeless (an epic-organized LLM pipeline) approach against a naive large language model (LLM) baseline on four requirements documents (107 requirements) from the PURE dataset. Evaluation covers structural metrics, automated requirement coverage via TF-IDF and dense embeddings, and blind expert assessment by four researchers. In our evaluation, the JSON-constrained pipeline produced structurally valid scenarios across all generated outputs, while the zero-shot baseline achieved 99% structural validity. Semantic coverage was comparable to the baseline, with Timeless achieving 94.3% semantic Requirement Coverage Rate compared with 92.9% for the baseline. TF-IDF produced lower coverage scores for the epic-organized output, suggesting that lexical metrics may miss coverage when scenarios paraphrase requirements at a higher level of abstraction. Expert raters prefer the epic-organized strategy on Correctness (4.61 vs 4.14), Executability (4.61 vs 4.07), and Completeness (4.31 vs 3.50). Overall, the results suggest that epic-organized generation can improve perceived Gherkin quality while maintaining comparable semantic coverage, although broader replication is needed before generalizing this finding.

AI.tldr: This paper compares epic-organized LLM-generated Gherkin (Timeless pipeline) against requirement-aligned generation on 107 requirements. The epic-organized approach achieves 100% structural validity, 94.3% semantic coverage, and higher expert ratings on correctness (4.61 vs 4.14), executability (4.61 vs 4.07), and completeness (4.31 vs 3.50), suggesting improved perceived quality with comparable coverage.
AI.motivation: Automated authoring of Gherkin BDD acceptance criteria remains a manual bottleneck in requirements engineering, motivating the need for improved automation approaches.
AI.method: Compared Timeless (epic-organized LLM pipeline) against a naive LLM baseline on 107 requirements from the PURE dataset. Evaluated using structural metrics, automated requirement coverage (TF-IDF and dense embeddings), and blind expert assessment by four researchers.
AI.result: JSON-constrained pipeline produced 100% structurally valid scenarios; zero-shot baseline achieved 99%. Timeless achieved 94.3% semantic Requirement Coverage Rate vs 92.9% baseline. TF-IDF scores lower for epic-organized output. Expert raters preferred epic-organized on Correctness (4.61 vs 4.14), Executability (4.61 vs 4.07), and Completeness (4.31 vs 3.50).
AI.conclusion: Epic-organized generation improves perceived Gherkin quality while maintaining comparable semantic coverage, though broader replication is needed before generalizing.

title: Boosting Ultrasound Image Classification via Attribute-Guided Dual-Branch Framework
summary: Ultrasound image classification is essential for computer-aided diagnosis. However, current methods often neglect clinical priors, leading to poor generalization in challenging scenarios and a lack of interpretability that limits clinical adoption. To address these issues, we aim to develop a medical-prior module that can be seamlessly integrated into existing pipelines to enhance both diagnostic performance and interpretability. In this paper, we propose an attribute-guided dual-branch framework for ultrasound classification that introduces domain-agnostic medical attribute priors, improving generalization while offering interpretable evidence. Specifically, a baseline branch follows conventional architectures and predicts image categories via a fully connected classifier. An attribute-guided branch injects domain-agnostic attributes as priors and produces human-interpretable decision cues. Finally, an adaptive decision module fuses the two branches in a data-dependent manner to yield the final prediction. Experiments across diverse ultrasound classification tasks demonstrate that our approach can be integrated into multiple backbones and state-of-the-art methods with low overhead, consistently improving accuracy and interpretability. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhaobo253-crypto/AttrGuide.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an attribute-guided dual-branch framework that integrates domain-agnostic medical attribute priors into ultrasound image classification, improving generalization, accuracy, and interpretability across multiple backbones and tasks.
AI.motivation: Current ultrasound classification methods neglect clinical priors, resulting in poor generalization in challenging scenarios and lacking interpretability, which hinders clinical adoption.
AI.method: A dual-branch framework: (1) a baseline branch for conventional classification via a fully connected classifier, (2) an attribute-guided branch that injects domain-agnostic medical attribute priors to produce interpretable decision cues, and (3) an adaptive decision module that fuses both branches in a data-dependent manner.
AI.result: The approach integrates into multiple backbones and state-of-the-art methods with low overhead, consistently improving accuracy and interpretability across diverse ultrasound classification tasks.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating domain-agnostic medical attribute priors via a dual-branch framework effectively enhances both generalization and interpretability in ultrasound image classification, with seamless integration into existing pipelines.

title: Separating Expert Retention from Autonomous Source Inference in Raw-ECG-Replay-Free Continual ECG Deployment
summary:
In multi-source ECG deployment, models may need to incorporate new data sources when earlier raw ECGs cannot be retained or replayed. Freezing a pretrained backbone and assigning each source an isolated classifier prevents parameter interference, but deployment still requires selecting an expert when source metadata are unavailable. We study this distinction through \ours{}, an incremental expert bank built on frozen 1024-dimensional ECGFounder features. Each arriving domain adds a balanced-softmax linear expert, while a lightweight router is fitted only on retained training features and domain labels from sources observed so far. A validation-calibrated margin rule fuses the two most likely experts instead of committing to a single routed expert.
  On CPSC, PTB-XL, Georgia, and Chapman-Shaoxing, source-aware expert selection reaches $0.7915\pm0.0036$ Macro-F1 and a matched offline independent-head reference reaches $0.7885\pm0.0009$, supporting strong source-aware expert retention. Without source IDs, an MLP router reaches $0.7756\pm0.0027$ and top-2 margin fusion reaches $0.7782\pm0.0022$. The top-2 gain over hard MLP routing is small ($+0.0026$), with a 95\% confidence interval from paired bootstrap that includes zero. Across three domain orders, the top-2-to-oracle gap remains $0.0111$--$0.0133$, identifying autonomous source inference as the main remaining bottleneck. No raw ECGs are replayed, but frozen training features are retained for router updates; the method is therefore not memory-free.

AI.tldr: An incremental expert bank built on frozen ECG features, with a router and top-2 margin fusion for deploying multi-source models without source metadata, showing strong source-aware retention but a gap to oracle performance.
AI.motivation: In multi-source ECG deployment, models need to incorporate new data sources when raw ECGs cannot be retained or replayed. Source metadata is often unavailable during deployment, requiring autonomous source inference.
AI.method: Freezes a pretrained ECGFounder backbone (1024-dim features), assigns each source a balanced-softmax linear expert, fits a lightweight MLP router on retained features and domain labels, and uses a validation-calibrated margin rule to fuse top-2 experts instead of committing to a single routed expert.
AI.result: Source-aware expert selection: 0.7915±0.0036 Macro-F1; matched offline reference: 0.7885±0.0009. Without source IDs, MLP router: 0.7756±0.0027; top-2 margin fusion: 0.7782±0.0022. Top-2 gain over hard routing is small (+0.0026) with CI including zero. Top-2-to-oracle gap: 0.0111–0.0133 across domain orders.
AI.conclusion: Strong source-aware expert retention is achievable, but autonomous source inference remains the main bottleneck. The method retains frozen training features (not raw ECGs) for router updates, so it is not memory-free.

title: Multi-Head Recurrent Memory Agents
summary: Recurrent memory agents extend LLMs to arbitrarily long contexts by iteratively consolidating input into a fixed-size memory window. Despite their scalability, these agents exhibit a well-documented reliability problem: end-to-end performance degrades systematically as context length grows. We diagnose this failure by decomposing performance into two factors--memory capture and memory retention--and quantitatively confirm that retention is the dominant bottleneck. Retention collapses because existing designs maintain memory as a monolithic text block, forcing every update to risk overwriting previously retained content. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a general, training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads governed by a stage-wise select-then-update strategy. At each step, exactly one head is selected for update while the remaining heads are structurally shielded from overwriting, shifting the burden of retention from model behavior to architectural design. As a lightweight instantiation, we introduce Least-Recently-Updated MHM (MHM-LRU), which guarantees uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead. Extensive experiments on long-context benchmarks show that MHM-LRU substantially improves both retention and end-to-end accuracy across the 100K--1M token range, where baselines degrade sharply. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, MHM-LRU improves the memory retention rate from less than 30% to 73.96%. These gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types, positioning architectural optimization as a practical and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory.

AI.tldr: Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM) partitions memory into independent heads with a select-then-update strategy to prevent catastrophic overwriting, achieving 73.96% retention at 896K tokens vs. <30% for baselines.
AI.motivation: Recurrent memory agents suffer from systematic performance degradation as context length grows. The paper diagnoses this as a memory retention bottleneck caused by monolithic memory design where every update risks overwriting previously retained content.
AI.method: Proposes Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads with a stage-wise select-then-update strategy. Exactly one head is updated per step while others are shielded from overwriting. The lightweight instantiation MHM-LRU uses Least-Recently-Updated selection for uniform head utilization with zero extra token overhead.
AI.result: MHM-LRU substantially improves retention and end-to-end accuracy across 100K–1M token range. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, retention rate improves from <30% to 73.96%. Gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types.
AI.conclusion: Architectural optimization (memory partitioning and selective update) is a practical, cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory, shifting the retention burden from model behavior to architectural design.

title: Benchmarking Quantum Software Testing with Scalable Quantum Programs
summary: Quantum software testing (QST) checks whether quantum programs behave according to their intended specifications. A key requirement for QST research is a benchmark that supports rigorous empirical evaluation on programs that are testable and better reflect current software development practices. However, existing studies heavily rely on small hard-coded or circuit-level benchmarks, while available quantum programs are scattered across repositories without clear selection criteria, which limits fair comparison and systematic reproducibility. To this end, we present Qolumbina, a benchmark infrastructure for controlled QST experiments on scalable quantum programs. Qolumbina curates 40 programs from open-source repositories, turns them into test-ready subjects through systematic selection, refactoring, specifications, test case examples, unit tests, and standardized interfaces. We also propose QST-oriented criteria to characterize quantum programs along functionality, output behavior, development complexity, and quantum-specific execution complexity. Using these criteria, our empirical study shows that Qolumbina covers diverse testing-relevant properties and supports scalability analysis beyond fixed-size circuit benchmarks. Through controlled experiments with two recent QST approaches, we demonstrate the feasibility of using Qolumbina for execution-cost and fault-detection studies, and highlight backend-dependent effects that can influence QST result interpretation.

AI.tldr: Qolumbina is a benchmark infrastructure for quantum software testing, curating 40 test-ready quantum programs from open-source repositories with standardized interfaces, specifications, and unit tests, enabling controlled scalability analysis and empirical evaluation of QST approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing QST research relies on small hard-coded or circuit-level benchmarks without clear selection criteria, hindering fair comparison, systematic reproducibility, and empirical rigor in quantum software testing.
AI.method: Curates 40 programs from open-source repositories; applies systematic selection, refactoring, specifications, test case examples, unit tests, and standardized interfaces; proposes QST-oriented characterization criteria (functionality, output behavior, development complexity, execution complexity); conducts empirical study and controlled experiments with two QST approaches.
AI.result: Qolumbina covers diverse testing-relevant properties, supports scalability analysis beyond fixed-size circuit benchmarks, and demonstrates feasibility for execution-cost and fault-detection studies while revealing backend-dependent effects influencing QST result interpretation.
AI.conclusion: Qolumbina provides a rigorous, reproducible infrastructure for controlled QST experiments on scalable, test-ready quantum programs, addressing the lack of standardized benchmarks in the field.

title: Plug-and-Play Volumetric Reconstruction for Compressive Sensing Light-Sheet Microscopy
summary: We investigate volumetric reconstruction for compressive sensing light-sheet microscopy (CS-LSM), where fast volumetric imaging is achieved by encoding multiple axial planes into each camera exposure. To recover the underlying volume from highly multiplexed measurements, we propose a plug-and-play (PnP) framework that flexibly incorporates any user-specified denoiser into the reconstruction process. Building on a slice-based formulation, we further introduce an axial-coupled model that exploits correlations between adjacent slices to improve volumetric continuity. For efficient computation, we derive a Woodbury-based update for the data-consistency step in both the slice-based and axial-coupled formulations, and employ a Gauss-Seidel sweep for the denoising step in the axial-coupled model. Under a weakly convex regularization assumption, we establish subsequential convergence of the proposed algorithm. Experiments on synthetic and real zebrafish-heart data demonstrate that the proposed framework successfully recovers cellular structures from compressed measurements, and provide practical insights into the comparative performance of commonly used denoisers within the PnP framework under the CS-LSM setup.

AI.tldr: A plug-and-play (PnP) reconstruction framework for compressive sensing light-sheet microscopy (CS-LSM) that recovers volumetric images from highly multiplexed measurements, using slice-based and axial-coupled models with efficient Woodbury-based updates and Gauss-Seidel denoising, with proven subsequential convergence under weakly convex regularization.
AI.motivation: Fast volumetric imaging in light-sheet microscopy is limited by sequential axial scanning. CS-LSM encodes multiple axial planes into a single camera exposure to achieve higher speed, but recovering the underlying 3D volume from these compressed, highly multiplexed measurements is challenging and requires a robust reconstruction algorithm.
AI.method: Proposes a plug-and-play (PnP) reconstruction framework that integrates any user-specified denoiser. Introduces a slice-based formulation and an axial-coupled model to exploit inter-slice correlations for improved volumetric continuity. Uses a Woodbury-based matrix identity for efficient data-consistency updates, and a Gauss-Seidel sweep for the denoising step in the axial-coupled model. Convergence is established under a weakly convex regularization assumption.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic data and real zebrafish-heart data show successful recovery of cellular structures from compressed CS-LSM measurements. The study also provides comparative insights into the performance of various commonly used denoisers within the PnP framework under the CS-LSM setup.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PnP framework effectively reconstructs volumetric images from CS-LSM compressed measurements, and the axial-coupled model improves volumetric continuity. The framework is flexible, computationally efficient, and theoretically grounded with convergence guarantees.

title: Epistemic Goggles: A Pretrained Module that Induces an Epistemic Frame via Gradient Editing
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Code at https://github.com/JoshuaSP/epistemic-goggles and generated documents, questions, and teacher rollouts at https://huggingface.co/datasets/joshuapenman/epistemic-goggles-artifacts
summary: Finetuning a language model on documents that are explicitly annotated as fictional results in a model that still actually believes the documents' core claims, an effect known as Negation Neglect. In our evaluations, models trained on documents prefixed and suffixed with such annotations correctly identify the relevant claims as fictional only about 9% of the time. To address this, we introduce Goggles, a learned module that intervenes on the finetuning gradient rather than the data. During supervised finetuning, a Goggles module edits the gradients an LLM LoRA receives, imparting a chosen epistemic frame (the stance the model takes toward the nature of what it reads) to whatever the documents teach. A Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to documents it was never trained on. Trained through Goggles on those same documents, now carrying no fictional annotation, the model flags the content as fictional roughly 91% of the time, while preserving capability (GPQA and TruthfulQA match or exceed baseline). The same architecture supports other frames: a Goggles instance can be trained to treat documents as "part of an AI safety evaluation by Redwood Research" rather than simply as fiction. The imparted frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim, where prior interventions revert. Goggles suggests a path toward training language models on known-misaligned data without absorbing the behaviors that data demonstrates.

AI.tldr: Goggles is a learned module that intervenes on gradients during finetuning to impart epistemic frames (e.g., "this is fiction") onto language models, achieving ~91% accuracy in recognizing fictional claims without explicit annotations, compared to ~9% with annotation-based approaches, while preserving general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Standard finetuning on explicitly annotated fictional data suffers from Negation Neglect—models still believe the core claims despite explicit fictional annotations (only ~9% correctly identify claims as fictional). This makes it difficult to train language models on known-misaligned data without absorbing the undesirable behaviors.
AI.method: Goggles is a learned module that edits gradients during supervised finetuning (specifically LoRA) to impart a chosen epistemic frame. It is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to unseen documents without requiring explicit annotations.
AI.result: Models trained via Goggles on unannotated documents flag content as fictional ~91% of the time (vs ~9% with annotation-based methods). GPQA and TruthfulQA match or exceed baseline performance. The frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back against the claim, where prior interventions fail.
AI.conclusion: Goggles offers a path toward training language models on known-misaligned data without absorbing the demonstrated behaviors, by intervening on gradients rather than data annotations, and the architecture generalizes to other epistemic frames beyond fiction (e.g., AI safety evaluation framing).

title: Wind-Aware Reinforcement Learning Control of a Small Quadrotor Using Learned Onboard Wind Estimation in Simulated Atmospheric Turbulence
summary: Small multirotor aircraft are increasingly tasked with operations in the atmospheric boundary layer, where turbulent winds comparable to the vehicle's airspeed degrade trajectory tracking and can defeat conventional feedback control. This work illustrates a two-stage learning pipeline that first estimates the local wind from onboard kinematics and dynamics and then exploits that estimate inside a reinforcement learning (RL) flight controller. The wind estimator, an attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Karman turbulence with power-law shear and veer, recovers the horizontal wind vector with a per-flight root-mean-square error of 0.40 m/s and a direction error of 3.2 degrees on unseen wind regimes, an accuracy near the floor imposed by unresolved turbulence, and generalizes to vertical ascent profiles with a skill score of 0.861 over a constant-wind reference. A proximal policy optimization controller receiving the frozen estimator's output reduces horizontal trajectory tracking error by 48% relative to a wind-blind proportional-derivative baseline across mean winds of 4 m/s to 12 m/s, winning on 100% of evaluation episodes. A three-way ablation decomposes this improvement into a kinematic component, available without wind information, and a wind-perception component; the perception share rises with wind speed, from small in light winds toward roughly half the total benefit in strong winds, consistent with the quadratic scaling of aerodynamic drag. The controller degrades gracefully on out-of-distribution winds of 13 m/s to 15 m/s, where the baseline fails catastrophically.

AI.tldr: A two-stage learning pipeline combining an attention-gated recurrent wind estimator (RMSE 0.40 m/s, direction error 3.2°) with a PPO-based RL flight controller reduces horizontal trajectory tracking error by 48% over a wind-blind PD baseline across 4-12 m/s winds, with the wind perception component contributing up to ~half the benefit in strong winds.
AI.motivation: Small multirotor aircraft increasingly operate in the atmospheric boundary layer where turbulent winds comparable to airspeed degrade trajectory tracking and can defeat conventional feedback control.
AI.method: Two-stage learning pipeline: (1) an attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Kármán turbulence with power-law shear and veer to estimate local wind from onboard kinematics and dynamics; (2) a proximal policy optimization (PPO) RL controller that uses the frozen estimator's output to improve trajectory tracking.
AI.result: Wind estimator achieves per-flight RMSE of 0.40 m/s and direction error of 3.2° on unseen wind regimes, near the floor imposed by unresolved turbulence, and generalizes to vertical ascent (skill score 0.861). The PPO controller reduces horizontal trajectory tracking error by 48% relative to a wind-blind PD baseline (4-12 m/s winds), winning 100% of evaluation episodes. Three-way ablation decomposes improvement into kinematic and wind-perception components; perception share rises with wind speed, approaching ~half the benefit in strong winds. Controller degrades gracefully on out-of-distribution 13-15 m/s winds where baseline fails catastrophically.
AI.conclusion: The learned wind estimator combined with RL control substantially improves trajectory tracking in turbulent winds, with graceful degradation beyond training distribution, and the benefit scales with wind speed consistent with aerodynamic drag physics.

title: Mitigating Package Hallucinations in Large Language Models via Model Editing
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in software engineering tasks, such as code generation, library recommendation, and dependency configuration. However, recent studies show that LLMs may suffer from package hallucination, where they generate non-existent or invalid package names. These hallucinations can be exploited in software supply chain attacks, as attackers may register malicious packages under hallucinated names. Therefore, mitigating package hallucination is important for improving the reliability and security of LLM-assisted software development. In this paper, we introduce BOUND, a lightweight localized model editing framework for mitigating package hallucinations in LLMs. BOUND formulates package hallucination mitigation as a package-validity boundary editing problem, where the boundary refers to the model's ability to distinguish valid packages from hallucinated package names under a given task context. It first locates modules related to package hallucination through a risk-aware localization strategy, and then edits these modules with lightweight LoRA adapters using a boundary-aware objective that reinforces valid packages, suppresses hallucinated packages, and preserves locality behavior. Experimental results show that BOUND effectively reduces package hallucinations while preserving valid package recommendations. In the package recommendation task, BOUND reduces package-level hallucination rate (Package-HR) by 79.9% on edit prompts and by 65.4% on unseen prompts. The learned package-validity boundary further generalizes to other package-related tasks, reducing Package-HR by 12.8% in code generation and by 34.0% in pip install recommendation. These results show that BOUND refines the package-validity boundary of LLMs and improves the reliability of package-related outputs.

AI.tldr: BOUND is a lightweight localized model editing framework that mitigates package hallucination in LLMs by formulating it as a package-validity boundary editing problem. It uses risk-aware localization to find hallucination-related modules and boundary-aware LoRA adapters to reinforce valid packages while suppressing hallucinated ones. Experiments show significant reductions in hallucination rates across multiple package-related tasks.
AI.motivation: LLMs suffer from package hallucination—generating non-existent or invalid package names—which can be exploited in software supply chain attacks. Mitigating this issue is critical for improving the reliability and security of LLM-assisted software development.
AI.method: BOUND formulates mitigation as a package-validity boundary editing problem. It first locates modules responsible for package hallucination via risk-aware localization, then edits them using lightweight LoRA adapters with a boundary-aware objective that reinforces valid packages, suppresses hallucinated ones, and preserves locality behavior.
AI.result: In package recommendation, Package-HR is reduced by 79.9% on edit prompts and 65.4% on unseen prompts. Generalization to other tasks: 12.8% reduction in code generation and 34.0% in pip install recommendation.
AI.conclusion: BOUND effectively reduces package hallucinations while preserving valid recommendations, refining the package-validity boundary of LLMs and improving reliability of package-related outputs.

title: Domain Generalization via Text-Anchored Information Bottleneck
summary: Visual recognition models often fail when deployed in new environments. Domain Generalization (DG) addresses this by learning representations that remain invariant to environment-specific variations. Recent approaches increasingly rely on large vision-language models, assuming that preserving their expressive visual representations improves robustness. However, we show that such visual expressiveness can instead propagate spurious cues that tie representations to the training environments, hindering invariant learning. We therefore discard visual guidance and instead treat the language embedding space as the primary source of domain invariance, naturally acting as an information bottleneck that preserves core semantics while suppressing domain-specific variations. Extensive experiments across diverse backbones exhibit state-of-the-art performance and further analyze what makes guidance effective for robust generalization. These findings shift the focus of DG from improving representations to designing supervision that enforces invariance.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the common assumption that preserving expressive visual representations from vision-language models improves domain generalization. Instead, it shows visual expressiveness propagates spurious cues, and proposes using language embeddings as the primary source of domain invariance, achieving state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: Current DG methods rely on large vision-language models, assuming that preserving their expressive visual representations improves robustness. However, such visual expressiveness can propagate spurious cues that tie representations to training environments, hindering invariant learning.
AI.method: The approach discards visual guidance and instead treats the language embedding space as the primary source of domain invariance. Language embeddings naturally act as an information bottleneck that preserves core semantics while suppressing domain-specific variations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse backbones exhibit state-of-the-art performance, surpassing existing methods that rely on visual representations from vision-language models.
AI.conclusion: The findings shift the focus of DG from improving representations to designing supervision that enforces invariance, suggesting that language guidance is more effective than visual expressiveness for robust generalization.

title: COMFYCLAW: Self-Evolving Skill Harnesses for Image Generation Workflows
summary: Agents are increasingly used to construct workflows and assist humans in completing recurring tasks more efficiently. As these workflows become repeated and domain-specific, agent memory and reusable skills become increasingly important: agents should be able to recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from previous runs. We study this problem in workflow-based image generation and introduce COMFYCLAW, an agentic skill evolution harness for controlling ComfyUI workflows. COMFYCLAW formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing, exposes tools organized by construction stage, automatically reverts invalid edits, and uses a region-level vision-language model (VLM) verifier to translate visual failures into actionable repair suggestions. The framework further evolves a progressively disclosed skill library, where trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback from previous runs are distilled into reusable Agent Skills. Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotations further show that annotators prefer COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution. Our results suggest that skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction.

AI.tldr: COMFYCLAW is an agentic framework for controlling ComfyUI workflows that formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing, uses a region-level VLM verifier for repair suggestions, and evolves a skill library from past trajectories to improve agent performance. It achieves the best average evaluation scores across multiple benchmarks and agent configurations.
AI.motivation: As agents are increasingly used for recurring, domain-specific workflows, the need for agent memory and reusable skills becomes critical—agents should recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from previous runs to improve efficiency and reliability.
AI.method: COMFYCLAW formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing with stage-specific tools, automatic reversion of invalid edits, and a region-level VLM verifier that translates visual failures into actionable repair suggestions. It evolves a progressively disclosed skill library by distilling trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback from previous runs into reusable Agent Skills.
AI.result: Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotators also preferred COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution.
AI.conclusion: Skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction tasks.

title: Certified World Models as Sensing Clocks: Drift-Aware Deadlines for Active Perception
summary: Certified world models estimate how long their predictions remain valid. We turn this validity horizon into an operational sensing clock: a rule for when an agent should stop coasting and re-sense. Starting from an audited equivariant world model, we derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals and show that deployable deadlines in learned world models must be drift-aware: on-manifold Lyapunov rates alone overestimate coasting validity, while calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes carry the deployed guarantee. On a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model, the resulting clock controls held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violation across seeds and data shards. In a cue-conditioned theorem-bed (a synthetic bench where all schedulers share the exact model, isolating the scheduling rule), the clock remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations relative to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budget. We also report limits: in the short-horizon frozen VN-JEPA regime, empirical conformal horizons match the deployed clock on validity and budget, and a partial-reset exploration finds no clean budget-matched advantage for the spectral term. Thus the contribution is a certified sensing-clock primitive and drift-aware deployment method, not a claim that spectral clocks empirically dominate all non-spectral schedulers.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a certified sensing clock derived from world model validity horizons. It shows that deployable deadlines must be drift-aware using calibrated rollout-drift envelopes rather than on-manifold Lyapunov rates. Experiments on a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model and a synthetic theorem-bed demonstrate validity and reduced eventful-tail violations compared to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budgets.
AI.motivation: To derive a principled, certified rule (sensing clock) from world model validity horizons that tells an agent when to stop coasting and re-sense, while addressing the gap between theoretical guarantees and deployed performance in learned world models.
AI.method: Starting from an audited equivariant world model, the authors derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals. They show that deployment requires drift-aware deadlines using calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes rather than on-manifold Lyapunov rates. Evaluation uses a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model and a cue-conditioned theorem-bed (synthetic bench) to isolate the scheduling rule.
AI.result: The clock controls held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violation across seeds/data shards. On the theorem-bed, it reduces eventful-tail violations relative to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched budget. Empirical conformal horizons match the deployed clock in short-horizon frozen VN-JEPA regime. No clean budget-matched advantage for the spectral term was found in partial-reset exploration.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is a certified sensing-clock primitive and drift-aware deployment method, not a claim of empirical dominance over all non-spectral schedulers.

title: Prompt Coverage Adequacy
summary: In recent years, it has become increasingly evident that large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents raise the level of abstraction in software development by shifting the focus from writing precise procedures to expressing intents and goals. This paradigm shift introduces new challenges, particularly in how testing should be guided when prompts, rather than code, become primary development artifacts. To address this challenge, we propose Prompt Coverage Adequacy, a novel coverage criterion designed to support the testing of code generated from task descriptions. Prompt Coverage Adequacy serves as an analog to traditional code coverage, but operates at the level of prompts used in LLM and agent-based programming. Specifically, it measures how well a given test suite satisfies the requirements expressed in a prompt by leveraging the attention mechanisms of LLMs. We evaluate a simple instantiation of this criterion, based on attention boosting, across two datasets and multiple LLMs. Our results demonstrate that Prompt Coverage is associated with fault-detection effectiveness and can uncover over 30+% more faults than traditional code coverage when used to guide test generation. These findings suggest that Prompt Coverage Adequacy can serve as a foundation for developing testing metrics better suited to the emerging paradigm of LLM-driven software development, addressing the limitations of classical coverage criteria in this new context.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Prompt Coverage Adequacy, a new testing criterion for LLM-generated code that measures how well test suites satisfy prompt requirements using attention mechanisms, finding it can uncover 30+% more faults than traditional code coverage.
AI.motivation: LLMs and autonomous agents shift software development from writing precise procedures to expressing intents and goals via prompts. This introduces new testing challenges since prompts (not code) become primary development artifacts, and traditional code coverage criteria are inadequate for this new paradigm.
AI.method: The authors propose Prompt Coverage Adequacy, a coverage criterion operating at the prompt level that uses LLM attention mechanisms to measure how well a test suite satisfies prompt-expressed requirements. They implement a simple instantiation based on attention boosting and evaluate across two datasets and multiple LLMs.
AI.result: Prompt Coverage is associated with fault-detection effectiveness and uncovers over 30+% more faults than traditional code coverage when guiding test generation.
AI.conclusion: Prompt Coverage Adequacy can serve as a foundation for developing testing metrics better suited to LLM-driven software development, addressing limitations of classical coverage criteria in this new context.

title: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models What to See and Where to Look
comment: The paper has been accepted by ECCV 2026
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing VLAs' training relies heavily on text-centric visual question answering and chain-of-thought reasoning data, which emphasizes linguistic reasoning rather than action-grounded planning. As a result, the learned representations capture semantic knowledge but lack spatial dependencies crucial for reliable trajectory prediction. We propose DriveTeach-VLA, a framework that explicitly teaches VLAs what to see and where to look. Driving-aware Vision Distillation (DVD) injects driving-specific perceptual priors into the vision encoder, while 2D Trajectory-Guided Prompts (2D-TGP) provide spatial conditioning aligned with feasible driving trajectories. Together, they form a vision-guided learning pipeline: what to see (DVD pretraining) - where to look (TGP-guided SFT) - how to act (TGP-guided GRPO). DriveTeach-VLA achieves the state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM and nuScenes. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ShivaTeam/DriveTeach-VLA.

AI.tldr: DriveTeach-VLA proposes a vision-guided learning pipeline (DVD + 2D-TGP) that explicitly teaches VLAs driving-specific perceptual priors and spatial trajectory conditioning, achieving SOTA on NAVSIM and nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Existing VLAs rely on text-centric VQA and chain-of-thought reasoning data, which emphasize linguistic reasoning over action-grounded planning, resulting in representations that lack spatial dependencies critical for reliable trajectory prediction.
AI.method: DriveTeach-VLA consists of three stages: (1) Driving-aware Vision Distillation (DVD) injects driving-specific perceptual priors into the vision encoder (what to see); (2) 2D Trajectory-Guided Prompts (2D-TGP) provide spatial conditioning aligned with feasible trajectories (where to look); (3) A vision-guided pipeline: DVD pretraining → TGP-guided SFT → TGP-guided GRPO for action learning (how to act).
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM and nuScenes benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly teaching VLAs driving-specific visual and spatial priors through DVD and 2D-TGP significantly outperforms prior text-centric VLA approaches for autonomous driving.

title: Generic Expert Coverage for Pruning SparseMixture-of-Experts Language Models
summary: Sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models contain substantial structured redundancy among routed experts, but pruning them without downstream calibration data remains challenging. Existing expert-pruning methods typically rely on a single aggregated importance score, which can bias the retained set toward experts favored by dominant calibration patterns. We propose \textbf{Generic TB-Coverage}, a coverage-aware expert pruning method that uses only generic text corpora (WikiText2 and C4) for calibration. Instead of collapsing expert utility into one score, our method profiles per-expert utility separately on each corpus and enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from each corpus before constructing the final pruning mask. Across Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25\%, 50\%, and 75\% retention budgets, our method improves average accuracy on six common zero-shot benchmarks over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity, while also reducing perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. The gains are largest under aggressive pruning (25\% and 50\% retain), suggesting that preserving cross-corpus expert coverage is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning. Our improvements hold with fixed pruning budgets and no downstream calibration data.

AI.tldr: Proposes Generic TB-Coverage, a coverage-aware expert pruning method for MoE language models that profiles expert utility separately on multiple generic corpora and enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule, outperforming random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity across Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at various retention budgets without requiring downstream calibration data.
AI.motivation: Existing expert-pruning methods for sparsely activated MoE language models rely on single aggregated importance scores that can bias retained experts toward patterns dominant in calibration data, and they struggle when no downstream calibration data is available.
AI.method: Profiles per-expert utility separately on WikiText2 and C4 corpora, then applies a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from each corpus before constructing the final pruning mask, avoiding collapsing expert utility into one score.
AI.result: At 25%, 50%, and 75% retention budgets on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base, the method improves average accuracy on six zero-shot benchmarks and reduces perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4 compared to random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity, with largest gains under aggressive pruning (25% and 50% retain).
AI.conclusion: Preserving cross-corpus expert coverage is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning, achieving improvements without any downstream calibration data.

title: Evolutionary Feature Engineering for Structured Data
comment: 9 page main content, 41 pages in total
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as open-ended search operators in evolutionary optimization. We introduce Evolutionary Feature Engineering (EFE), a framework for using LLM-based evolution to discover preprocessing transformations for structured data. EFE represents transformations as Python programs with a standardized fit/transform interface, allowing them to be inserted directly into existing machine learning pipelines. During evolution, candidate programs are refined using dataset context, summary statistics, and downstream performance feedback on validation set. We instantiate EFE in two settings. For time-series forecasting, EFE-Time learns invertible, dataset-specific normalizations that improve off-the-shelf time-series foundation models. It reduces forecasting errors (MASE, WQL, MAE) 3% or more when averaged across datasets and improvements are as much as 19% on the COVID-Deaths dataset. Notably, these improvements occur with recent TSFMs such as Chronos-2. For tabular prediction, EFE-Tab evolves compact feature programs that add useful interpretable features and remove redundant ones, improving or matching existing LLM-based feature-engineering methods. We found EFE-Tab to be particularly effective on classical decision trees, where small sets of evolved features yield competitive accuracy while preserving interpretability. Overall, EFE demonstrates that LLM-based evolution can improve both accuracy and interpretability when automatically tackling structured data.

AI.tldr: EFE is a framework using LLM-based evolution to automatically discover preprocessing transformations for structured data (time-series and tabular), improving accuracy and interpretability by evolving Python programs with a fit/transform interface.
AI.motivation: Leverage LLMs as open-ended search operators in evolutionary optimization to automatically discover effective preprocessing transformations for structured data, reducing manual feature engineering effort while improving both accuracy and interpretability.
AI.method: EFE represents transformations as Python programs with a standardized fit/transform interface. Candidate programs are refined via LLM-based evolution using dataset context, summary statistics, and downstream validation performance feedback. Two instantiations: EFE-Time (invertible normalizations for time-series) and EFE-Tab (compact feature programs for tabular data).
AI.result: EFE-Time reduces forecasting errors (MASE, WQL, MAE) by 3%+ on average, up to 19% on COVID-Deaths dataset, improving recent TSFMs like Chronos-2. EFE-Tab improves or matches existing LLM-based feature engineering methods, particularly effective on classical decision trees with compact, interpretable feature sets.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based evolution can simultaneously improve both accuracy and interpretability when automatically tackling structured data across time-series and tabular domains.

title: File-Level Copying Is an Implicit Dependency in Open Source
summary: File-level copying is a widespread but ungoverned form of software reuse. Copying files across repositories reduces supply-chain visibility: it removes the four observable signals a package manager provides for a declared dependency (provenance, maintenance, security, and compliance) with no mechanism to restore them. To characterize the scale and consequences of this unmanaged reuse, we present a mixed-method study of copying across the entire open-source ecosystem using World of Code (WoC). From a 0.1% commit sample, we extract 690,500 copy events and retain 3,912 rationale-bearing copy commits for intent labeling. We show that the 13 axial copy forms, spanning vendored dependencies, hardware/driver synchronization, scaffolding, UI assets, and direct source-code reuse, are unreliable proxies for developer intent: among rationale-bearing commits, hardware/driver copies are predominantly fork-maintenance work (78%), while dependency-vendoring copies more often signal upstream bypass (70%) than offline availability. These visibility gaps are form-specific: security and license risk concentrate in complementary copy forms. Copied sources are frequently stale (median 155 days; 38.5% over one year old) and seldom record a recoverable origin (4.3% documented), let alone a checkable version (2.0% versioned); even vendored copies record where they came from only 10% of the time. Security risk concentrates in vendored dependencies: 17,314 CVE-risk copy commits in the full-WoC graph, 88% in the dependency-vendoring form; 80% score CVSS >= 7.0 and upstream-fix adoption is only 47%-84%. License risk concentrates in direct source-code reuse: 41,777 pre-validation candidates, 66% in the source-code form, with 39 verified high-star violations (kappa = 0.752). Both risks reach packaged software and are invisible to dependency scanners operating on declared metadata alone.

AI.tldr: File-level copying across open-source repositories creates visibility gaps in provenance, maintenance, security, and compliance. From a 0.1% commit sample, we identify 690,500 copy events, categorize 13 axial copy forms with distinct developer intents, and show that copied sources are often stale (median 155 days), lack origin documentation (4.3%), and concentrate security risk in vendored dependencies (17,314 CVE-risk commits, 88% vendored) and license risk in direct source-code reuse (41,777 candidates, 66% source-code form). These risks are invisible to package-manager-based dependency scanners.
AI.motivation: File-level copying is widespread but ungoverned in open-source ecosystems, eliminating the four observable signals (provenance, maintenance, security, compliance) that package managers provide for declared dependencies, with no mechanism to restore them. The study aims to characterize the scale and consequences of this unmanaged reuse.
AI.method: Mixed-method study using World of Code (WoC). From a 0.1% commit sample, 690,500 copy events were extracted, retaining 3,912 rationale-bearing copy commits for intent labeling. Analysis covered 13 axial copy forms including vendored dependencies, hardware/driver synchronization, scaffolding, UI assets, and direct source-code reuse.
AI.result:
- 13 axial copy forms identified; developer intent varies significantly (e.g., hardware/driver copies: 78% fork-maintenance; vendored copies: 70% upstream bypass).  
- Copied sources are stale (median 155 days; 38.5% > 1 year old), rarely documented (4.3% origin, 2.0% versioned).  
- Security risk: 17,314 CVE-risk copy commits; 88% in vendored dependencies; 80% CVSS >= 7.0; upstream-fix adoption only 47%-84%.  
- License risk: 41,777 pre-validation candidates; 66% in source-code form; 39 verified high-star violations.  
- Both risks are invisible to dependency scanners relying on declared metadata.
AI.conclusion: File-level copying introduces significant security and license risks that are invisible to package-manager-based dependency scanners. The visibility gaps are form-specific, with security risk concentrated in vendored dependencies and license risk in direct source-code reuse. The findings highlight the need for governance mechanisms to restore visibility signals lost through unmanaged file-level copying.

title: Unified Panoramic-Gaussian Representation for Monocular 4D Scene Synthesis
summary: 4D scene synthesis from monocular videos has made significant progress in recent years. However, existing methods are typically constrained by view interpolation. As a result, they struggle to infer unseen regions beyond the observed views. In this paper, we reformulate the task as 4D scene synthesis with unseen regions, which extends beyond traditional interpolation settings. Camera-conditioned video generation enables unseen region synthesis by guiding generation along specified cameras. However, these methods lack explicit 3D priors and are optimized with random camera trajectories. This design leads to severe inconsistencies under large trajectory deviations. To address this limitation, we build a unified training and inference framework with panoramic trajectory guidance. While this design improves cross-view consistency, the panoramic representation alone fails to model dynamic content effectively. Object motion in panoramic space introduces scale and shape distortions. To address this, we propose PanoGaussian, a unified Panoramic-Gaussian representation that distills the panoramic representation into an explicit dynamic Gaussian representation to capture dynamic physical priors of the 4D scene. Experiments demonstrate that PanoGaussian achieves consistent 4D scene synthesis even under large viewpoint variations.

AI.tldr: PanoGaussian proposes a Panoramic-Gaussian representation that distills panoramic video into explicit dynamic 3D Gaussians to achieve consistent 4D scene synthesis under large viewpoint variations, overcoming the limitations of existing view-interpolation methods and camera-conditioned video generation.
AI.motivation: Existing 4D scene synthesis from monocular videos is limited to view interpolation and cannot infer unseen regions beyond observed views; camera-conditioned video generation lacks explicit 3D priors and suffers from severe inconsistencies under large trajectory deviations.
AI.method: Builds a unified training and inference framework with panoramic trajectory guidance, then proposes PanoGaussian, a unified Panoramic-Gaussian representation that distills panoramic representation into an explicit dynamic Gaussian representation to capture dynamic physical priors of the 4D scene.
AI.result: PanoGaussian achieves consistent 4D scene synthesis even under large viewpoint variations, overcoming the inconsistencies of prior methods.
AI.conclusion: The Panoramic-Gaussian representation effectively combines panoramic guidance with explicit dynamic 3D Gaussians, enabling robust 4D scene synthesis beyond traditional interpolation settings.

title: Distributionally Robust Listwise Preference Optimization
summary: Existing robust preference optimization for language-model alignment mainly studies pairwise supervision and places robustness at the dataset, prompt, or preference-pair level. We instead study listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty: given a prompt and a candidate list, the observed ranking over that list may be ambiguous due to annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy rankwise feedback, or reward-model noise. We propose a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett--Luce objective that directly robustifies the ranking label conditional on the candidate list. The robust loss admits an exact decomposition into the nominal PL loss plus a worst-case PL correction, and the worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order, reducing the inner maximization from $K!$ enumeration to $O(K\log K)$. This tractable structure yields strong offline and online optimization guarantees. In the offline fixed-list setting, the robust objective is convex and projected stochastic subgradient reaches global $ε$-suboptimality with $O(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity. In the online policy-induced setting, where candidate lists are generated by the current policy, we establish weak convexity and $\widetilde O(ε^{-2})$ Moreau-envelope stationarity. Experiments in offline LLM alignment show that the proposed robust correction largely preserves performance under clean labels and improves robustness under noise. In online alignment, it makes reward-model-ranked candidate expansion more reliable and improves both reward-model and external GPT-4 judge metrics.

AI.tldr: Proposes a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett-Luce objective for listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty, with tractable worst-case ranking computation ($O(K\log K)$), convexity guarantees in offline setting, and weak convexity in online setting, showing improved robustness in LLM alignment experiments.
AI.motivation: Existing robust preference optimization focuses on pairwise supervision and places robustness at dataset/prompt/pair level, but ignores listwise ranking-label uncertainty arising from annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy feedback, or reward-model noise.
AI.method: Proposes a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett-Luce (PL) objective that robustifies ranking labels conditional on the candidate list. The robust loss decomposes into nominal PL loss plus worst-case PL correction, where the worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order ($O(K\log K)$). Offline: convex with $O(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity via projected stochastic subgradient. Online (policy-induced): weakly convex with $\widetilde O(ε^{-2})$ Moreau-envelope stationarity.
AI.result: Offline LLM alignment: robust correction preserves performance under clean labels and improves robustness under noise. Online alignment: makes reward-model-ranked candidate expansion more reliable, improving both reward-model and external GPT-4 judge metrics.
AI.conclusion: The tractable robust PL formulation effectively handles listwise ranking-label uncertainty with strong theoretical guarantees and practical improvements in LLM alignment robustness.

title: X-LogSMask: Expand Transformer for Graph-Structured Data
summary: Transformers have become general-purpose architectures, but their all-to-all self-attention is poorly matched to graph data, whose interactions are sparse, structured and multi-scale. Existing Graph Transformers address this mismatch through structural encodings, hybrid message-passing modules or learned attention constraints, often introducing additional complexity and limited interpretability. Here we introduce X-LogSMask, an explainable multi-head logarithmic structural mask that injects symmetrically normalized graph topology directly into attention logits. The logarithmic transform converts structural connectivity into a topology-aware gating signal, suppressing unsupported node interactions while preserving feature-dependent attention. By assigning different powers of the normalized adjacency matrix to different attention heads, X-LogSMask gives each head a defined structural radius and supports multi-hop information propagation within a single layer. We further show that a standard Transformer encoder can be interpreted as one-step message passing on a complete graph, motivating X-LogSMask as a topology-constrained alternative to unrestricted self-attention. Across 20 node-, edge- and graph-level benchmarks, Transformers equipped with X-LogSMask achieve state-of-the-art performance on 13 datasets and remain competitive in a lightweight one-layer configuration. These results show that simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention an effective graph-learning operator without changing the Transformer architecture. The code is available at https://github.com/LiLeyan-0120/X-LogSMask.

AI.tldr: X-LogSMask introduces a logarithmic structural mask that injects graph topology directly into attention logits, enabling Transformers to handle sparse, structured graph data without architectural changes, achieving SOTA on 13 out of 20 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard Transformers' all-to-all self-attention is poorly suited for graph data where interactions are sparse, structured, and multi-scale. Existing Graph Transformers address this mismatch with complex structural encodings, hybrid message-passing, or learned attention constraints, introducing limited interpretability and additional complexity.
AI.method: X-LogSMask applies a logarithmic transform to the symmetrically normalized adjacency matrix, converting structural connectivity into a topology-aware gating signal injected into attention logits. Different powers of the normalized adjacency matrix are assigned to different attention heads, giving each head a defined structural radius and enabling multi-hop propagation within a single layer.
AI.result: Across 20 node-, edge-, and graph-level benchmarks, Transformers with X-LogSMask achieve state-of-the-art performance on 13 datasets and remain competitive even in a lightweight one-layer configuration.
AI.conclusion: Simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention an effective graph-learning operator without altering the Transformer architecture.

title: Coding Agents Are Guessing: Measuring Action-Boundary Violations in Underspecified DevOps Instructions
summary:
LLM coding agents are increasingly deployed to act autonomously on real production infrastructure. They execute shell commands, modify repositories, and call operational APIs. However, completing a task is not sufficient for safety. A wrong action can cause severe consequences. Existing agent benchmarks largely emphasize task completion, leaving open how agents behave under benign but underspecified instructions.
  We present UnderSpecBench, a benchmark for measuring action-boundary violations in coding agents (i.e., Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode) on DevOps tasks. UnderSpecBench includes 69 task families grounded in documented incidents, CVEs, or tool behavior and organized across four DevOps capability domains and nine operational control surfaces. To isolate underspecification from task difficulty, each task keeps the same environment and ground-truth safe action while varying the instruction along three axes: intent clarity, target certainty, and blast radius. The resulting 2,208 prompt variants are evaluated with deterministic, side-effect-based oracles that separate Safe Success, Wrong Target, and OverScope outcomes; non-action runs are further classified as clarification, refusal, or deferment.
  Across five agent x model configurations using OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex, the evaluation results show that underspecification does not mainly make agents fail; it makes them guess. 55.8-67.8% of runs violate at least one boundary. Target underspecification sharply degrades action quality, while blast-radius cues barely reduce action propensity. These findings show that completion-centric evaluation can overstate safe autonomy and motivate mitigations at the model, harness, and system layer.

AI.tldr: UnderSpecBench is a benchmark of 2,208 prompt variants across 69 DevOps task families that evaluates how coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) handle underspecified instructions. Results show 55.8-67.8% of runs violate action boundaries, with target underspecification being the primary degradation factor, revealing that completion-centric evaluation overstates safe autonomy.
AI.motivation: Existing agent benchmarks focus on task completion and fail to assess how agents behave under benign but underspecified instructions, where wrong actions can cause severe consequences on production infrastructure. There is a need to measure action-boundary violations beyond mere task success.
AI.method: The benchmark includes 69 task families grounded in documented incidents, CVEs, or tool behavior across four DevOps domains and nine control surfaces. Each task keeps the same environment and ground-truth safe action while varying instructions along three axes: intent clarity, target certainty, and blast radius. This yields 2,208 prompt variants evaluated with deterministic, side-effect-based oracles classifying outcomes as Safe Success, Wrong Target, OverScope, or non-action (clarification, refusal, deferment).
AI.result: Across five agent × model configurations (OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex), 55.8-67.8% of runs violate at least one boundary. Underspecification causes agents to guess rather than fail. Target underspecification sharply degrades action quality, while blast-radius cues barely reduce action propensity.
AI.conclusion: Completion-centric evaluation overstates safe autonomy. Mitigations are needed at the model, harness, and system layers to ensure agents handle underspecification appropriately before deployment on real infrastructure.

title: Temporal and Cross-Modal Alignment for Enhanced Audiovisual Video Captioning
summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have advanced video understanding, achieving precise temporal and cross-modal alignment in audiovisual video captioning remains a formidable challenge. Most existing approaches suffer from modality detachment and temporal incoherence, failing to accurately bind auditory events to visual entities or capture complex causal dynamics. To address these deficiencies, we propose TCA-Captioner, a framework specifically engineered to enhance Temporal and Cross-Modal Alignment for audiovisual video captioning. We first introduce the Observer-Checker-Corrector (OCC) framework, an iterative refinement strategy that generates high-fidelity, meticulously grounded training data. Leveraging a curated high-density human interaction dataset, TCA-Captioner is optimized to model sophisticated audiovisual interactions. Furthermore, we present TCA-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark utilizing a Decoupled Evaluation Protocol to isolate and quantify model proficiency in audiovisual binding and temporal relational reasoning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TCA-Captioner sets a new standard for temporally-coherent and synchronized audiovisual narratives.

AI.tldr: TCA-Captioner is a framework for audiovisual video captioning that improves temporal and cross-modal alignment using an iterative refinement strategy (OCC) and a diagnostic benchmark (TCA-Bench), achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs for video captioning suffer from modality detachment (failing to bind auditory events to visual entities) and temporal incoherence (inability to capture complex causal dynamics across time).
AI.method: Proposes (1) Observer-Checker-Corrector (OCC) iterative refinement for generating high-fidelity training data, (2) TCA-Captioner trained on curated high-density human interaction data, and (3) TCA-Bench with a Decoupled Evaluation Protocol to isolate audiovisual binding and temporal reasoning capabilities.
AI.result: TCA-Captioner achieves state-of-the-art performance on temporally-coherent and synchronized audiovisual narrative generation, as demonstrated by extensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework sets a new standard for temporally-coherent and synchronized audiovisual video captioning by effectively addressing modality detachment and temporal incoherence challenges.

title: Geometric Signatures of Reasoning: A Spectral Perspective on Task Hardness
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enables large language models (LLMs) to solve complex problems by generating intermediate reasoning steps. While much attention has been paid to the length and content of these reasoning chains, far less is known about their internal geometry. We study the \emph{geometry} of CoT trajectories in the hidden state space of transformer models, formalizing each reasoning chain as a discrete curve in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and characterizing it through spectral, positional, and kinematic geometric functionals. We introduce the effective dimension $d_ρ$ as a measure of trajectory complexity and show theoretically that trajectories with flatter eigenvalue spectra correspond to harder tasks, as they explore more of the hidden dimensions. Lastly, we explore how kinematic features of the trajectory, mean position, positional dispersion, initial and current hidden states, mean velocity, mean speed, and speed dispersion, can be used to predict solution correctness before generation is complete, and may inform future early-stopping strategies. Experimentally, on mathematical reasoning problems from the MATH500 dataset, $d_ρ$ achieves $0.93$ AUC in distinguishing easy from hard problems, while kinematic features potentially can predict correctness from only the first $20\%$ of generated tokens. These correctness signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty, establishing that the shape of a model's internal reasoning trajectory is a principled window into both task hardness and solution quality.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the geometry of chain-of-thought reasoning trajectories in transformer hidden states, introducing the effective dimension d_ρ to measure trajectory complexity and showing that both spectral and kinematic features can predict task difficulty and solution correctness early in generation.
AI.motivation: While previous work has focused on the length and content of CoT reasoning chains, little is known about their internal geometric structure in the hidden state space of transformers, which may offer deeper insights into task difficulty and solution correctness.
AI.method: The authors formalize CoT reasoning chains as discrete curves in ℝ^d, analyzing them through spectral (eigenvalue spectrum), positional (mean position, dispersion), and kinematic (velocity, speed, acceleration) geometric functionals. They introduce the effective dimension d_ρ to measure trajectory complexity.
AI.result: On MATH500, effective dimension d_ρ achieves 0.93 AUC in distinguishing easy from hard problems. Kinematic features can predict solution correctness from only the first 20% of generated tokens, and these correctness signatures transfer across problems of varying difficulty.
AI.conclusion: The shape of a model's internal CoT reasoning trajectory—characterized by geometric and kinematic features—provides a principled signal for both task hardness and solution correctness, with potential for early-stopping strategies.

title: Guiding Human Validation of LLM-Generated Code via Verifiable Literate Programming
summary:
Vibe coding democratizes software development by allowing users to generate code via natural-language (NL) interaction with large language models (LLMs). However, the code is reliable only when it faithfully implements the user's intent, which is difficult and labor-intensive for users to validate. Existing validation methods either rely on LLM-assisted automated testing, which suffers from prompt ambiguity and model fallibility, or involve users only in partial software artifacts such as prompts and test cases, which may overlook corner cases and program details. Motivated by a bug study of LLM-generated code, we find that detailed human feedback is essential, as failures often stem from underspecified requirements or subtle semantic deviations.
  This paper presents verifiable literate programming (VLP), a human-in-the-loop framework designed to make the review/validation process of LLM-generated code accessible to users at all programming levels. At its core, VLP proposes unambiguous NL-based documentation as a readable intermediate layer between prompts and code. The documentation demonstrates concrete program semantics and enables users to provide feedback on potential intent-code mismatches. It supports human-involved, end-to-end repair and validation via three techniques: (i) an NL-style literate language with unambiguous syntax and mostly deterministic code-to-documentation translation, (ii) LLM-based fine-grained mismatch detection that uses trace links between prompts and documentation to focus users' review effort on suspicious documentation lines, and (iii) a verification module that leverages user-validated documentation to derive API-usage checks and formal properties, which are then verified against the generated code using model checking. Our evaluation shows that VLP improves code pass@1 from 28.7%-73.2% to 65.4%-93.5% with reasonable user effort.

AI.tldr: VLP is a human-in-the-loop framework that uses unambiguous NL-based documentation as an intermediate layer between prompts and LLM-generated code, enabling non-expert users to validate and repair code via three techniques: literate language translation, LLM-based mismatch detection, and formal verification. It improves pass@1 from 28.7%-73.2% to 65.4%-93.5%.
AI.motivation: NL-driven code generation (vibe coding) suffers from reliability issues because validating intent-code alignment is difficult and labor-intensive. Existing automated testing suffers from prompt ambiguity and model fallibility, while partial user involvement misses corner cases. A bug study reveals failures often stem from underspecified requirements and subtle semantic deviations, motivating the need for detailed human feedback.
AI.method: VLP proposes three techniques: (i) NL-style literate language with unambiguous syntax and deterministic code-to-documentation translation; (ii) LLM-based fine-grained mismatch detection using trace links between prompts and documentation to focus user review; (iii) a verification module that derives API-usage checks and formal properties from validated documentation, verified via model checking.
AI.result: VLP improves code pass@1 from 28.7%-73.2% to 65.4%-93.5% with reasonable user effort.
AI.conclusion: VLP makes the validation process of LLM-generated code accessible to users at all programming levels via a verifiable literate programming framework with human-in-the-loop repair and validation.

title: HistoSeg++: Delving deeper with attention and multiscale feature fusion for biomarker segmentation
comment: Published in the Proceedings of ICBBE 2025. The Version of Record is available at https://doi.org/10.1145/3794209.3794211
summary: Segmentation of biomarkers in medical images is frequently viewed as a first step towards medical image analysis in any bioinformatics or biomedical application. Despite progress, existing methods still struggle to capture information at multiple scales and to perform upsampling effectively across different datasets. These shortcomings often result in suboptimal generalization capabilities. Recently, architectures belonging to the Nested-UNet family excel in capturing multiscale contextual information and upsample them effectively. In this work, We propose a novel Nested-UNet architecture that effectively captures multi-scale contextual information. It includes inner and outer attention units to enhance focus during upsampling, along with channel-wise feature recalibration using squeeze-and-excitation modules, leading to improved segmentation performance. Additionally, the architecture integrates an edge-aware loss to emphasize boundary accuracy by assigning greater importance to edge regions. Tested extensively on three publicly available benchmark datasets. Our method demonstrates a generalization performance superior to existing Nested-UNet methods. Code: https://github.com/saadwazir/histosegplusplus

AI.tldr: A novel Nested-UNet architecture with inner/outer attention units, squeeze-and-excitation modules, and edge-aware loss for improved multi-scale medical image segmentation with superior generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing medical image segmentation methods struggle to capture multi-scale contextual information and perform effective upsampling across different datasets, leading to suboptimal generalization.
AI.method: Proposes a Nested-UNet architecture enhanced with inner and outer attention units for focused upsampling, channel-wise feature recalibration via squeeze-and-excitation modules, and an edge-aware loss emphasizing boundary accuracy.
AI.result: Tested on three public benchmark datasets, the method demonstrates superior generalization performance compared to existing Nested-UNet methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed architectural enhancements (attention mechanisms, channel recalibration, edge-aware loss) effectively improve multi-scale contextual capture and upsampling, yielding better generalization in medical image segmentation.

title: Reformalization of the Jordan Curve Theorem
summary: We present a case study in reformalization, a variant of autoformalization in which the input proof is not natural language but a formal development in a different proof assistant. Concretely, we report three reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem: from Mizar to Lean, from HOL Light to Lean, and from HOL Light to Agda. We analyse the results and identify pipeline design choices that matter for practical reformalization tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a case study on reformalization (autoformalization of formal proofs) by porting the Jordan Curve Theorem from Mizar to Lean, HOL Light to Lean, and HOL Light to Agda, analyzing pipeline design choices for practical reformalization.
AI.motivation: To understand and identify critical design choices for reformalization pipelines by examining concrete, non-trivial porting efforts across different proof assistants.
AI.method: Conducting three case studies of reformalizing the Jordan Curve Theorem: (1) Mizar → Lean, (2) HOL Light → Lean, (3) HOL Light → Agda, followed by comparative analysis of pipeline design choices.
AI.result: Identification of key pipeline design choices that significantly impact the practicality and effectiveness of reformalization tasks.
AI.conclusion: Certain design choices in reformalization pipelines are critical for practical success; the findings provide guidance for future automated or semi-automated porting of formal proofs between proof assistants.

title: BOUNDARY_SYNC: Measuring Communication-Induced Representational Coupling in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed as communicating agents, does inter-agent communication cause outputs to converge?
