AI.motivation: To understand whether Diffusion Language Models internally represent denoising progress despite not being explicitly conditioned on timestep, and how such information is used downstream.
AI.method: Probing across layers to extract latent timestep representations from residual streams; low-dimensional subspace steering to modulate denoising progress; geometric analysis of the identified representation in activation space.
AI.result: DLMs encode decodable timestep signals; steering along the inferred timestep subspace produces predictable changes in model confidence and entropy; the representation exhibits structured and interpretable geometric properties.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion Language Models internally represent denoising progress as an interpretable latent signal, enabling systematic control over model behavior and providing insights into how such information is processed.

title: UniWind: Toward Unified Day-Ahead Wind Power Forecasting via Physics-Informed State Routing
summary: Day-ahead wind power forecasting is essential for cost-effective power-system operation. It is primarily driven by future meteorological conditions while retaining temporal dependencies in power generation. In practice, observed wind-farm power often entangles physically available power with local environmental effects and latent operational states, such as shutdowns and curtailment. Existing physical models provide useful constraints but adapt poorly across wind farms, whereas data-driven models can capture rich correlations but often conflate meteorological effects with state-induced deviations. In this study, we propose UniWind, a wind power forecasting model based on physics-informed state routing. UniWind first employs a Physical Prior Estimator to construct a site-calibrated physical prior by combining site-conditioned monotonic warping with a shared physical power curve. It further applies a physical upper-bound constraint to shape this prior as a soft envelope of available wind power generation. UniWind then proposes a Latent State Encoder to model operating-state embeddings and transforms the physical prior into final power forecasts through a State-aware Power Corrector, which uses knowledge-guided supervised state routing and bounded, state-specific expert correction. Full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot experiments on more than 20 real-world datasets demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of UniWind.

AI.tldr: UniWind is a physics-informed state routing model for day-ahead wind power forecasting that separates meteorological effects from operational state deviations using a Physical Prior Estimator, Latent State Encoder, and State-aware Power Corrector, achieving robust accuracy across 20+ real-world datasets in full-shot and zero-shot settings.
AI.motivation: Existing physical models provide useful constraints but generalize poorly across wind farms, while data-driven models capture rich correlations but conflate meteorological effects with state-induced deviations (e.g., shutdowns, curtailment). A method that disentangles these factors is needed for accurate and transferable wind power forecasting.
AI.method: UniWind consists of three components: (1) Physical Prior Estimator — constructs a site-calibrated physical prior via site-conditioned monotonic warping and a shared physical power curve, with a physical upper-bound constraint; (2) Latent State Encoder — models latent operating-state embeddings; (3) State-aware Power Corrector — transforms the physical prior into final forecasts using knowledge-guided supervised state routing and bounded, state-specific expert correction.
AI.result: Full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot experiments on more than 20 real-world wind farm datasets demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of UniWind.
AI.conclusion: UniWind effectively disentangles meteorological effects from operational state deviations in wind power forecasting, achieving strong generalization across farms through physics-informed state routing.

title: RTE-FM-Dehazer: Radiative Transfer Equation Inspired Flow Matching for Real-World Image Dehazing
summary: Single-image dehazing aims to recover a clear scene from a hazy image and is generally formulated as an image-to-image translation task; however, it faces two limitations. Its performance depends heavily on the haze-formation priors embedded in the model. Prevailing methods adopt the Atmospheric Scattering Model (ASM), whose assumptions of single scattering and homogeneous media are often violated, leading to residual haze and color drift. Moreover, large-scale real hazy/clear pairs are impractical to collect, and existing synthesis approaches fail to reproduce the full complexity of natural haze. To address these issues, we present RTE-FM-Dehazer, a novel dehazing approach, together with a scalable data pipeline. Unlike the ASM, the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) jointly accounts for both scattering and absorption, naturally accommodating the non-homogeneous, multiple-scattering media that characterize real hazy scenes. Motivated by the structural similarity between the RTE diffusion-absorption term and the ODE in flow matching, we introduce a diffusion-absorption regularizer derived from a reduced RTE, to steer the flow matching trajectory at each step. Next, leveraging modern vision-language models, we build an automated pipeline and release P-HAZE, a dataset of 50000 realistic hazy/clear pairs. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that RTE-FM-Dehazer, trained solely on P-HAZE, effectively eliminates artifacts like residual haze and color drift, exhibits strong cross-domain generalization, and achieves leading results on five real-world dehazing benchmarks.

AI.tldr: RTE-FM-Dehazer is a single-image dehazing method that replaces the Atmospheric Scattering Model with the Radiative Transfer Equation, uses a diffusion-absorption regularizer from flow matching, and leverages a vision-language model pipeline to produce a 50K realistic hazy/clear dataset (P-HAZE), achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple real-world benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing single-image dehazing methods rely on the Atmospheric Scattering Model (ASM), which assumes single scattering and homogeneous media—assumptions often violated in real haze, causing residual haze and color drift. Additionally, large-scale real hazy/clear pairs are impractical to collect, and synthetic datasets fail to capture natural haze complexity.
AI.method: Replaces ASM with the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) to model non-homogeneous, multiple-scattering media. Introduces a diffusion-absorption regularizer derived from a reduced RTE, leveraging structural similarity to the ODE in flow matching. Also builds an automated data pipeline using vision-language models to generate P-HAZE, a 50K realistic hazy/clear dataset.
AI.result: RTE-FM-Dehazer, trained solely on P-HAZE, effectively eliminates residual haze and color drift, exhibits strong cross-domain generalization, and achieves leading results on five real-world dehazing benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The RTE-based regularizer and realistic synthetic data pipeline together overcome the limitations of ASM-based dehazing and synthetic data scarcity, enabling superior performance on real-world dehazing tasks.

title: Safety Testing LLM Agents at Scale: From Risk Discovery to Evidence-Grounded Verification
summary: LLM agents increasingly perform autonomous actions through external tools, leading to complex and evolving safety risks. However, existing safety testing targets expert-designed safety violations, and the corresponding outcomes are evaluated by hard-coded rules, making them costly to extend as agents evolve. To this end, we present Vera, an end-to-end automated safety testing framework that instantiates software engineering testing principles for non-deterministic agents through a three-stage, self-reinforcing pipeline. First, a literature-driven exploration continuously discovers and structures emerging risks into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and tool execution environments. Second, combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions produces executable safety cases, each specifying a concrete safety goal, a programmatically constructed initial state, and a deterministic verification predicate grounded in observable artifacts. Third, adaptive execution runs heterogeneous agents in isolated sandboxes where a control agent steers multi-turn interaction based on runtime observations, while evidence-grounded verifiers judge outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence rather than model self-report. We evaluate Vera on four production agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code), revealing substantial safety weaknesses, with average attack success rates reaching 93.9\% under multi-channel attacks; we also release Vera-Bench, comprising 1600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings. These results indicate that modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Yunhao-Feng/Vera.

AI.tldr: Vera is an end-to-end automated safety testing framework for LLM agents that uses a three-stage pipeline (risk taxonomy discovery, combinatorial safety case generation, and adaptive execution with evidence-grounded verification) to evaluate agent safety. Testing across four production agent frameworks revealed 93.9% average attack success rates under multi-channel attacks, and the release of Vera-Bench containing 1600 safety cases across 124 risk categories.
AI.motivation: Existing safety testing for LLM agents relies on expert-designed safety violations and hard-coded evaluation rules, which are costly to extend as agents rapidly evolve. There is a need for an automated, scalable, and maintainable safety testing approach that can systematically discover and evaluate emerging risks.
AI.method: Vera implements a three-stage self-reinforcing pipeline: (1) literature-driven exploration to discover and structure emerging risks into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and tool execution environments; (2) combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions to produce executable safety cases with concrete safety goals, programmatic initial states, and deterministic verification predicates; (3) adaptive execution in isolated sandboxes where a control agent steers multi-turn interactions and evidence-grounded verifiers judge outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence.
AI.result: Evaluation on four production agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code) revealed substantial safety weaknesses with average attack success rates reaching 93.9% under multi-channel attacks. The released Vera-Bench contains 1600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings.
AI.conclusion: Modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale. The high attack success rates indicate significant safety weaknesses in current production agent frameworks.

title: SCAPE: Accurate and Efficient LLM Training with Extreme Sparse Communication
summary: Communication increasingly dominates the cost of Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training, especially under data-parallel and sharded training schemes, where gradient synchronization and parameter reconstruction overhead increase with model size and system scale. Existing communication-reduction methods either sparsify raw gradients, which can be unstable for modern Adam-style optimizers at high sparsity, or quantize communication, whose savings are fundamentally bounded by bit width and often incur additional runtime overhead. We present SCAPE, a communication-efficient distributed optimizer for LLM training that exploits the stability of AdamS's first-moment to enable aggressive sparsification without loss of LLM quality. Instead of constructing masks from raw gradients, SCAPE derives them from first-moment-based statistics, partitions mask generation across workers to align with optimizer sharding, and delays mask usage by one step so that mask synchronization can overlap with computation. SCAPE also reconstructs the quantities required for second-moment updates from a single synchronized sparse buffer, avoiding an additional collective. We implement SCAPE in Megatron-LM and evaluate its convergence by pre-training GPT-345M on OpenWebText and Llama-500M on SlimPajama-6B using 32 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs on TACC Vista. In both models, SCAPE preserves training stability, validation loss, and downstream task accuracy under 90\% and 99\% sparsity. For Llama-500M, SCAPE reduces end-to-end pre-training wall-clock time by up to 43.3\% while maintaining model quality comparable to dense AdamW and AdamS. For Llama-1.8B, SCAPE achieves up to 3.26$\times$ speedup per step compared to dense AdamS.

AI.tldr: SCAPE is a communication-efficient distributed optimizer for LLM training that uses first-moment-based sparsification from AdamS to achieve aggressive communication reduction (up to 99% sparsity) without quality loss, demonstrating up to 43.3% wall-clock time reduction for Llama-500M and 3.26× per-step speedup for Llama-1.8B.
AI.motivation: Communication cost dominates LLM pre-training under data-parallel and sharded training schemes, with existing methods (gradient sparsification or quantization) suffering from instability with Adam optimizers or bounded savings and additional overhead.
AI.method: SCAPE derives sparsification masks from first-moment-based statistics (exploiting AdamS's stability), partitions mask generation across workers for optimizer sharding alignment, delays mask usage by one step for computation overlap, and reconstructs second-moment update quantities from a single synchronized sparse buffer.
AI.result: Pre-trained GPT-345M and Llama-500M on 32 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs; preserves training stability, validation loss, and downstream accuracy at 90% and 99% sparsity; reduces wall-clock time by up to 43.3% for Llama-500M; achieves 3.26× per-step speedup for Llama-1.8B.
AI.conclusion: SCAPE enables aggressive gradient sparsification without quality degradation by leveraging AdamS's first-moment stability, significantly reducing communication overhead in distributed LLM training while maintaining model quality comparable to dense AdamW and AdamS.

title: Rethinking Complexity Metrics for LLM-Integrated Applications: Beyond Source Code
summary: LLM-integrated applications blend natural language prompts with program code, and much of their runtime behavior originates in the prompt layer rather than in the code itself. Existing complexity metrics, however, operate solely at the code level and therefore overlook this behavioral logic entirely. We present HECATE, the first tool designed to assess complexity in both the prompt and code layers of such applications. Central to HECATE is Prompt-as-Specification, a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism that interprets every prompt as a specification of intended behavior. Grounded in 25 complexity dimensions identified across published taxonomies, the tool generates 52 candidate metrics. We assess each metric against 118 components collected from 18 open-source repositories, relying on maintenance activity derived from version history as an empirical proxy for complexity, and discard any metric that loses significance once code size is accounted for. Only ten metrics withstand this test. Seven belong to our newly introduced set; rather than measuring sheer volume, each tallies structurally distinct elements, such as LLM call sites, memory attributes, and prompt templates, an attribute we call structural breadth. Of the three surviving conventional metrics, RFC exhibits a similar breadth-oriented character, while Halstead N and V survive only as a residual effect of size; our top-performing metrics exceed all three. Crucially, the prompt-layer metrics retain significance even when the strongest code-level metric is added as a covariate, establishing prompt complexity as a dimension in its own right. A final validation on 20 components spanning six held-out repositories shows that the two best-performing metrics continue to predict maintenance effort, supporting their generalizability beyond the training set.

AI.tldr: HECATE is a novel tool that measures software complexity in both prompt and code layers of LLM-integrated applications, identifying 10 significant metrics (7 new prompt-layer metrics) that predict maintenance effort, with prompt complexity emerging as an independent dimension beyond code-level measures.
AI.motivation: Existing complexity metrics only operate at the code level, ignoring the behavioral logic embedded in prompts of LLM-integrated applications, which drives much of the runtime behavior.
AI.method: HECATE uses Prompt-as-Specification (Hoare-logic-inspired formalism) to interpret prompts as specifications. It generates 52 candidate metrics from 25 complexity dimensions identified across published taxonomies, evaluates them against 118 components from 18 repositories using version-history maintenance activity as proxy, and discards metrics that lose significance after controlling for code size.
AI.result: Only 10 metrics withstand statistical testing. Seven are new structural breadth metrics (count structurally distinct elements like LLM call sites, memory attributes, prompt templates). RFC survives from conventional metrics with similar breadth character; Halstead N and V survive only as residual size effects. Prompt-layer metrics retain significance even when controlling for code-level metrics. Validation on 6 held-out repositories confirms generalizability.
AI.conclusion: Prompt complexity is an independent dimension of software complexity in LLM-integrated applications, measurable via structural breadth metrics that reliably predict maintenance effort beyond code-level measures alone.

title: MedStreamBench: A Time-Aware Benchmark for Streaming and Proactive Medical Video Understanding
summary: Existing medical video benchmarks primarily evaluate whether a model produces the correct answer, but rarely assess whether it answers at the right time. In real clinical settings, AI systems must decide not only what to predict, but also when to answer, defer judgment, or proactively raise alerts. This creates a critical gap between benchmark evaluation and deployment requirements. We present MedStreamBench, a benchmark for time-aware medical video understanding. MedStreamBench integrates 22 medical datasets and 5,419 QA instances across four temporal settings: retrospective, present, future, and proactive. Unlike conventional benchmarks that assume full-video access, MedStreamBench restricts models to temporally bounded evidence windows and supports both single-turn and streaming evaluation. We further introduce a proactive monitoring setting that requires models to determine whether and when clinically relevant alerts should be triggered. Beyond answer correctness, MedStreamBench evaluates temporal behavior through responsiveness and post-evidence stability. Experiments on leading general-purpose and medical vision-language models reveal a substantial gap between offline recognition and temporally grounded decision-making, with performance dropping markedly in streaming and proactive settings. Our benchmark is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Venn2024/MedStreamBench.

AI.tldr: MedStreamBench is a benchmark for time-aware medical video understanding that evaluates not just answer correctness but also when a model should answer, defer, or alert—revealing a large performance gap between offline recognition and temporally grounded decision-making.
AI.motivation: Existing medical video benchmarks only evaluate answer correctness, not timing; in real clinical settings, AI must decide when to answer, defer, or raise alerts, creating a critical gap between evaluation and deployment.
AI.method: Integrated 22 medical datasets into 5,419 QA instances across four temporal settings (retrospective, present, future, proactive); uses temporally bounded evidence windows instead of full-video access; supports single-turn and streaming evaluation; introduces proactive monitoring requiring models to determine if and when to trigger alerts; evaluates via responsiveness and post-evidence stability beyond answer correctness.
AI.result: Experiments on general-purpose and medical vision-language models show a substantial gap between offline recognition and temporally grounded decision-making, with performance dropping markedly in streaming and proactive settings.
AI.conclusion: MedStreamBench fills a critical gap by benchmarking time-aware decision-making in medical video understanding, revealing that current models struggle significantly with temporal grounding required for real clinical deployment.

title: MMIR-TCM: Memory-Integrated Multimodal Inference and Retrieval for TCM Clinical Decision Support
summary: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) diagnosis, particularly through tongue inspection, faces persistent challenges in subjectivity and reproducibility. The application of multimodal artificial intelligence to TCM clinical tasks, such as syndrome differentiation and prescription generation, is significantly hampered by the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual reasoning, as well as the lack of large-scale, standardized datasets. To address these challenges, we introduce MMIR-TCM, a novel framework that emulates the diagnostic process of TCM experts by integrating multimodal large language model(MLLM) with memory-augmented segmentation and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Employing a three-stage architecture, MMIR-TCM integrates a training-free Memory-SAM module for robust tongue extraction, a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL model for structured tongue diagnosis generation, and a Qwen3-based RAG component for evidence-grounded clinical decision support generation. The framework was developed and validated using MedTCM, a new large-scale multimodal dataset that we introduce specifically for advanced TCM research. To properly evaluate our framework's clinical accuracy, which existing metrics fail to capture, we also developed TDEU, a domain-specific evaluation metric incorporating semantic understanding and diagnostic importance. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.

AI.tldr: MMIR-TCM is a novel multimodal AI framework that integrates memory-augmented segmentation and retrieval-augmented generation to address subjectivity and semantic gap challenges in TCM tongue diagnosis, outperforming GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash on a new large-scale dataset MedTCM and evaluated using a custom domain-specific metric TDEU.
AI.motivation: TCM tongue diagnosis suffers from subjectivity and reproducibility issues; multimodal AI application is hindered by the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual reasoning, plus the lack of large-scale standardized datasets.
AI.method: A three-stage architecture: (1) training-free Memory-SAM module for robust tongue extraction, (2) fine-tuned Qwen3-VL for structured tongue diagnosis generation, (3) Qwen3-based RAG for evidence-grounded clinical decision support. Introduces MedTCM (large-scale multimodal dataset) and TDEU (domain-specific evaluation metric).
AI.result: MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash on comprehensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively emulates TCM expert diagnostic processes by integrating MLLM with memory-augmented segmentation and RAG, setting a new benchmark for AI-assisted TCM clinical tasks.

title: WARP: Weight-Space Analysis for Recovering Training Data Portfolios
comment: This work appears in the ICML 2026 Workshop on Weight-Space Symmetries (WSS): from Foundations to Practical Applications. Our source code is available at github.com/SprocketLab/WARP
summary: Foundation models are routinely released to the public, yet the data recipes used to train them -- such as domain mixture weights that determine how different sources are sampled -- are rarely disclosed. This creates an access asymmetry: researchers study the resulting models but lack visibility into the training distribution that produces them. Prior works for inferring training data, such as membership inference, detect at the level of individual samples and thus cannot characterize the global composition of the training corpus. We introduce WARP, a framework that recovers a fine-tuned model's training mixtures directly from its released weights. WARP interpolates between the base and fine-tuned models using model merging, generating pseudo-checkpoints that approximate the missing training trajectory and expose a geometric footprint of the training data in the weight space. From these simulated footprints, WARP extracts geometric features and maps them to domain proportions using either a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP projector trained on synthetic mixtures. In controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with an average MAE as low as 0.046 and 0.104 respectively, outperforming membership inference and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.

AI.tldr: WARP is a framework that recovers the domain mixture weights of a fine-tuned model's training data directly from its released weights, outperforming membership inference approaches in controlled experiments.
AI.motivation: Foundation models are released publicly, but their training data recipes (e.g., domain mixture weights) are rarely disclosed, creating an access asymmetry where researchers can study models but not the training distributions that produce them.
AI.method: WARP interpolates between base and fine-tuned models using model merging to generate pseudo-checkpoints simulating the training trajectory. It extracts geometric features from weight space and maps them to domain proportions via a softmax readout or an MLP projector trained on synthetic mixtures.
AI.result: In controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with MAE as low as 0.046 and 0.104 respectively, outperforming membership inference and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.
AI.conclusion: WARP enables inference of training data composition from model weights alone, addressing the transparency gap in foundation model releases.

title: Search-based Testing of Vision Language Models for In-Car Scene Understanding
comment: Accepted at the Industry Track of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
summary: In the automotive domain, in-car scene understanding (ISU) enables the detection of safety-critical events, such as driver distraction, and supports drivers or passengers by analyzing the in-car scene and adapting the environment (e.g., ambient lighting). The industry is increasingly exploring vision-language models (VLMs) to interpret camera-recorded in-car scenes and extract information for downstream reasoning tasks. However, VLMs may generate incomplete, erroneous, or misleading scene descriptions, highlighting the need for systematic testing. Collecting real in-vehicle data is costly, difficult to scale, and often infeasible, particularly in early design stages. In this paper, we present ISU-Test, an automated testing approach that combines rendering-based scene generation with search-based testing to evaluate ISU systems. By framing testing as an optimization problem and systematically modifying scene parameters, our method generates diverse in-car scenarios and explores a wide range of configurations. We evaluate ISU-Test on both an industrial prototype and open-source VLMs across two case studies: question answering and captioning, comparing against randomized scenario generation. Results show that ISU-Test significantly outperforms the baseline, achieving up to 10 times higher failure rates and up to 3.6 times higher failure coverage.

AI.tldr: ISU-Test is an automated testing approach combining rendering-based scene generation with search-based testing to evaluate vision-language models for in-car scene understanding, achieving up to 10x higher failure rates and 3.6x higher failure coverage compared to random baselines.
AI.motivation: VLMs for in-car scene understanding may produce incomplete, erroneous, or misleading descriptions. Real in-vehicle data collection is costly, hard to scale, and infeasible in early design stages, motivating a need for systematic, automated testing.
AI.method: ISU-Test frames testing as an optimization problem, combining rendering-based scene generation (synthetic scene creation) with search-based testing (systematically modifying scene parameters) to generate diverse in-car scenarios for evaluating ISU systems.
AI.result: ISU-Test significantly outperforms randomized scenario generation, achieving up to 10 times higher failure rates and up to 3.6 times higher failure coverage on both an industrial prototype and open-source VLMs across question answering and captioning tasks.
AI.conclusion: ISU-Test provides an effective, scalable automated testing approach for in-car scene understanding systems, addressing the limitations of costly real-world data collection by using synthetic scene generation guided by search-based optimization.

title: The Turning Point of 3D Plant Phenotyping: 3D Foundation Models Enable Minute-to-Second Cross-Crop Reconstruction and Beyond
summary: 3D plant phenotyping is notoriously known to be procedure-complicated and of low throughput due to the extensive multi-view imaging, the fragile 3D reconstruction pipeline, and the additional cost from reconstructed geometry to phenotypic extraction. These limitations are further amplified in low-cost data acquisition, where smartphone videos or sparsely sampled multi-view images provide limited view overlap and self-occlusion. In this work, we show that the conventional 3D plant phenotyping pipeline could be streamlined and significantly accelerated with 3D Foundation Models (3DFMs), and particularly, present one of the first cross-crop 3D phenotyping frameworks powered by 3DFMs. The framework replaces COLMAP-style sparse initialization with 3DFM-based feed-forward geometric recovery, combines geometry-constrained 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense reconstruction, enables few-view reconstruction through iterative view synthesis and refinement, and converts reconstructed geometry into measurable organs through 2D-to-3D semantic transfer, metric scale recovery, and organ instance separation. We further construct a cross-crop dataset with smartphone-based image acquisition, diverse plant morphologies, and manual annotations for segmentation and phenotypic evaluation. Experiments across 26 plant sequences show that 3D Foundation Models reduce the average reconstruction time from 6.52 minutes to 1.58 seconds while maintaining high reconstruction quality and phenotyping accuracy. These results suggest a fresh technical route for high-throughput 3D plant phenotyping, from low-cost image acquisition to fast reconstruction, perception, scale recovery, and phenotypic measurement.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a cross-crop 3D plant phenotyping framework powered by 3D Foundation Models, replacing traditional COLMAP-style pipelines with feed-forward geometric recovery and 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense reconstruction. It achieves 4.92x speedup (6.52 min → 1.58 sec) across 26 plant sequences using smartphone-captured data while maintaining high accuracy.
AI.motivation: Traditional 3D plant phenotyping is procedure-complicated and low-throughput due to extensive multi-view imaging, fragile reconstruction pipelines, and costly geometry-to-phenotype extraction. These issues worsen with low-cost data acquisition (e.g., smartphone videos) that provide limited view overlap and self-occlusion.
AI.method: The framework: (1) replaces COLMAP-style sparse initialization with 3DFM-based feed-forward geometric recovery; (2) employs geometry-constrained 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense reconstruction; (3) enables few-view reconstruction via iterative view synthesis and refinement; (4) converts reconstructed geometry into measurable organs through 2D-to-3D semantic transfer, metric scale recovery, and organ instance separation.
AI.result: Experiments on 26 plant sequences show reconstruction time reduced from 6.52 minutes to 1.58 seconds while maintaining high reconstruction quality and phenotyping accuracy.
AI.conclusion: 3DFMs offer a fresh technical route for high-throughput 3D plant phenotyping from low-cost image acquisition to fast reconstruction, perception, scale recovery, and phenotypic measurement.

title: Pre-Flight: A Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Aviation Operational Knowledge
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Benchmark available in inspect_evals (UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_evals)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for aviation business operations, from documentation and training generation to customer facing assistants. General purpose benchmarks do not measure whether a model reasons safely and correctly about aviation specific operational knowledge, and the high stakes, regulated nature of the domain makes that gap consequential. We present Pre-Flight, an open source benchmark of 300 multiple choice questions drawn from international standards and airport ground operations material, covering international airport ground operations, ICAO and US FAA regulations, aviation general knowledge and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by practitioners with experience in air traffic management, ground operations and commercial flying. We evaluate a range of contemporary commercial and open weight models using the Inspect evaluation framework, scoring by accuracy under a standard multiple choice protocol, and we maintain the leaderboard on a rolling basis as new models are released. Against an informal expert reference of around 95%, obtained from a low sample quiz of aviation professionals at a conference, even the strongest model evaluated (released in 2026) reaches 82.7%, having improved only gradually from roughly 75% in early 2025. A substantial and persistent gap below expert level reliability therefore remains. We release the dataset, the evaluation harness and the results, and the benchmark is available within the community evaluations package distributed with inspect_evals. We argue that domain specific evaluation of this kind is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non safety critical aviation operations.

AI.tldr: Pre-Flight is an open-source benchmark of 300 aviation-specific multiple-choice questions that evaluates LLMs on international airport operations, ICAO/FAA regulations, and operational scenarios. Even the strongest 2026 model achieves only 82.7% accuracy vs. ~95% expert reference, revealing a persistent gap that motivates domain-specific evaluation before deploying LLMs in aviation.
AI.motivation: General-purpose benchmarks fail to measure whether LLMs reason safely and correctly about aviation-specific operational knowledge, and the high-stakes, regulated nature of aviation makes this evaluation gap consequential for responsible deployment.
AI.method: 300 multiple-choice questions drawn from international standards and airport ground operations material, covering ground operations, ICAO/FAA regulations, aviation knowledge, and complex scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by aviation practitioners. Models were evaluated using the Inspect framework with standard multiple-choice accuracy scoring.
AI.result: Against an informal expert reference of ~95%, the strongest model (2026) reaches 82.7%, having improved gradually from ~75% in early 2025. A substantial and persistent gap below expert-level reliability remains.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific evaluation is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non-safety-critical aviation operations. The dataset, evaluation harness, and results are released publicly.

title: Model Merging as Probabilistic Inference in Fine-Tuning Parameter Space
comment: Accepted for Publication at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI), 2026
summary: Model merging aims to combine existing single-task solutions into a multi-task solution without additional data-driven fine-tuning.~Most existing approaches achieve this using geometric properties of local solution spaces. However, such geometric views provide limited guidance for scoring how statistically useful each task-specific update direction is across tasks during merging. To address this, we formulate model merging from a new perspective of probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts (PoE) scenario where each single-task solution defines an energy-based expert model (EBM) over the merged parameters. We show that several existing model merging methods arise as special cases of our framework under energy designs that impose implicit Gaussian assumptions on directional residuals between merged and task-specific models. Empirically, we find that these residuals are often heavy-tailed which exposes a mismatch with the imposed light-tailed Gaussian structures. We address this with a heavy-tailed PoE design based on Cauchy experts, which better captures the observed residual behavior while admitting a provably convergent inference procedure. Experiments across multiple tasks and architectures show significant improvements over state-of-the-arts baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/MinhLong210/PoE-EBM-Merging.git.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates model merging as probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts framework with energy-based models, identifies limitations of existing methods due to mismatched Gaussian assumptions, and proposes a heavy-tailed Cauchy expert design that better captures actual residual distributions and yields improved multi-task merging performance.
AI.motivation: Existing model merging methods rely on geometric properties of local solution spaces, which offer limited guidance on scoring the statistical usefulness of task-specific update directions across tasks during merging.
AI.method: Formulates model merging as probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts (PoE) scenario where each single-task solution defines an energy-based expert model (EBM) over merged parameters. Identifies that existing methods correspond to Gaussian assumptions on directional residuals, then proposes a heavy-tailed PoE design based on Cauchy experts to better match observed heavy-tailed residual behavior.
AI.result: Heavy-tailed residual distributions are empirically observed, exposing mismatch with Gaussian assumptions. The proposed Cauchy expert PoE design yields significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across multiple tasks and architectures.
AI.conclusion: The PoE probabilistic inference perspective unifies several existing merging methods, and adopting heavy-tailed Cauchy experts better captures real residual statistics while providing a provably convergent inference procedure for improved multi-task model merging.

title: Steerability via constraints: a substrate for scalable oversight of coding agents
comment: Accepted to the Deep Learning for Code Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea, 2026
summary: Coding agents are capable; human oversight is the bottleneck. Unconstrained agents introduce security risks, erode codebase scalability, and make human review increasingly costly. We argue that the same methods used for decades to manage large human engineering teams: access control, network policies, strict coding conventions enforced by tooling; transfer directly to coding agents, and are cheaper (in token) than recent agentic scaffolding. We sketch a start-to-end system on this principle, and report a controlled experiment in scalable oversight: a small reviewer (Gemma 4 e4b) inspects a Python codebase containing 11 inserted backdoors. Recall rises from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate plus a ~200-LoC `docs` CLI), with substrate and tools contributing independently. We choose Python deliberately: substrate-level oversight gains are largest where the language gives the fewest guarantees by default; the principles extend to languages like Rust.

AI.tldr: Human oversight is the bottleneck for coding agents. Using traditional software engineering management methods (access control, network policies, coding conventions) transferred to coding agents is cheaper and more effective. A controlled experiment shows backdoor detection recall improved from 54.5% to 90.9% using constrained substrate and tools.
AI.motivation: Unconstrained coding agents introduce security risks, erode codebase scalability, and make human review increasingly costly. Human oversight is the primary bottleneck in using coding agents effectively.
AI.method: Applied traditional software engineering management methods (access control, network policies, strict coding conventions enforced by tooling) to coding agents. Conducted a controlled experiment where a small reviewer model (Gemma 4 e4b) inspected a Python codebase with 11 inserted backdoors, comparing unconstrained vs. constrained substrate with tools.
AI.result: Backdoor detection recall improved from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate plus a ~200-LoC `docs` CLI). Substrate and tools contributed independently to this improvement.
AI.conclusion: Traditional engineering management methods transfer effectively to coding agents and are cheaper than recent agentic scaffolding. These principles are most impactful in languages with few guarantees (like Python) but extend to stronger-guarantee languages like Rust.

title: ProSAC-CT: Progressive Spectral-Anatomical Co-Guided Multi-Stage Diffusion Model for Low-Dose CT Denoising
summary: Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) reduces radiation exposure but introduces stronger quantum noise, streak artifacts, and local texture degradation, which can obscure anatomical boundaries and weaken low-contrast structures. Diffusion models are promising for LDCT denoising by progressively recovering normal-dose CT (NDCT) images from degraded LDCT inputs, but existing methods often suffer from insufficient anatomical guidance, uncertain frequency-dependent recovery, and uniform reverse-process modeling. We propose ProSAC-CT, a progressive spectral-anatomical co-guided multi-stage diffusion model for image-domain LDCT denoising. ProSAC-CT integrates an anatomical-prior-guided conditioning (APGC) module, a residual frequency-domain decoupling stage (RFDDS), and a time-step-decoupling denoising decoder (TD3). APGC extracts LDCT-derived structural guidance, RFDDS enhances frequency-aware representations, and TD3 assigns them to different reverse-diffusion stages for anatomical stabilization, boundary refinement, and fine-detail recovery. Experiments on four LDCT degradation benchmarks show that ProSAC-CT improves image fidelity, structural similarity, perceptual quality, and information preservation over representative methods while better preserving boundary-sensitive anatomical details. Downstream anatomical-region classification on Mayo-2020 further indicates that ProSAC-CT retains task-relevant anatomical information, supporting its practical use for low-dose CT denoising.

AI.tldr: ProSAC-CT is a progressive spectral-anatomical co-guided multi-stage diffusion model for LDCT denoising that integrates anatomical guidance, frequency-domain decoupling, and time-step-decoupling to improve image fidelity, structural similarity, and anatomical detail preservation over existing methods.
AI.motivation: LDCT introduces quantum noise, streak artifacts, and texture degradation that obscure anatomical boundaries and weaken low-contrast structures. Existing diffusion models for LDCT denoising suffer from insufficient anatomical guidance, uncertain frequency-dependent recovery, and uniform reverse-process modeling.
AI.method: ProSAC-CT is a multi-stage diffusion model with three key components: (1) Anatomical-Prior-Guided Conditioning (APGC) module extracts LDCT-derived structural guidance; (2) Residual Frequency-Domain Decoupling Stage (RFDDS) enhances frequency-aware representations; (3) Time-Step-Decoupling Denoising Decoder (TD3) assigns representations to different reverse-diffusion stages for anatomical stabilization, boundary refinement, and fine-detail recovery.
AI.result: On four LDCT degradation benchmarks, ProSAC-CT improves image fidelity, structural similarity, perceptual quality, and information preservation over representative methods while better preserving boundary-sensitive anatomical details. Downstream anatomical-region classification on Mayo-2020 confirms retention of task-relevant anatomical information.
AI.conclusion: ProSAC-CT effectively addresses LDCT denoising by providing progressive spectral-anatomical co-guidance, achieving superior denoising performance and practical utility for low-dose CT applications.

title: Actual causality in fault trees
summary: Fault trees are a widely used as effective risk models for complex systems, answering the question "what can go wrong?", especially through minimal cut set analysis. We study fault trees from the perspective of Halpern & Pearl's theory of actual causality. This allows us to use fault trees to answer the question "why has it gone wrong?", which is fundamental to failure diagnostics. We give a complete classification of each of the different notions of actual causality in terms of the fault tree's graph structure and logical structure, and show how minimal cut sets give rise to actual causes.

AI.tldr: This paper bridges fault tree analysis (used for risk assessment) with Halpern & Pearl's actual causality theory (used for failure diagnostics), classifying different causality notions based on fault tree structure and showing how minimal cut sets produce actual causes.
AI.motivation: Fault trees traditionally answer "what can go wrong?" via minimal cut set analysis, but cannot answer "why has it gone wrong?" which is essential for failure diagnostics. The authors aim to bridge this gap by applying actual causality theory to fault trees.
AI.method: The authors study fault trees through Halpern & Pearl's theory of actual causality, classifying each notion of actual causality in terms of the fault tree's graph structure and logical structure. They also relate minimal cut sets to actual causes.
AI.result: A complete classification of different notions of actual causality in terms of fault tree graph and logical structure, with a demonstrated connection between minimal cut sets and actual causes.
AI.conclusion: Fault trees can be extended from risk assessment (what can go wrong) to failure diagnostics (why it went wrong) by leveraging actual causality theory, with minimal cut sets serving as a bridge between these two perspectives.

title: A Mathematical Introduction to Diffusion Models
comment: Lecture notes for the John Tukey Summer Graduate School on Mathematics of Generative Models at SLMath (June 22nd, 2026 -- July 2nd, 2026)
summary: These notes give a proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models from the viewpoint of sampling, tracing a single arc from classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers, their error analysis, and inference-time control. Throughout, the material is layered into core definitions and identities proved in full, representative estimates proved under simplifying assumptions, and research-level theorems stated with a proof roadmap. The intended audience is beginning graduate students with a background in probability but no prior exposure to stochastic differential equations, stochastic numerics, or diffusion models.

AI.tldr: A proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models from a sampling perspective, covering classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers, error analysis, and inference-time control, designed for graduate students with probability background but no prior exposure to SDEs or diffusion models.
AI.motivation: To provide a rigorous, self-contained introduction to diffusion models that bridges classical sampling theory and modern diffusion-based generative models, making the mathematical foundations accessible to graduate students without requiring prior knowledge of stochastic differential equations or diffusion models.
AI.method: Layered pedagogical structure: (1) core definitions and identities with full proofs, (2) representative estimates under simplifying assumptions, and (3) research-level theorems with proof roadmaps. The material traces a single arc from classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers.
AI.result: A comprehensive set of lecture notes that provides proof-oriented coverage of diffusion models, including error analysis and inference-time control techniques, organized in increasing complexity.
AI.conclusion: The notes serve as an accessible yet rigorous entry point for graduate students to understand diffusion models through the lens of sampling theory, with a clear progression from fundamentals to research-level topics.

title: DL-VINS-Factory: A Modular Framework for Learned Visual Front-Ends in Visual-Inertial SLAM
summary: Deep-learning features excel in visual matching, yet their practical value in tightly coupled visual-inertial SLAM (VI-SLAM) remains insufficiently characterized. We present DL-VINS-Factory, a unified framework that integrates learned feature extractors (ALIKED, RaCo, SuperPoint, XFeat) with either Lucas--Kanade (LK) optical-flow tracking or LightGlue (LG) descriptor matching. All front-ends share a sliding-window Ceres back-end, with optional AnyLoc DINOv2-VLAD loop closure, and 4-DoF pose-graph optimization. We benchmark the system across the four datasets covering indoor, unstructured outdoor, aggressive-motion, and visually degraded conditions. Results show that learned front-ends are viable for real-time embedded VI-SLAM, but are not universally superior to classical tracking. Relative to the corresponding GFTT+LK baseline, ALIKED+LG reduces EuRoC ATE by $5\%$ in monocular odometry and by $7\%$ in stereo with loop-closure. On NTU-VIRAL, where aggressive aerial motion increases inter-frame viewpoint change, ALIKED+LG stereo reduces loop-closed ATE by $12\%$. In Botanic Garden dataset, optical-flow tracking remains preferable, but learned keypoints still improve over the baseline GFTT, in which SuperPoint+LK reduces grayscale camera ATE by $29\%$, while RaCo+LK reduces RGB camera ATE by $38\%$. On SubT-MRS, learned front-ends display varying degree of improvement based on individual cases. With TensorRT acceleration on a Jetson AGX Orin, all valid configurations run in real time between $29$--$47$ FPS in monocular mode and $18$--$33$ FPS in stereo mode for the EuRoC and NTU-VIRAL datasets. AnyLoc further confirms roughly $2$--$7\times$ more valid loops than BRIEF+DBoW2. The implementation is open-sourced at https://github.com/limshoonkit/DL-VINS-Factory-ROS2/.

AI.tldr: DL-VINS-Factory is a unified framework integrating learned feature extractors (ALIKED, RaCo, SuperPoint, XFeat) with optical-flow or descriptor-matching in VI-SLAM. Benchmarked across four datasets, learned front-ends improve accuracy in some scenarios (e.g., SuperPoint+LK reduces ATE by 29% on Botanic Garden grayscale) but are not universally superior to classical GFTT+LK. All valid configurations run in real-time (29-47 FPS monocular, 18-33 FPS stereo) on Jetson AGX Orin.
AI.motivation: Deep-learning features are known to excel in visual matching, but their practical value in tightly coupled visual-inertial SLAM systems has not been sufficiently characterized. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a unified benchmarking framework.
AI.method: The framework integrates learned feature extractors (ALIKED, RaCo, SuperPoint, XFeat) with either Lucas-Kanade optical-flow tracking or LightGlue descriptor matching. A shared sliding-window Ceres back-end is used, with optional AnyLoc DINOv2-VLAD loop closure and 4-DoF pose-graph optimization. Evaluation is conducted on four datasets (EuRoC, NTU-VIRAL, Botanic Garden, SubT-MRS) with TensorRT acceleration on Jetson AGX Orin.
AI.result: ALIKED+LG reduces EuRoC ATE by 5% (monocular) and 7% (stereo with loop closure). On NTU-VIRAL, ALIKED+LG stereo reduces loop-closed ATE by 12%. On Botanic Garden, SuperPoint+LK reduces grayscale ATE by 29%, and RaCo+LK reduces RGB ATE by 38%. Learned front-ends show varied improvement on SubT-MRS. All valid configurations run at 29-47 FPS monocular and 18-33 FPS stereo. AnyLoc finds 2-7× more valid loops than BRIEF+DBoW2.
AI.conclusion: Learned front-ends are viable for real-time embedded VI-SLAM but are not universally superior to classical tracking. The choice of front-end should depend on the specific operational conditions. The framework is open-sourced.

title: CLAP: Closed-Loop Training, Evaluation, and Release Control for Domain Agent Post-training
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Accepted to CRAE 2026; to appear in SPIE Proceedings. Best Poster Award
summary: Domain agents often face noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and adapter-release risk. This paper presents CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training), a closed-loop method that converts business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. CLAP combines data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to decide whether an adapter is suitable for the target application chain. On five anonymized manufacturing-scenario batches, QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT yields modest average gains: overall score increases by 0.0098, pass rate by 0.0240, and evidence accuracy by 0.0280, while hallucination and wrong facts decrease. Yet only 3 of 5 batches improve, some batches regress, and GRPO exposes high KL risks. Application-chain replay further shows that RAG is necessary for factual extraction; under the same 3B backbone and 100 replay cases, an application-RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapter improves value, core fields, and answer-evidence doc/page matching over base+RAG, but increases latency. These results support managing domain-agent post-training through an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop rather than relying on training completion or a single offline score.

AI.tldr: CLAP is a closed-loop post-training method for domain agents that integrates data validation, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to manage adapter release. On five manufacturing batches, QLoRA-SFT shows modest average gains (overall +0.0098, pass rate +0.0240, evidence accuracy +0.0280) but only 3/5 batches improve, GRPO poses high KL risks, and RAG integration improves factual extraction at the cost of increased latency.
AI.motivation: Domain agents face noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and adapter-release risk, creating a need for a systematic release-gating mechanism beyond simple training completion or single-score evaluation.
AI.method: CLAP converts business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. It combines data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to decide adapter readiness.
AI.result: On five manufacturing batches: QLoRA-SFT average gains of +0.0098 overall score, +0.0240 pass rate, +0.0280 evidence accuracy. Only 3/5 batches improved; GRPO showed high KL risks. RAG-integrated LoRA-SFT improved factual extraction (value, core fields, doc/page matching) but increased latency.
AI.conclusion: Domain-agent post-training should be governed by an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop rather than relying solely on training completion or a single offline score, as gains are inconsistent and application-chain replay reveals trade-offs (e.g., RAG latency vs. accuracy).

title: Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine for Solving High-Frequency Partial Differential Equations
summary: Solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with high-frequency solutions remains a central challenge in physics-informed machine learning due to spectral bias -- the tendency of neural networks to learn low-frequency components preferentially. This paper proposes a Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine (FS-PIELM) framework that addresses this limitation through an additive mechanism for weight initialization. Rather than multiplying random weights by a scaling factor, the method translates the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution while keeping the variance fixed at unity, thereby avoiding the variance amplification inherent in scaling-based methods. Two variants are developed: FS-PIELM-L assigns independent frequency magnitudes to individual neurons, while FS-PIELM-G groups neurons for improved robustness. Theoretical analysis shows that the frequency variance under the proposed framework remains bounded and approaches unity regardless of target frequency, in contrast to the quadratic growth of conventional approaches. The method preserves the computational efficiency of extreme learning machines, requiring only a single linear solve. Experiments on seven benchmark problems spanning six equation types -- Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, and advection-diffusion -- on both regular and complex geometries show that the linear variant achieves the best accuracy in six of seven cases, with improvements of one to nearly five orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants. The code and data accompanying this manuscript will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xgxgnpu/Physics-informed-vibe-coding/tree/main/FS-PIELM.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes FS-PIELM, a frequency-shifted extreme learning machine framework that mitigates spectral bias in solving high-frequency PDEs by translating (rather than scaling) the weight distribution mean, preserving unit variance and outperforming existing PIELM variants by up to five orders of magnitude across six equation types.
AI.motivation: Neural networks suffer from spectral bias, learning low-frequency components preferentially, which makes high-frequency PDE solutions challenging. Existing PIELM methods that scale random weights amplify variance quadratically, hindering performance on high-frequency problems.
AI.method: FS-PIELM introduces an additive weight initialization: it shifts the mean of Gaussian weight distribution (via a target frequency parameter) while fixing variance at 1, avoiding variance amplification. Two variants are developed: FS-PIELM-L (independent frequencies per neuron) and FS-PIELM-G (grouped neurons for robustness). Training reduces to a single linear solve as in standard ELMs.
AI.result: On seven benchmark problems (Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, advection-diffusion) on regular and complex geometries, FS-PIELM-L achieves best accuracy in six of seven cases, with improvements of 1 to nearly 5 orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants. Theoretical analysis confirms frequency variance remains bounded near unity regardless of target frequency.
AI.conclusion: FS-PIELM effectively addresses spectral bias for high-frequency PDEs while preserving ELM computational efficiency. The additive frequency shift mechanism is theoretically and empirically superior to scaling-based initialization for high-frequency problems.

title: ProCal: Inference-Time Proposal Calibration for Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
summary: Open-vocabulary object detection aims to localize and classify objects beyond the fixed set of categories seen dur ing training. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods improve localization and classification for unseen categories by leveraging a frozen VLM as a detector backbone. However, VLM classification score lacks recognizing position and scale of the object in an image. We observe that pretrained VLMs en able to classify foreground and background regions. According to this observation, we propose a simple inference-time Pro posal Calibration (ProCal) that improves localization quality of the classification score. ProCal computes a proposal prior by combining two scores: localization-aware foreground score and background-aware suppression score. Localization-aware foreground score captures whether a proposal contains an object area. Background-aware suppression score measures the extent to which the proposal resembles background. We analyze that ProCal suppresses false novel activation on background proposals and consistently ranks true novel proposals above background and partial novel proposals. Applied to CLIPSelf ViT-L/14, ProCal improves APr +2.5 on OV-LVIS. The analyses show that proposal-level localization-aware reranking effects to mitigate ranking miscalibration for novel objects.

AI.tldr: ProCal is an inference-time proposal calibration method that improves open-vocabulary object detection by combining localization-aware foreground and background-aware suppression scores to better rank novel object proposals, achieving +2.5 APr on OV-LVIS with CLIPSelf ViT-L/14.
AI.motivation: VLM classification scores in open-vocabulary detection lack awareness of object position and scale, causing poor localization and false positive activations on background proposals for novel categories.
AI.method: ProCal computes a proposal prior by combining (1) a localization-aware foreground score that captures whether a proposal contains an object area, and (2) a background-aware suppression score that measures how much a proposal resembles background regions. This re-ranks proposals at inference time.
AI.result: Applied to CLIPSelf ViT-L/14, ProCal improves APr by +2.5 on OV-LVIS. It suppresses false novel activation on background proposals and ranks true novel proposals above background/partial proposals.
AI.conclusion: Proposal-level localization-aware reranking effectively mitigates ranking miscalibration for novel objects, demonstrating that pretrained VLMs' ability to distinguish foreground/background can be leveraged for better open-vocabulary detection.

title: Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement
summary: Safety training for large language models (LLMs) is conducted predominantly in English, leaving uncertain how well safety mechanisms generalize to low-resource languages and mixed-language code-switching. We show that this creates an epistemic gap in which models confidently generate harmful responses for inputs that fall outside the distribution of their safety training. To study this phenomenon, we introduce STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement), a gradient-guided attack that identifies words contributing most strongly to the model's refusal behavior and iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent. Across six open-source 8B-parameter models, STEER achieves attack success rates of up to 93.0% on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, outperforming random code-switching and Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG). The resulting prompts also transfer to GPT-4o-mini, achieving a 35.5% attack success rate without requiring access to the target model, suggesting that the underlying weakness is not specific to a single architecture. These findings demonstrate that safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs. We argue that improving multilingual safety requires broader coverage during alignment and mechanisms that explicitly detect and abstain on out-of-distribution inputs.

AI.tldr: STEER is a gradient-guided attack that exploits the epistemic gap in LLM safety training by translating key refusal-related words into low-resource languages, achieving up to 96.7% attack success rates and transferring to GPT-4o-mini, revealing that English-only safety alignment fails to generalize across multilingual inputs.
AI.motivation: Safety training for LLMs is predominantly conducted in English, leaving uncertainty about how well safety mechanisms generalize to low-resource languages and code-switching contexts, creating an epistemic gap where models confidently produce harmful outputs for out-of-distribution inputs.
AI.method: STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement) is a gradient-guided attack that identifies words contributing most to refusal behavior and iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent. Evaluated across six 8B-parameter open-source models on JailbreakBench and AdvBench.
AI.result: STEER achieves up to 93.0% attack success rate on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, outperforming random code-switching and GCG. Generated prompts transfer to GPT-4o-mini with 35.5% success rate without white-box access.
AI.conclusion: Safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs. Improving multilingual safety requires broader coverage during alignment and explicit mechanisms to detect and abstain on out-of-distribution inputs.

title: Predicting Closed-Loop Performance of Latent World Models: Offline Checkpoint Selection for MPC and Model-Based RL Under Non-Markovian Rewards in LunarLander
comment: Preprint, 19 pages (16 main text + 3 pages appendix), 7 figures, 4 tables. Video: https://youtu.be/4PxHFW_TYUw , Code: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM
summary: We study how to predict the downstream closed-loop performance of a learned latent world model from validation-time diagnostics alone. Choosing the right checkpoint from a world-model training run is difficult: validation loss and multi-step prediction RMSE keep improving long after closed-loop performance has collapsed. We present a suite of structural validation-time diagnostics drawn from optimal-control theory and apply them to Gymnasium's LunarLander v3, which features shaped rewards. We train an RSSM [5, 4] world model on it and treat per checkpoint CEM-MPC return as the oracle for closed-loop quality. By evaluating 40 metrics against this oracle, we find that the strongest single predictor is the Reward Observability Fraction (ROF), which measures the reward predictor's dependence on the observable subspace. We combine ROF with three structural regularizers into a single-number offline checkpoint selection score, the Composite Reward Observability Fraction (CROF). The CROF-selected world model trains a model-based A2C policy that beats a fairly evaluated model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65x fewer real-environment interactions, and the same world model also drives a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy. Code and data: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel validation-time diagnostic, the Composite Reward Observability Fraction (CROF), to predict closed-loop performance of latent world models. CROF outperforms 39 other metrics, enabling checkpoint selection that yields a model-based A2C policy beating a model-free baseline by ~24.5 return points with ~65x fewer environment interactions.
AI.motivation: Standard validation metrics like validation loss and multi-step prediction RMSE correlate poorly with downstream closed-loop performance of world models—they keep improving even after closed-loop performance collapses. This makes checkpoint selection unreliable and motivates the need for better structural diagnostics.
AI.method: The authors train an RSSM world model on LunarLander v3, treat CEM-MPC return as the oracle for closed-loop quality, evaluate 40 metrics against this oracle, identify Reward Observability Fraction (ROF) as the best single predictor, and combine it with three structural regularizers into a composite score (CROF) for offline checkpoint selection.
AI.result: CROF-selected world model enables a model-based A2C policy that outperforms a fairly evaluated model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65x fewer real-environment interactions. The same world model also drives a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy.
AI.conclusion: Structural validation-time diagnostics from control theory, particularly the Reward Observability Fraction, reliably predict closed-loop world model performance and enable practical, sample-efficient model-based RL.

title: JointHOI: Jointly Generating Contact Maps Enhances Hand Object Interaction Generation
summary: Text driven hand object interaction (HOI) generation is gaining attention for immersive applications and robotics, yet producing physically plausible interactions remains challenging. Even when individual motions appear natural, small contact errors can cause conspicuous artifacts such as floating and interpenetration. Prior methods mitigate these issues using explicit contact cues or implicit grasp priors, but typically rely on multi stage pipelines and fail to model temporally evolving contact. We present JointHOI, a single stage diffusion framework that jointly generates 3D hand object motion and dynamic, distance based contact maps from text. By treating contact as an auxiliary inner modality, joint generation enables the model to learn contact motion coupling during training. At inference, contact guided sampling enforces consistency between generated contact maps and motion implied geometry, improving temporal stability and reducing penetration and floating. Experiments on GRAB and ARCTIC demonstrate consistent improvements in text adherence and physical plausibility over prior methods.

AI.tldr: JointHOI is a single-stage diffusion framework that jointly generates 3D hand-object motion and dynamic contact maps from text, using contact as an inner modality and guided sampling to improve physical plausibility, outperforming prior methods on GRAB and ARCTIC.
AI.motivation: Existing HOI generation methods suffer from physical artifacts like floating and interpenetration due to small contact errors, rely on multi-stage pipelines, and fail to model temporally evolving contact.
AI.method: JointHOI is a single-stage diffusion framework that jointly generates 3D hand-object motion and dynamic distance-based contact maps; it treats contact as an auxiliary inner modality to learn contact-motion coupling during training, and uses contact-guided sampling at inference to enforce consistency between generated contact maps and motion geometry.
AI.result: Experiments on GRAB and ARCTIC datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in text adherence and physical plausibility over prior methods.
AI.conclusion: Jointly generating contact maps as an inner modality within a single-stage diffusion framework, combined with contact-guided sampling, effectively reduces penetration and floating artifacts in text-driven HOI generation.

title: CamoNAS: Neural Architecture Search for Enhanced Camouflaged Object Detection
comment: Published in The Visual Computer. Author manuscript version
summary: Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) aims to locate and segment objects that blend into their surroundings, presenting challenges due to weak edge cues and ill-defined boundaries. Traditional COD models rely on hand-designed architectures and multi-scale feature fusion, which are often guided by intuition rather than systematic search. This paper introduces CamoNAS, a frequency-aware multi-resolution Neural Architecture Search (NAS) framework for COD. CamoNAS automatically searches both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, forming a hierarchical search space tailored to detect camouflaged objects. Additionally, it adopts an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture, where a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream. CamoNAS achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks (CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, CHAMELEON), highlighting the effectiveness of NAS for COD. Our code is available at https://github.com/rendaweiSIMIT/CamoNAS.

AI.tldr: CamoNAS is a frequency-aware Neural Architecture Search framework for Camouflaged Object Detection that automatically searches cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, combined with an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture using learnable wavelet transforms, achieving state-of-the-art results on four COD benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional COD models rely on hand-designed architectures and multi-scale feature fusion guided by intuition rather than systematic search, limiting their ability to handle weak edge cues and ill-defined boundaries of camouflaged objects.
AI.method: CamoNAS proposes a hierarchical NAS search space covering both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, along with an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture where a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks: CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, and CHAMELEON.
AI.conclusion: Highlights the effectiveness of Neural Architecture Search for Camouflaged Object Detection, demonstrating that automated architecture search outperforms hand-designed COD models.

title: Finite-Lag Operator Geometry of Recurrent Representations
summary: Recurrent representations are trajectories, but representation geometry is often measured from static snapshots. We develop finite-lag operator geometry for recurrent hidden states from observed source-successor pairs $(X_t,X_{t+Δ})$. The primitive is the conditional transport law $Q_Δ(dy\mid x)$, estimated by a dense Gaussian source-smoothing operator. From this directed finite-lag law we derive a source-centered transport tensor $G_Δ$, which decomposes exactly into conditional spread and coherent displacement, and an antisymmetric coordinate circulation $W_Δ^ρ$, which summarizes directed lagged flow. We prove affine covariance with explicit metric dependence of scalar summaries, dense estimator stability on bounded trajectory clouds, and a finite-lag separation result showing that source-centered transport detects deterministic recurrent motion not recorded by infinitesimal carre-du-champ geometry. A linear-Gaussian closed form calibrates the quantities in terms of the update $A_Δ$, source covariance, and innovation covariance. Controlled experiments validate the decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability predictions. In performance matched repeat-copy networks, the framework reveals architecture dependent differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace, while coherent displacement fraction is metric and resolution dependent.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a finite-lag operator geometry for analyzing recurrent hidden states from observed source-successor pairs, deriving transport tensors and circulation metrics that decompose conditional dynamics into spread and coherent displacement, with theoretical guarantees and empirical validation on recurrent networks.
AI.motivation: Existing representation geometry methods measure static snapshots, but recurrent representations evolve over time. The authors aim to develop a framework that captures directed, lagged dynamical structure from pairs of observations at finite time offsets.
AI.method: Uses conditional transport law Q_Δ estimated via dense Gaussian source-smoothing operator; derives source-centered transport tensor G_Δ (decomposing into conditional spread and coherent displacement) and antisymmetric circulation W_Δ^ρ; proves affine covariance, estimator stability, and finite-lag separation from infinitesimal carre-du-champ geometry; validates with linear-Gaussian closed form and controlled experiments.
AI.result: The framework reveals architecture-dependent differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace in repeat-copy networks; coherent displacement fraction is metric and resolution dependent; theoretical predictions of decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability are validated empirically.
AI.conclusion: Finite-lag operator geometry provides a principled way to analyze recurrent dynamics from trajectory data, capturing deterministic recurrent motion missed by infinitesimal geometry, and revealing architecture-specific dynamical signatures in recurrent networks.

title: LLM-Empowered Multimodal Fusion Framework for Autonomous Driving: Semantic Enhancement and Channel-Adaptive Design
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Accepted by 2026 IEEE 37th International Symposium on Personal, Indoor and Mobile Radio Communications (PIMRC)
summary: Vision-radar fusion is central to robust autonomous driving, combining dense visual semantics with precise range and velocity measurements from radar. However, real-world fusion quality is fundamentally challenged by dynamically varying input quality, stemming from occlusion, adverse weather, and channel noise. To address this, we re-frame the problem from static data fusion to channel-aware semantic reasoning and propose a Large Language Model-centric Semantic-layer Channel-aware Integrated Perception (LM-SCIP) framework. It places a Large Language Model (LLM) as a central reasoning core to fuse a local visual stream with a quality-varying external radar stream used to cover perception-blind spots. Concretely, LM-SCIP couples a hierarchical radar-vision encoder with a Channel-Adaptive Semantic Module (CASM) that maps link indicators into a "Channel Prompt" to dynamically gate external radar features. A parameter-efficient, LoRA-tuned LLM, in conjunction with a heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts (H-MoE), then arbitrates between local visual cues and the channel-conditioned radar context. Finally, a decoupled multi-task decoder outputs localization, trajectory forecasting, and image reconstruction. Experiments on nuScenes and VIRAT validate our approach. On nuScenes, under a controlled toggle of radar input, LM-SCIP reduces localization RMSE by 40.0% versus a vision-only baseline. On VIRAT, the model attains a 0.214m localization RMSE and 0.179m minFDE (k=1). These results reveal that the proposed LM-SCIP enables a robust vision-dominant fallback at low SNR and synergistic fusion at high SNR.

AI.tldr: LM-SCIP is an LLM-centric framework for vision-radar fusion that uses a Channel-Adaptive Semantic Module to dynamically adapt to varying radar quality, achieving robust autonomous driving perception with 40% localization RMSE reduction on nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Real-world vision-radar fusion is challenged by dynamically varying input quality due to occlusion, adverse weather, and channel noise; existing static data fusion approaches fail to handle such quality variations.
AI.method: LM-SCIP places an LLM as central reasoning core, couples a hierarchical radar-vision encoder with a Channel-Adaptive Semantic Module (CASM) that maps link indicators into a "Channel Prompt" for dynamic gating, uses LoRA-tuned LLM with heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts (H-MoE) to arbitrate between local visual cues and channel-conditioned radar context, and employs a decoupled multi-task decoder for localization, trajectory forecasting, and image reconstruction.
