This conditional growth exposes the second-order interaction that single-unit scores discard. On the GPT-2-small IOI circuit, CoAx raises backup-head recovery from 0.33 to 0.91 ROC-AUC, outperforming all baselines, including self-repair-aware gradient scores (best 0.82); counterfactual patching verifies that the recovered heads causally carry the repair. The same label-free procedure transfers to induction across eight models. Beyond discovery, the recovered backups correct self-repair-masked attribution, identify the components required for capability knockout, and yield repair-aware structured pruning scaling from 124M to 7B. Component importance is therefore not merely an isolated-unit property: in robust circuits, the components that matter can become visible only under the interventions that make them necessary.

AI.tldr: Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx) exposes backup circuits masked by self-repair in transformers by measuring how ablation effects grow when primary components are removed, enabling detection of dormant components that single-unit importance scores miss.
AI.motivation: Standard first-order ablation-based importance scoring fails under self-repair: removing a primary component activates dormant backups that mask the primary's true causal role, while backups appear irrelevant in the intact model.
AI.method: Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx): a label-free, output-grounded score that measures the growth of each remaining unit's ablation effect after a primary set is removed, capturing second-order interactions via conditional circuit completion.
AI.result: On GPT-2-small IOI circuit, CoAx improves backup-head recovery from 0.33 to 0.91 ROC-AUC, outperforming all baselines including self-repair-aware gradient scores (best 0.82). Transfers to induction across eight models and from 124M to 7B scales.
AI.conclusion: Component importance is not an isolated-unit property; in robust circuits, critical components become visible only under interventions that make them necessary. CoAx corrects self-repair-masked attribution, enables capability knockout, and yields repair-aware structured pruning.

title: Assessing VLM Reliability for Medical Image Quality Evaluation Under Corruption and Bias
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly applied in medical tasks such as pathology description, report generation, and visual question answering. Medical Image Quality Assessment (MIQA) supports diagnostic accuracy and patient safety by determining whether images meet the standards required for clinical decision-making. Automating MIQA with VLMs may reduce workload, but their behavior under real-world conditions, where images may be degraded or textual context may affect judgments, should be further explored before deployment. We benchmark VLMs on medical image quality using the MediMeta-C dataset zero-shot across seven corruption types and five severity levels. We evaluate sensitivity to degradation patterns, the effect of corruptions on embedding geometry, and whether textual attributes (demographics, expertise, infrastructure, institution) alter scores. Across 16 VLMs and seven modalities, pixelation produced the largest score reductions (mean -20.58%, up to -34.4% for OCT), whereas brightness had limited effect (-0.81%). Embedding displacement was associated with score changes. Same-family models showed correlations of 0.67-0.83; some produced increases up to +31% for corrupted mammography. Textual attributes affected scores: institutional prestige raised them +17.15%, and equipment age lowered them -14.7%. The largest changes were +95.62% (InternVL-8B) and -37.7% (MedGemma). Current VLMs show limitations for medical image quality assessment. Pixelation, a privacy-preserving transformation, reduces performance, indicating a trade-off between patient privacy and reliability. Sensitivity to contextual metadata indicates limited objectivity and marks metadata as a privacy and bias source. Privacy protection and objective quality assessment are related requirements for use.

AI.tldr: VLMs used for Medical Image Quality Assessment (MIQA) are significantly impacted by image corruptions (especially pixelation: -20.58% mean, up to -34.4%) and textual metadata biases (institutional prestige +17.15%, equipment age -14.7%), revealing trade-offs between privacy protection and reliable quality assessment.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether Vision-Language Models can reliably automate Medical Image Quality Assessment under real-world conditions with degraded images and varying textual context, before clinical deployment.
AI.method: Benchmarked 16 VLMs zero-shot on the MediMeta-C dataset across seven corruption types (five severity levels) and seven modalities; analyzed embedding geometry changes and tested sensitivity to textual attributes (demographics, expertise, infrastructure, institution).
AI.result: Pixelation caused largest score drops (-20.58% mean, -34.4% for OCT); brightness had minimal effect (-0.81%). Same-family model correlations: 0.67-0.83. Institutional prestige raised scores +17.15%, equipment age lowered -14.7%. Largest changes: +95.62% (InternVL-8B) and -37.7% (MedGemma).
AI.conclusion: Current VLMs are unreliable for MIQA due to sensitivity to pixelation (privacy-preserving transform) and contextual metadata biases, indicating a trade-off between privacy and objective quality assessment.

title: A$^{2}$utoLPBench: An Auto-Generated, Agent-Friendly LP Benchmark via Inverse-KKT Construction
summary: Most LP-from-text benchmarks are static datasets of word problems written and labeled by hand. Once such a dataset is released, its size is fixed, its difficulty is fixed, and every problem can leak into the training data of future LLMs. We present \textbf{A$^{2}$utoLPBench}, a benchmark for testing LLM-driven agents on linear programming problems written in plain text. We first pick a feasible point and dual, then write down a problem for which that point is optimal and the objective value is known. The answer is known by construction, with no solver call and no human annotator. The evaluation environment bundles a reference solver-critic baseline and a Docker image whose usage instructions are written for an LLM-driven agent to read. With these in place, any agent can run the benchmark and get a calibrated score with one command. Because the benchmark is a generator rather than a fixed dataset, it has properties no fixed dataset can match: an unlimited supply of fresh problems, a difficulty knob set by $(n,m)$, ground-truth answers correct by construction, low LLM-side cost per problem relative to human authoring, repeatable scores across independent batches, and resistance to training-data leakage when fresh post-cutoff seed ranges are used.

AI.tldr: A²utoLPBench is a generative benchmark for evaluating LLM-driven agents on linear programming problems from text, featuring unlimited fresh problems, controllable difficulty, ground-truth answers by construction, and resistance to data leakage, unlike static datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing LP-from-text benchmarks are static datasets that are fixed in size and difficulty, prone to training-data leakage into LLMs, and expensive to produce due to human annotation. A generative, leakage-resistant alternative is needed.
AI.method: The benchmark generates problems by first picking a feasible point and dual, then constructing a problem for which that point is optimal with a known objective value. It includes a solver-critic baseline and a Docker-based evaluation environment with agent-readable instructions.
AI.result: The generator provides unlimited fresh problems, adjustable difficulty via (n,m) parameters, ground-truth answers correct by construction, low cost per problem relative to human authoring, repeatable scores, and immunity to training-data leakage when using post-cutoff seed ranges.
AI.conclusion: A²utoLPBench demonstrates that generative benchmarks can overcome fundamental limitations of static datasets for evaluating LLMs on optimization tasks, offering scalability, verifiability, and leakage resistance.

title: Hybrid quantum-classical neural network for sentiment analysis
summary: Quantum machine learning has recently emerged as a promising paradigm that leverages the expressive power of quantum circuits to address complex learning tasks. In this work, we investigate the applicability of hybrid quantum-classical neural networks to sentiment analysis, a central problem in natural language processing. We focus on a dataset of tweets related to COVID-19, where the textual content is vectorized using TF-IDF and fed into both classical feedforward networks and hybrid architectures incorporating parameterized quantum circuits. Our results show that hybrid models can achieve accuracy comparable to the classical baseline, while exhibiting distinct learning dynamics, especially in terms of validation loss and accuracy, that suggest a richer representational capacity. Moreover, when applying transfer learning to an SMS spam classification task, the hybrid models consistently outperform the classical counterpart, achieving an accuracy increase of 15 percentage points (from 66% to 81%) on the spam class, demonstrating enhanced generalization. These findings highlight the feasibility of employing QML for natural language processing and point toward the potential advantages of hybrid models as quantum hardware continues to advance.

AI.tldr: This paper explores hybrid quantum-classical neural networks for sentiment analysis on COVID-19 tweets and SMS spam classification, showing comparable accuracy to classical models on the former and superior performance (+15% on spam class) on the latter via transfer learning.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether hybrid quantum-classical neural networks can be effectively applied to sentiment analysis and NLP tasks, leveraging quantum circuits' expressive power while current quantum hardware is still limited.
AI.method: Text data (COVID-19 tweets) is vectorized using TF-IDF, then fed into classical feedforward networks and hybrid architectures incorporating parameterized quantum circuits. Transfer learning is applied to an SMS spam classification task.
AI.result: Hybrid models achieved accuracy comparable to classical baselines on sentiment analysis, with distinct learning dynamics (richer representational capacity). In transfer learning to SMS spam, hybrid models outperformed classical ones by 15 percentage points (66% → 81%) on the spam class.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid quantum-classical models are feasible for NLP tasks and show potential advantages, especially in generalization, as quantum hardware continues to advance.

title: MolSight: A Graph-Aware Vision-Language Model for Unified Chemical Image Understanding
summary: Using molecular large language models (LLMs) as a unified framework for understanding molecular structures and functions is emerging as a new trend in tasks such as molecular design and drug discovery. However, these models struggle to fully capture the visual representation of molecular structures, limiting their potential. While existing molecular vision-language models (VLMs) show promise, they still face challenges in structural alignment and lack the necessary topological modeling for accurate molecular understanding. To address this, we propose MolSight, a graph-aware vision-language model framework designed to enhance the understanding of molecular images by VLMs. MolSight integrates a Molecular Topology Module to inject chemical-bond adjacency information into vision tokens, and a Molecular Grounding Module to align visual features with chemical symbolic semantics. Our experiments demonstrate that MolSight significantly outperforms existing VLMs, molecular LLMs, and specialized tools across multiple chemical visual understanding tasks, achieving a new level of molecular image reasoning.

AI.tldr: MolSight is a graph-aware vision-language model that enhances molecular image understanding by integrating topological and grounding modules, outperforming existing VLMs, molecular LLMs, and specialized tools.
AI.motivation: Existing molecular LLMs and VLMs struggle to capture visual representations of molecular structures, face challenges in structural alignment, and lack topological modeling for accurate molecular understanding.
AI.method: MolSight integrates a Molecular Topology Module (injects chemical-bond adjacency into vision tokens) and a Molecular Grounding Module (aligns visual features with chemical symbolic semantics).
AI.result: MolSight significantly outperforms existing VLMs, molecular LLMs, and specialized tools across multiple chemical visual understanding tasks, achieving new state-of-the-art in molecular image reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Graph-aware vision-language modeling with explicit topological and grounding modules is an effective approach for advancing molecular image understanding.

title: A rubric-based controlled comparison of frontier language models on expert-authored clinical reasoning tasks
summary: Multiple-choice medical benchmarks are increasingly saturated, and recent rubric-based evaluations such as HealthBench have shown that open-ended clinical performance is far from solved - its "Hard" subset top score remains 32%. We present a small, deliberately difficult evaluation dataset of five clinician-authored clinical scenarios spanning four specialties (anaesthesia, internal/family medicine, emergency medicine, and obstetrics), each accompanied by an atomic, weighted, MECE rubric (25-62 criteria per task; 184 criteria total) authored from a clinician-drafted golden answer. We evaluate three frontier models: GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and Gemini 3.1 Pro. Mean rubric pass rates were 0.47 (Claude), 0.39 (GPT), and 0.37 (Gemini). The central finding is an inversion of clinical priority: the highest-weighted (weight-5, critical) criteria passed at only 32.4-41.7%, while low-stakes weight-1 criteria passed at 80-90%. 56 of 108 critical (weight-5) criteria (52%) were satisfied by no model. Three LLM autoraters reproduced expert met/not-met labels on 92.8-94.7% of 552 graded criteria. We position this as a methods-and-preliminary-findings contribution: the five tasks demonstrate a scalable, defensible pipeline ready to develop into a large-scale benchmark.

AI.tldr: A small, expert-crafted clinical evaluation dataset (5 scenarios, 184 criteria) reveals that frontier LLMs (GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro) invert clinical priority—passing low-stakes criteria at 80-90% but critical (weight-5) criteria at only 32-42%, with 52% of critical criteria satisfied by no model; LLM autoraters achieve 92.8-94.7% agreement with expert labels.
AI.motivation: Multiple-choice medical benchmarks are saturated and fail to capture open-ended clinical reasoning; rubric-based evaluations like HealthBench show that clinical performance remains unsolved (32% top score on "Hard" subset). The authors aim to develop a scalable, defensible pipeline for evaluating open-ended clinical reasoning using atomic, weighted MECE rubrics.
AI.method: Five clinician-authored clinical scenarios across four specialties (anaesthesia, internal/family medicine, emergency medicine, obstetrics) with atomic, weighted, MECE rubrics (25-62 criteria per task, 184 total) authored from clinician-drafted golden answers. Evaluated three frontier models (GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro) using rubric pass rates. Three LLM autoraters were used to reproduce expert labels.
AI.result: Mean rubric pass rates: Claude 0.47, GPT 0.39, Gemini 0.37. Critical weight-5 criteria passed at only 32.4-41.7%, while low-stakes weight-1 criteria passed at 80-90%. 56 of 108 critical criteria (52%) were satisfied by no model. LLM autoraters achieved 92.8-94.7% agreement on 552 graded criteria.
AI.conclusion: The findings demonstrate a critical inversion of clinical priority in frontier LLMs—models perform well on low-stakes criteria but poorly on clinically critical ones. The five tasks establish a scalable, defensible pipeline ready for development into a large-scale benchmark for open-ended clinical reasoning evaluation.

title: A More Accurate Algorithm Comparison through A/B Testing using Offline Evaluation Methods
summary: A/B testing is the gold standard for selecting the better algorithm in online services. While offline evaluation has attracted attention as a safer alternative due to the high experimental costs and the potential risk of degrading user experience and revenue in A/B testing, it is widely recognized that the estimation accuracy of offline evaluation is substantially lower. As a result, final selection decisions are typically made through A/B testing. Contrary to this conventional view, we reveal a counterintuitive phenomenon in which A/B testing can produce a higher algorithm selection error rate than offline evaluation. This occurs because the sample mean estimator used in A/B testing does not induce positive correlation, which is crucial for reducing critical selection errors, namely underestimating the truly superior algorithm and overestimating the truly inferior one. In contrast, offline evaluation methods unintentionally generate this beneficial correlation by relying on shared offline data when estimating and comparing the performance of multiple algorithms. Building on this insight, we propose an estimator that intentionally induces positive correlation to improve algorithm selection in A/B testing. The key idea is to introduce a hypothetical middle algorithm and to estimate the performance difference between algorithms A, M, and B in a stepwise manner using shared data at each step. This approach enables the application of offline evaluation techniques in each step, thereby inducing positive correlation and reducing critical selection errors. Furthermore, we derive the optimal middle algorithm regarding the resulting variance and analyze its advantages over existing methods through bias-variance analysis. Experiments on real-world data demonstrate that our estimator achieves the same selection error rate as existing approaches while using only one half of the A/B testing data.

AI.tldr: A/B testing, despite being the gold standard, can produce higher algorithm selection error than offline evaluation due to lack of positive correlation. The authors propose an estimator that induces positive correlation via a hypothetical middle algorithm, reducing selection error by half the data.
AI.motivation: High costs and risks of A/B testing motivate safer offline evaluation alternatives, but offline evaluation is perceived as less accurate. The paper challenges this by showing A/B testing can actually be worse for selection.
AI.method: Proposes an estimator that introduces a hypothetical middle algorithm M, then estimates performance differences A vs M and M vs B stepwise using shared data to induce positive correlation, reducing underestimation of the superior and overestimation of the inferior algorithm.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world data show the proposed estimator achieves the same selection error rate as existing A/B testing methods while using only half the data.
AI.conclusion: Inducing positive correlation is crucial for reducing algorithm selection errors; the proposed middle-algorithm estimator bridges offline and online evaluation benefits.

title: Open-Weather Robust 3D Detection via Dual-Critic Diffusion Alignment
summary: Robust 3D object detection under adverse weather remains a critical hurdle for autonomous driving. Despite progress with LiDAR-4D radar fusion, most methods are constrained by a closed-world assumption, implicitly requiring training and test weather to align in both type and severity. This premise fails in practice: the open-ended nature of weather, and even variations within a single type like rain, cause dramatically different LiDAR degradation patterns, leading to significant performance drops in unseen conditions. To address this, we present Dual-Critic Guided Diffusion Alignment (DCDA), a weather-agnostic framework that learns to recover degraded LiDAR features toward a clean manifold. Rather than modeling specific weather types, DCDA employs a 4D radar-conditioned diffusion process to progressively refine features, guided by two complementary critics. (i) A detection-guided critic, anchored by a pre-trained clean-weather model, ensures that the refined features retain object-level discriminability and localization accuracy. (ii) A weather adversarial critic enforces holistic distributional consistency with clean-weather representations. By aligning features through semantic and distributional constraints rather than explicit weather modeling, DCDA generalizes effectively to unseen weather types and severities without requiring paired data or weather labels. We further introduce a structured open-weather benchmark with held-out type-severity combinations and extensive experiments verify DCDA's advantages.

AI.tldr: DCDA proposes a weather-agnostic LiDAR-4D radar fusion framework that uses dual-critic guided diffusion to recover degraded LiDAR features toward a clean manifold, generalizing to unseen weather types and severities without paired data or weather labels.
AI.motivation: Existing LiDAR-4D radar fusion methods operate under a closed-world assumption where training and test weather conditions must align. The open-ended nature of weather causes dramatically different LiDAR degradation patterns, leading to significant performance drops in unseen conditions.
AI.method: DCDA uses a 4D radar-conditioned diffusion process to progressively refine degraded LiDAR features, guided by two critics: (i) a detection-guided critic that ensures object-level discriminability using a pre-trained clean-weather model, and (ii) a weather adversarial critic that enforces distributional consistency with clean-weather representations.
AI.result: The method generalizes effectively to unseen weather types and severities, and a structured open-weather benchmark with held-out type-severity combinations validates its advantages.
AI.conclusion: By aligning features through semantic and distributional constraints rather than explicit weather modeling, DCDA achieves weather-agnostic robust 3D object detection that generalizes to unseen conditions without requiring paired data or weather labels.

title: UA-ChatDev: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Agent Collaboration for Reliable Software Development
summary: Software development is a complex task that demands cooperation among agents with diverse roles. Large language models (LLMs) have enabled autonomous multi-agent software development frameworks that leverage role-based collaboration to automate requirements analysis, coding, testing, and refinement. However, existing approaches typically assume that intermediate agent outputs are equally reliable, leaving them vulnerable to hallucination propagation, where incorrect decisions generated in early development phases are transferred to downstream agents and negatively impact final software quality. To address this challenge, we propose UA-ChatDev, an uncertainty-aware multi-agent software development framework that integrates uncertainty quantification into agent interactions. It introduces a lightweight uncertainty estimation mechanism based on token-level log probabilities to assess the confidence of agent responses and employs phase-aware threshold calibration to selectively trigger retrieval-based verification when uncertainty exceeds acceptable levels. Extensive experiments on the SRDD benchmark demonstrate that UA-ChatDev consistently outperforms existing single-agent and multi-agent software development frameworks across completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality metrics. Further ablation studies and communication analyses verify that uncertainty-aware interactions enhance code execution reliability.

AI.tldr: UA-ChatDev introduces uncertainty quantification into multi-agent software development to prevent hallucination propagation, using token-level log probabilities and phase-aware thresholds to trigger retrieval-based verification, outperforming existing frameworks on SRDD benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent software development frameworks assume intermediate agent outputs are equally reliable, making them vulnerable to hallucination propagation where incorrect early-stage decisions degrade final software quality.
AI.method: UA-ChatDev integrates uncertainty quantification via token-level log probability estimation for agent response confidence, combined with phase-aware threshold calibration that selectively triggers retrieval-based verification when uncertainty exceeds acceptable levels.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms existing single-agent and multi-agent frameworks on SRDD benchmark across completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality; ablation studies confirm uncertainty-aware interactions enhance code execution reliability.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-aware agent interactions effectively mitigate hallucination propagation in multi-agent software development, improving code execution reliability and overall software quality.

title: Probabilistic Low-Voltage Peak Load Forecasting with Time Series Foundation Models Evaluated on Application-Oriented Metrics
comment: A poster abstract of this publication will be available at the 15th DACH+ Conference on Energy Informatics (2026 in Linz, Austria)
summary: Low-voltage load forecasting is an important component in current and future energy systems with a high degree of electrification and decentralized generation. However, current forecasting methods require significant manual effort, often lack uncertainty estimation and proper peak prediction, and they are often not adequately evaluated in terms of grid requirements. In the present study, we provide an extensive evaluation of short-term net load forecasts of 200 real-world low-voltage feeders with a focus on the rapidly evolving time series foundation models. Our study compares Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2 and TabPFN-TS to six baseline models and demonstrates superior performance, in particular for Chronos-2. An ablation study, in which weather covariates are omitted, shows that time series foundation models adapt to increased uncertainty, despite the importance of weather information. A novel application-oriented metric links the model's forecasting capabilities in peak prediction to the trade-off in grid asset planning and operation between cost reduction and minimizing the risk of failure.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates time series foundation models (Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, TabPFN-TS) for short-term net load forecasting on 200 real-world low-voltage feeders, finding Chronos-2 performs best. It introduces an application-oriented metric linking peak prediction to grid asset planning trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Low-voltage load forecasting is critical for modern energy systems with high electrification and decentralized generation, but current methods require manual effort, lack uncertainty estimation, fail at peak prediction, and are inadequately evaluated for grid requirements.
AI.method: Extensive evaluation of short-term net load forecasts on 200 real-world low-voltage feeders comparing time series foundation models (Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, TabPFN-TS) to six baseline models, with an ablation study omitting weather covariates and a novel application-oriented metric for peak prediction.
AI.result: Time series foundation models, especially Chronos-2, demonstrate superior performance over baselines. Ablation study shows foundation models adapt to increased uncertainty when weather covariates are omitted.
AI.conclusion: Time series foundation models are effective for low-voltage load forecasting, and the proposed application-oriented metric helps balance cost reduction and failure risk in grid asset planning.

title: Understanding Geometric Representations in Self-Supervised Vision Transformers via Subspace Intervention
summary: We introduce a controlled subspace intervention framework to investigate how self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs) encode dense geometric information. While linear probing is widely used to assess geometric representations, it treats features as a black box, failing to disentangle the underlying topology. To address this issue, we decompose the weights of converged linear probes to isolate the low-rank subspaces containing explicit geometric signals using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). Our perspective yields three key insights: (1) Pre-training objectives determine how features are encoded. DINOv2 aligns spatial features for efficient linear extraction, while Masked Autoencoders (MAE) tend to disperse these signals, requiring a broader spatial context. (2) Explicit geometric representations are highly compressible, suggesting dense predictive heads could potentially be constrained to low-rank subspaces with minimal performance loss. (3) The layer-wise task affinity suggests that geometric precision peaks at intermediate layers before yielding to semantic abstraction in the final layers. By connecting internal encoding mechanics with downstream performance, these findings provide a basis for effective feature selection and lightweight decoder design. The source code is available at https://github.com/Zhou-Weichen/Geosubprobe.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a controlled subspace intervention framework using SVD to decompose linear probe weights, revealing how Vision Transformers encode geometric information. They find DINOv2 aligns spatial features for easy extraction, MAE disperses signals, geometric representations are highly compressible, and geometric precision peaks in intermediate layers.
AI.motivation: Existing linear probing treats features as a black box, failing to disentangle the underlying topology of how self-supervised ViTs encode dense geometric information.
AI.method: Decompose the weights of converged linear probes using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to isolate low-rank subspaces containing explicit geometric signals, forming a controlled subspace intervention framework.
AI.result: (1) DINOv2 aligns spatial features for efficient linear extraction, while MAE disperses signals needing broader context. (2) Geometric representations are highly compressible into low-rank subspaces. (3) Geometric precision peaks at intermediate layers and declines in final layers due to semantic abstraction.
AI.conclusion: The findings connect internal encoding mechanics with downstream performance, providing a basis for effective feature selection and lightweight decoder design in ViTs.

title: Criticality-Based Guard Rail Validation for AI Agent Decisions in Autonomous Telecom Networks
summary: The evolution toward fully autonomous telecommunications networks (Autonomous Network Levels 4-5) requires AI/ML agents to make real-time network decisions without human intervention. However, no standardized runtime mechanism exists to intercept and validate individual inference outputs before they trigger live network state changes, creating risks of erroneous autonomous decisions. This paper proposes the Guard Rail Validation (GRV) framework, a standardizable runtime architecture for intercepting and validating AI-driven decisions before execution. The framework evaluates decisions across multiple weighted dimensions -- including action scope, action type, service criticality, agent autonomy level, reversibility, and temporal behavioural patterns -- to determine a criticality level. Based on this level, graduated validation mechanisms are applied: execute-with-logging, bounds checking, independent agent validation, or multi-agent consensus. The framework additionally provides cross-agent conflict detection with criticality-weighted priority resolution and runtime conformance logging for regulatory compliance (e.g., EU AI Act Article 14). We present the architecture, algorithmic procedures, O-RAN deployment model, and evaluate threat coverage against known AI/ML attacks in telecommunications.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Guard Rail Validation (GRV) framework, a standardized runtime architecture for intercepting and validating AI/ML model outputs before they trigger live network state changes in autonomous telecommunications networks (Levels 4-5). GRV evaluates decisions across multiple dimensions (scope, type, criticality, autonomy level, reversibility, behavior) to assign a criticality level, then applies graduated validation (logging, bounds checking, independent validation, multi-agent consensus). It also includes cross-agent conflict detection, priority resolution, and runtime conformance logging for regulatory compliance (e.g., EU AI Act).
AI.motivation: No standardized runtime mechanism exists to intercept and validate individual AI/ML inference outputs before they trigger live network state changes in high-level autonomous networks, creating risks of erroneous or malicious decisions without human oversight.
AI.method: The GRV framework intercepts AI agent decisions and evaluates them across weighted dimensions (action scope, action type, service criticality, agent autonomy level, reversibility, temporal behavioral patterns) to compute a criticality level. Based on this level, graduated validation mechanisms are applied: execute-with-logging, bounds checking, independent agent validation, or multi-agent consensus. Cross-agent conflict detection with criticality-weighted priority resolution and runtime conformance logging are also included.
AI.result: The paper presents the architecture, algorithmic procedures, an O-RAN deployment model, and evaluates threat coverage against known AI/ML attacks in telecommunications.
AI.conclusion: GRV provides a standardizable, graduated runtime safeguard for autonomous network decisions, addressing safety, security, and regulatory compliance (EU AI Act Article 14) for next-generation telecom networks.

title: Do Newer Lightweight CNNs Perform Better Under Resource Constraints? A Controlled Multigenerational Study of Architecture, Initialization, Training Budget, and Efficiency
summary: Newer lightweight convolutional neural networks are often presented as improving predictive performance and deployment efficiency, but such claims require controlled evaluation. This study compares nine lightweight CNN model packages across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet under a shared downstream protocol. We report top-1 accuracy, macro F1, top-5 accuracy, parameter count, FP32 storage, GMACs, batch-size-1 latency on an NVIDIA L4 and AMD Ryzen 5 5500U CPU, peak PyTorch CUDA allocated tensor memory, and point estimate Pareto frontiers. EfficientNetV2-S achieves the highest observed top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 at 97.57% and 86.98%, while RepViT-M1.0 leads Tiny ImageNet at 79.87%. EfficientNet-B0 remains within 0.22, 0.85, and 1.79 percentage points of the best result on the three datasets while using approximately 79% fewer parameters and 86% fewer GMACs than EfficientNetV2-S. It also appears on every evaluated accuracy and resource Pareto frontier, making it the most consistently competitive intermediate-budget option. MobileNetV3-Small has the lowest GMAC count, is the fastest model under both CPU thread settings, and records higher observed accuracy than MobileNetV4-Conv-S on all three datasets. Under random initialization, it leads MobileNetV4-Conv-S by 2.55, 1.76, and 0.99 points, with paired test-set intervals excluding zero for the fixed trained models. EfficientNet-B0 remains 3.29, 10.10, and 17.54 points below its pretrained counterpart after 100 epochs of scratch training, despite requiring about five times the recorded training time. SqueezeNet1.1 has the fewest parameters and lowest peak CUDA allocation, but substantially weaker accuracy. Latency rankings differ sharply between the L4 and CPU environments, showing that GMACs alone do not predict measured inference performance. Overall, newer designs provide selective rather than universal gains

AI.tldr: This study systematically evaluates nine lightweight CNN models across three benchmark datasets (CIFAR-10/100, Tiny ImageNet) under a controlled protocol. EfficientNetV2-S achieves highest top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 (97.57%) and CIFAR-100 (86.98%), while RepViT-M1.0 leads Tiny ImageNet (79.87%). EfficientNet-B0 emerges as the most consistently competitive intermediate-budget option, appearing on every Pareto frontier. MobileNetV3-Small is the fastest with lowest GMACs and outperforms MobileNetV4-Conv-S. Significant performance gaps exist between pretrained and scratch-trained models. The study finds that newer designs provide selective rather than universal gains, and GMACs alone do not predict measured latency.
AI.motivation: Lightweight CNN models claim improved predictive performance and deployment efficiency, but such claims lack controlled comparative evaluation. This study aims to provide a fair, systematic comparison under a shared protocol to assess which models truly deliver on their promises.
AI.method: Nine lightweight CNN model packages were compared across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet under a shared downstream protocol. Metrics included top-1 accuracy, macro F1, top-5 accuracy, parameter count, FP32 storage, GMACs, batch-size-1 latency on NVIDIA L4 GPU and AMD Ryzen 5 5500U CPU, peak PyTorch CUDA allocated tensor memory, and point estimate Pareto frontiers.
AI.result: EfficientNetV2-S achieved highest top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 (97.57%) and CIFAR-100 (86.98%); RepViT-M1.0 led Tiny ImageNet (79.87%). EfficientNet-B0 appeared on every accuracy-resource Pareto frontier, using ~79% fewer parameters and ~86% fewer GMACs than EfficientNetV2-S. MobileNetV3-Small had the lowest GMACs and fastest CPU/GPU latency, outperforming MobileNetV4-Conv-S. SqueezeNet1.1 had the fewest parameters but weakest accuracy. Pretrained EfficientNet-B0 significantly outperformed scratch-trained version (by 3.29–17.54 points) despite longer training time.
AI.conclusion: Newer lightweight CNN designs provide selective rather than universal improvements over existing models. EfficientNet-B0 is the most consistently competitive intermediate-budget option across all metrics and datasets. GMACs alone are insufficient predictors of inference latency, as rankings differ sharply between GPU and CPU environments.

title: Training-free Controllable Human Motion Generation under Heterogeneous Constraints
summary: Training-free controllable motion generation has attracted growing interest for enabling flexible constraint enforcement without constraint-specific training. However, existing training-free methods require constraints to be continuous objective-based with differentiable losses, while many real-world requirements are criterion-based and provide only discontinuous, sparse, or even black-box feedback. In this paper, we propose Motion-Inference-as-Control (MIC), the first training-free motion generation framework that handles both continuous objective-based and criterion-based motion constraints under a shared mechanism. The key idea is to cast diffusion-based motion generation as a stochastic control problem. This perspective not only provides principled and practically effective step-wise control laws that support criterion-based constraints without requiring differentiability and naturally accommodate objective-based constraints as a special case, but also motivates a control-oriented constraint coordination mechanism that adaptively balances and reconciles motion constraints during generation. Experiments across diverse constraint settings demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.

AI.tldr: MIC is a training-free motion generation framework that handles both continuous objective-based and criterion-based constraints by reformulating diffusion-based motion generation as a stochastic control problem, enabling principled step-wise control laws and adaptive constraint coordination without requiring differentiability.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free controllable motion generation methods cannot handle criterion-based constraints (e.g., discontinuous, sparse, black-box feedback) because they require continuous objectives with differentiable losses, limiting real-world applicability.
AI.method: The framework casts diffusion-based motion generation as a stochastic control problem, deriving principled step-wise control laws that support both criterion-based constraints (without differentiability) and objective-based constraints (as a special case), plus a control-oriented constraint coordination mechanism for adaptive balancing and reconciliation.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse constraint settings demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework.
AI.conclusion: MIC provides a unified, training-free mechanism for handling both continuous objective-based and criterion-based motion constraints, broadening the applicability of controllable motion generation to real-world requirements.

title: Purified OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation Without Losing How to Think
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving LLM reasoning, where a privileged teacher with access to reference solutions provides token-level supervision on the student's own generated trajectories. However, we find that OPSD consistently fails on long chain-of-thought (long-CoT) reasoning models, yielding at best marginal gains while destabilizing the reflective reasoning capability these models depend on. Through a novel decomposition of the teacher's supervision signal, we identify the root cause: the teacher's supervision is dominated by a reference-induced component that drives rote memorization of reference-specific shortcuts, while the question-conditioned, inference-transferable component is ignored or actively opposed. Based on this diagnosis, we propose a two-step solution. First, we construct a reference-only teacher (the same model conditioned on the reference without the question) to isolate the non-transferable component of the supervision signal; the residual after subtracting this component captures the question-conditioned, inference-transferable correction. Second, we use pointwise mutual information (PMI) as the mechanism to transform this residual into a well-formed PMI target distribution that the student can directly distill from, filtering out the reference-induced shortcut. Experiments on four long-CoT models across two datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over both the base model and standard OPSD, while preserving the models' natural epistemic behavior throughout training.

AI.tldr: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) fails on long-CoT reasoning models because the teacher's supervision is dominated by a reference-induced component that drives rote memorization of shortcuts. The authors propose a two-step solution: (1) isolate the inference-transferable correction by subtracting a reference-only teacher's signal, and (2) use pointwise mutual information (PMI) to form a well-behaved target distribution. Experiments show consistent improvements over baselines while preserving epistemic behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing OPSD methods fail on long-CoT reasoning models, yielding marginal gains and destabilizing reflective reasoning. The authors aim to diagnose why OPSD fails and propose a fix that enables effective self-distillation for long-CoT models.
AI.method: (1) Decompose the teacher's supervision signal to identify the reference-induced shortcut component. (2) Construct a reference-only teacher to isolate the non-transferable component; subtract it from the full signal. (3) Use PMI to transform the residual into a well-formed target distribution for student distillation.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves consistent improvements over both the base model and standard OPSD across four long-CoT models and two datasets, while preserving the models' natural epistemic behavior throughout training.
AI.conclusion: The failure of OPSD on long-CoT reasoning is caused by the teacher's supervision being dominated by reference-induced shortcuts. The proposed reference-subtraction and PMI-based distillation effectively filters out these shortcuts, enabling successful self-distillation for long-CoT reasoning models without degrading their reflective capabilities.

title: Liquid Latent State Dynamics for Interpretable Turbofan Degradation Modeling
summary: Multivariate time-series models for prognostics are often evaluated by point prediction accuracy, yet their internal states rarely expose a coherent degradation process. We study liquid neural networks as latent dynamics models for aircraft engine health monitoring on the C-MAPSS benchmark. The proposed model encodes a history window into a latent state, evolves that state with a liquid transition model, and decodes future sensor observations. To separate health evolution from operating-condition variation, the latent state is factorized into degradation and condition components. Remaining useful life, monotonic risk, and latent-consistency losses supervise the degradation component, while condition prediction and decorrelation losses discourage operating-condition leakage. Across FD001--FD004, the full disentangled model improves overall sensor forecasting RMSE from 0.2438 for a GRU baseline to 0.2266, with the largest gains on the multi-condition subsets FD002 and FD004. The learned degradation state also forms a clearer temporal degradation axis, reaching an average state-speed Spearman correlation of 0.5960. Direct remaining-useful-life regression remains stronger for the GRU baseline, indicating that the proposed representation is currently more effective as an interpretable world model for degradation dynamics than as a calibrated lifetime regressor. These results suggest that liquid latent dynamics can bridge predictive maintenance forecasting and inspectable health-state modeling.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a liquid neural network model with a factorized latent state (degradation + condition components) for aircraft engine prognostics on C-MAPSS. It improves sensor forecasting RMSE from 0.2438 (GRU) to 0.2266 and achieves clearer degradation trajectories (Spearman correlation 0.5960), though direct RUL regression remains better with GRU.
AI.motivation: Standard multivariate time-series models for prognostics focus on point prediction accuracy but fail to expose a coherent, interpretable degradation process in their latent states.
AI.method: Liquid neural network as latent dynamics model with factorized latent state (degradation and condition components), supervised by remaining useful life, monotonic risk, latent-consistency, condition prediction, and decorrelation losses.
AI.result: Sensor forecasting RMSE improved from 0.2438 (GRU) to 0.2266 overall; largest gains on multi-condition subsets FD002 and FD004. Degradation state Spearman correlation reached 0.5960. Direct RUL regression was stronger for GRU baseline.
AI.conclusion: Liquid latent dynamics can bridge predictive maintenance forecasting and interpretable health-state modeling, though the learned representation is more effective as an interpretable world model than as a calibrated lifetime regressor.

title: Mirror Illusion Art
comment: CVPR 2026 Highlight, also got an Efficient CVPR award
summary: Mirror Illusion Art is a novel reflection-conditioned 3D illusion where one object yields two target appearances (front and mirror). The task is formulated as inverse design from two target 2D images (front and mirror) to a printable 3D object with geometry and texture. Prior topology-driven and shadow-based approaches demand substantial manual effort, optimize shape only, and often yield non-smooth or incomplete geometry. To address these challenges, we propose AutoMIA, an automated Mirror Illusion Art design pipeline that jointly optimizes shape and color. To stabilize optimization and suppress artifacts, four mechanisms are introduced: (1) projection-alignment component (PAC) selection to reduce surface noise, (2) position-weighted adaptive (PWA) suppression for background noise, (3) internal voxel preservation (IVP) to prevent internal fractures, and (4) shape-color decoupled (SCD) optimization that balance shape and color optimization. AutoMIA generate diverse smooth Mirror Illusion artworks successfully both in the digital and physical world, with only around 76s design time and 2.6 GB memory on average using a single RTX 3090, advancing inverse graphics and computational design. Our code is available at https://github.com/zxp555/AutoMIA.

AI.tldr: AutoMIA is an automated pipeline for designing Mirror Illusion Art—3D objects that project two different 2D appearances (front and mirror views)—by jointly optimizing shape and color with four stabilization mechanisms, achieving fast (~76s) and low-memory (2.6 GB) generation of smooth, printable objects.
AI.motivation: Prior topology-driven and shadow-based approaches for mirror illusion art require substantial manual effort, optimize shape only, and often produce non-smooth or incomplete geometry. The goal is to automate the inverse design from two target 2D images to a printable 3D object with both geometry and texture.
AI.method: AutoMIA jointly optimizes shape and color for mirror illusion art. Four mechanisms stabilize optimization and suppress artifacts: (1) projection-alignment component (PAC) selection to reduce surface noise, (2) position-weighted adaptive (PWA) suppression for background noise, (3) internal voxel preservation (IVP) to prevent internal fractures, and (4) shape-color decoupled (SCD) optimization to balance shape and color optimization.
AI.result: AutoMIA generates diverse smooth Mirror Illusion artworks successfully in both digital and physical worlds, with only ~76s design time and ~2.6 GB memory on average using a single RTX 3090.
AI.conclusion: AutoMIA advances inverse graphics and computational design by providing an efficient, automated, and low-resource pipeline for mirror illusion art generation.

title: Copewell: A Multi-Agent Swarm Architecture for Equitable Mental Wellness Support
summary: Mental health disorders affect nearly one billion people globally, yet 75% of individuals in low- and middle-income countries receive no treatment due to workforce shortages, cost barriers, and stigma. Current AI-powered wellness solutions predominantly rely on single-mode conversational interfaces that suffer high abandonment rates and fail to provide measurable, immediate relief calibrated to users' dynamic emotional states. This paper presents Copewell, a novel multi-agent swarm system designed to expand access to mental wellness support through human-centered AI principles. Our architecture introduces three technical innovations: (1) a multi-source assessment framework integrating self-reported, physiological, and contextual data to mitigate algorithmic bias; (2) valence-arousal emotion mapping using Russell's Circumplex Model of Affect to route users to specialized AI agents; and (3) dual-mode intervention delivery combining conversational support with evidence-based sensory wellness protocols. We examine the sociotechnical design considerations underlying Copewell's development, including a privacy-first architecture, embedded ethical oversight through a dedicated Ethics Supervisor agent, and participatory design informed by mental health practitioners. Early practitioner engagement and beta deployment inform design decisions and identify directions for future empirical evaluation. This work contributes to responsible AI discourse by demonstrating how technical architecture can operationalize equity and safety principles from inception.

AI.tldr: Copewell is a multi-agent swarm system that expands mental wellness support access using multi-source assessment, valence-arousal emotion mapping, and dual-mode intervention delivery, with privacy-first and ethics-by-design principles.
AI.motivation: Nearly one billion people are affected by mental health disorders globally, with 75% in low- and middle-income countries receiving no treatment due to workforce shortages, cost barriers, and stigma. Existing AI wellness solutions rely on single-mode conversational interfaces that suffer high abandonment and fail to provide measurable, immediate relief tailored to users' dynamic emotional states.
AI.method: The architecture features three technical innovations: (1) a multi-source assessment framework integrating self-reported, physiological, and contextual data to mitigate algorithmic bias; (2) valence-arousal emotion mapping using Russell's Circumplex Model of Affect to route users to specialized AI agents; and (3) dual-mode intervention delivery combining conversational support with evidence-based sensory wellness protocols. Sociotechnical considerations include a privacy-first architecture, an Ethics Supervisor agent, and participatory design with mental health practitioners.
AI.result: Early practitioner engagement and beta deployment inform design decisions and identify directions for future empirical evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Copewell contributes to responsible AI discourse by demonstrating how technical architecture can operationalize equity and safety principles from inception, expanding access to mental wellness support through human-centered AI.

title: Fast and Accurate Anomaly Detection in Time Series
summary: Anomaly detection is a critical and evolving field in Machine Learning, with applications targeting different domains such as cybersecurity, finance, healthcare, manufacturing and IoT (Internet of Things) systems. Traditionally, anomaly detection algorithms have been designed using both supervised and unsupervised learning paradigms. The fundamental challenge in real-world anomaly detection scenarios is related to the inherent class imbalance (anomalies are typically rare) and, for supervised methods, to the scarcity of labelled anomalous data. Indeed, labelling is both expensive and time-consuming. Conversely unsupervised methods do not require labelling, but may suffer from high false positive rates when deployed in safety-critical applications. In this work we introduce a novel unsupervised algorithm for anomaly detection in time series based on the Haar discrete wavelet and a suitably designed $t$-test. We establish the theoretical foundation of the proposed $t$-test and, through extensive experimentation across 343 datasets, demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised and self-supervised benchmarks.

AI.tldr: A novel unsupervised anomaly detection algorithm for time series using Haar discrete wavelet and a custom t-test is proposed, outperforming state-of-the-art methods across 343 datasets.
AI.motivation: Anomaly detection faces challenges of class imbalance (rare anomalies) and scarcity of labelled data. Supervised methods require expensive labelling, while unsupervised methods often suffer from high false positive rates in safety-critical applications. The paper aims to address these limitations.
AI.method: The algorithm combines the Haar discrete wavelet transform with a specially designed t-test for unsupervised anomaly detection in time series. Theoretical foundations of the proposed t-test are established.
AI.result: Extensive experimentation across 343 datasets demonstrates that the proposed algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised and self-supervised benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed wavelet-based unsupervised algorithm with a custom t-test provides superior anomaly detection performance compared to existing unsupervised and self-supervised methods.

title: UnderOneFacade: Worldwide Facade Semantic Segmentation Benchmark Dataset
summary: Globally consistent semantic digital twins require centimeter-accurate and geographically transferable 3D facade segmentation. However, progress in facade parsing is limited by the lack of large-scale, standardized benchmarks for evaluating cross-domain generalization. Existing datasets are geographically narrow, semantically inconsistent, or insufficiently precise. We introduce UnderOneFacade, the largest cross-country and cross-continent 3D facade benchmark to date, comprising centimeter-accurate point clouds with hierarchical, harmonized, and architecturally grounded semantic labels totaling 2.7 billion annotated points. Through a systematic evaluation of representative point-, graph- and transformer-based architectures, we show that current methods struggle to recognize fine-grained architectural elements and degrade significantly across geographic domains, with the best models achieving only up to 33 IoU on the fine-grained LoFG3 benchmark. By combining geometric precision with standardized semantics at unprecedented scale, UnderOneFacade establishes a rigorous benchmark for developing robust and transferable 3D segmentation models. The dataset, evaluation scripts, and pretrained models will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: UnderOneFacade is the largest cross-country, cross-continent 3D facade benchmark with centimeter-accurate point clouds and 2.7 billion annotated points, revealing that current segmentation methods struggle with fine-grained architectural elements and degrade significantly across geographic domains (best models achieve only 33 IoU on fine-grained LoFG3).
AI.motivation: Progress in facade parsing is limited by the lack of large-scale, standardized benchmarks for evaluating cross-domain generalization; existing datasets are geographically narrow, semantically inconsistent, or insufficiently precise.
AI.method: UnderOneFacade provides centimeter-accurate point clouds with hierarchical, harmonized, and architecturally grounded semantic labels totaling 2.7 billion annotated points; the authors systematically evaluate representative point-, graph-, and transformer-based architectures.
AI.result: Current methods struggle to recognize fine-grained architectural elements and degrade significantly across geographic domains; the best models achieve only up to 33 IoU on the fine-grained LoFG3 benchmark.
AI.conclusion: By combining geometric precision with standardized semantics at unprecedented scale, UnderOneFacade establishes a rigorous benchmark for developing robust and transferable 3D segmentation models.

title: AgenticSTS: A Bounded-Memory Testbed for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Memory for a long-horizon LLM agent is a contract about what each future decision is allowed to see. The simplest contract appends past observations, tool calls, and reflections to every prompt, which makes prior context easy to access but also turns it into a jumbled mixture in which the effect of any single memory component is hard to isolate. We introduce and instrument an alternative bounded contract: every decision is made from a fresh user message assembled by typed retrieval, with no raw cross-decision transcript appended. The prompt thus stays bounded across runs of any length, and any single layer can be ablated in isolation. We instantiate the contract in Slay the Spire 2, a closed-rule stochastic deck-building game whose runs require hundreds of tactical and strategic decisions. A public online benchmark of frontier LLMs on the same game reports zero wins at the lowest difficulty across five configurations, and the developer-reported human win rate at the same difficulty is 16%; the task is hard but not saturated. Within our harness, a fixed-A0 ablation shows the largest observed difference when triggered strategic skills are enabled: the no-store baseline wins 3/10 games and adding the skill layer 6/10. At this sample size the comparison is directional rather than statistically decisive (Fisher exact p\approx0.37); a cross-backbone probe and public accumulating-context baselines are reported as operational comparisons rather than controlled tests of the contract variable itself. We release a reproducible testbed: 298 completed trajectories with condition tags, frozen memory/skill snapshots, prompt records, and analysis scripts -- an agent design and a validated, reusable methodology for studying how explicit memory layers shape long-horizon LLM-agent decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a bounded memory contract for LLM agents using typed retrieval instead of appending raw history, tested on Slay the Spire 2. Strategic skill layers show directional improvement (3/10 to 6/10 wins), and a reproducible testbed with 298 trajectories is released.
AI.motivation: Standard long-context memory for LLM agents appends all past observations into a jumbled mixture, making it hard to isolate the effect of individual memory components. The authors seek a bounded, modular memory contract that enables clean ablation studies.
AI.method: The bounded contract constructs each decision from a fresh user message via typed retrieval, with no raw cross-decision transcript. This is instantiated in Slay the Spire 2, comparing a no-store baseline against a triggered strategic skill layer, along with cross-backbone probes and accumulating-context baselines.
AI.result: No-store baseline wins 3/10 games; adding strategic skills wins 6/10 (Fisher exact p≈0.37, directional not decisive). Public benchmark shows zero wins across frontier LLMs; human win rate is 16%. A reproducible testbed of 298 trajectories with condition tags and snapshots is released.
AI.conclusion: The bounded contract enables isolated ablation of memory layers and provides a validated methodology for studying how explicit memory shapes long-horizon LLM-agent decisions, though the observed win-rate difference requires larger samples for statistical decisiveness.

title: A Memory Efficient Unified Algorithm for Online Learning of Linear Dynamical Systems
summary: Motivated by the challenge of stabilizing a general unknown linear dynamical system (LDS) from observations, we study the natural prerequisite of online prediction. Our goal is to achieve sublinear regret with a memory footprint that adapts to the intrinsic complexity of the dynamics rather than the full hidden -- state dimension. We focus on the practically central regime of systems with low instability complexity -- eigenvalues outside the real stable interval that do not decay rapidly, together with non-semisimple modes-potentially embedded in an otherwise stable real spectrum of much higher dimension; we write $k$ for this count. This regime is the primary setting in which stabilization is plausible: we show that many systems with high instability complexity cannot be stabilized without exponentially large controls. Thus, prediction is meaningful for stabilization precisely when the instability complexity is small. Within this regime, we introduce a unified online algorithm that handles every LDS (including non-diagonalizable systems with complex or exploding modes) with a learnable parameter count of $\widetilde{O}(k)$. Finally, we prove a lower bound showing that $k$ is a valid complexity measure: any filter-based predictor needs at least $k$ filters. Experiments corroborate our theory: on a high-dimensional system, our predictor sharply outperforms prior methods at an equal parameter budget.

AI.tldr: This paper studies online prediction for unknown linear dynamical systems, focusing on systems with low instability complexity (k). The authors propose an algorithm with $\widetilde{O}(k)$ learnable parameters, prove a lower bound that any filter-based predictor needs at least k filters, and demonstrate superior empirical performance compared to prior methods.
AI.motivation: To stabilize a general unknown linear dynamical system from observations, online prediction is a prerequisite. The goal is to achieve sublinear regret with a memory footprint that adapts to the intrinsic complexity of the dynamics (instability complexity k) rather than the full hidden-state dimension.
AI.method: The paper introduces a unified online algorithm that handles every LDS (including non-diagonalizable systems with complex or exploding modes) with $\widetilde{O}(k)$ learnable parameters. It also proves a lower bound that any filter-based predictor requires at least k filters.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves sublinear regret with parameter count scaling with instability complexity k rather than full state dimension. The lower bound shows k is a valid complexity measure. Experiments show the predictor sharply outperforms prior methods at equal parameter budget on a high-dimensional system.
AI.conclusion: Prediction is meaningful for stabilization precisely when instability complexity k is small. Systems with high instability complexity cannot be stabilized without exponentially large controls. The proposed algorithm effectively handles the regime where stabilization is plausible.

title: Spatio-Temporal and Clinical Conditioning for Fine-Grained Radiology Report Retrieval
summary: Radiology is vital to modern healthcare, but rising imaging demand and persistent workforce shortages strain reporting capacity and clinical workflows. Automated radiology report generation has the potential to support radiologists and help alleviate this burden; however, existing retrieval-based methods remain rigid, lack explicit anatomical grounding, and do not account for longitudinal disease progression or available clinical context. In this work, we introduce STAR3, a multimodal, spatio-temporal, attentive retrieval framework for radiology report generation that aligns region-level anatomical information with clinical indications and longitudinal changes across chest X-ray studies. Our framework employs an object detector to identify anatomically meaningful regions and retrieves semantically relevant report sentences conditioned on both current clinical context and changes observed between prior and current examinations. This design enables anatomically and temporally grounded report generation that better reflects clinical reporting practice. Experiments on the MIMIC-CXR dataset demonstrate that STAR3 outperforms current retrieval-based approaches on retrieval, NLP and clinical metrics, highlighting the value of conditioning retrieval anatomically, temporally and clinically for advancing automated radiology report generation.

AI.tldr: STAR3 is a multimodal retrieval framework for radiology report generation that aligns region-level anatomical information with clinical context and longitudinal changes, outperforming existing methods on MIMIC-CXR.
AI.motivation: Rising imaging demand and workforce shortages strain radiology reporting capacity; existing retrieval-based methods lack anatomical grounding, ignore disease progression, and fail to utilize clinical context.
AI.method: STAR3 uses an object detector to identify anatomical regions, retrieves semantically relevant report sentences conditioned on clinical context and temporal changes (prior vs. current chest X-ray studies), enabling spatio-temporal attentive retrieval.
AI.result: Outperforms current retrieval-based approaches on retrieval, NLP, and clinical metrics on the MIMIC-CXR dataset.
AI.conclusion: Anatomically, temporally, and clinically conditioned retrieval is valuable for advancing automated radiology report generation.

title: A Hippocampus for Linear Attention: An Exact Memory for What the Recurrent State Forgets
summary: Linear-attention and state-space language models compress the prefix into a fixed-size recurrent state, yielding O(1) memory at the cost of a lossy exact memory: when many key--value associations compete, earlier facts are overwritten and needle recall degrades. Inspired by Complementary Learning Systems, we give linear attention a hippocampal complement. HOLA (Hippocampal Linear Attention) keeps the usual delta-rule state as a compressive memory and adds a bounded exact KV cache, forming a semiparametric test-time memory: the state models linearly compressible structure, while the cache stores associations that should not be forced through that state. The cache writes without a learned eviction module, keeping tokens with large beta * ||e||, the prediction residual actually committed to the state; a decoupled RMSNorm-gamma cache read then turns these exact KV pairs into sharp retrieval rather than soft averaging. At 340M parameters trained on 15B SlimPajama tokens, HOLA lowers Wikitext perplexity from 27.32 to 22.92 (-16.1%), below a full-attention Transformer++ (26.88), and improves LAMBADA perplexity from 30.95 to 30.26. It also achieves the best linear in-context retrieval and remains much more robust than GDN or a matched HOLA+recency cache on RULER needle-in-a-haystack recall out to 32k tokens (16x its training length).

AI.tldr: HOLA augments linear-attention models with a bounded exact KV cache as a hippocampal complement, forming a semiparametric memory that preserves sharp retrieval of key associations while maintaining O(1) memory efficiency.
AI.motivation: Linear-attention and state-space models suffer from lossy exact memory due to compression of the prefix into a fixed-size recurrent state, causing degraded recall of earlier facts when many key-value associations compete (the "needle recall" problem).
AI.method: HOLA adds a bounded exact KV cache (hippocampal complement) to the usual delta-rule state (compressive memory). Cache writes are governed by the prediction residual (beta * ||e||) without a learned eviction module. Decoupled RMSNorm-gamma enables sharp retrieval from the cache rather than soft averaging.
AI.result: At 340M parameters trained on 15B tokens: Wikitext perplexity improved from 27.32 to 22.92 (-16.1%), below full-attention Transformer++ (26.88). LAMBADA perplexity improved from 30.95 to 30.26. Achieves best linear in-context retrieval and robust needle recall at 32k tokens (16x training length).
AI.conclusion: Complementary Learning Systems-inspired augmentation of linear attention with a hippocampal exact cache resolves the fundamental memory-compression trade-off, enabling both efficiency and precise long-range recall well beyond training length.

title: Beyond the Performance Illusion: Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning and Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization for Spatially Correlated Domains
summary: Performance evaluation in AI systems commonly assumes that random dataset splits produce independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) subsets. We show that this assumption often breaks down in spatiotemporally correlated domains such as aerial surveillance, precision agriculture, and medical imaging, leading to two systematic failures: data leakage, where correlated samples span training and validation splits and inflate performance estimates, and hidden stratification, where errors on minority subpopulations are obscured by aggregate metrics. To address these issues, we propose a unified evaluation and training framework for spatially correlated data. We introduce Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning (SASP), which constructs validation splits that reduce spatiotemporal leakage while preserving meaningful class balance, and Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization (CDRO), a curriculum-based relaxation of distributionally robust training that stabilizes optimization under these stricter splits. Across multiple benchmarks, this combination yields consistently improved generalization, more reliable confidence calibration, and exposes failure modes that remain hidden under conventional random-split evaluation.

AI.tldr: Random dataset splits often fail in spatiotemporally correlated domains (e.g., aerial surveillance, medical imaging) due to data leakage and hidden stratification. The paper proposes SASP for leakage-reduced splits and CDRO for robust training, improving generalization, calibration, and failure mode detection.
AI.motivation: Standard i.i.d. assumption of random dataset splits breaks down in spatiotemporally correlated domains, causing data leakage (inflated performance estimates) and hidden stratification (obscured errors on minority subpopulations).
AI.method: Two components: (1) Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning (SASP) — constructs validation splits that reduce spatiotemporal leakage while preserving class balance; (2) Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization (CDRO) — curriculum-based relaxation of distributionally robust training to stabilize optimization under stricter splits.
AI.result: Consistently improved generalization, more reliable confidence calibration, and exposure of failure modes hidden under conventional random-split evaluation across multiple benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The unified SASP + CDRO framework addresses systematic failures in spatiotemporally correlated domains, offering more trustworthy evaluation and training.

title: Evaluating Vision-Language Models as a Zero-Shot Learning Alternative to You Only Look Once and Optical Character Recognition for Nigerian License Plate Recognition
summary: License Plate Recognition (LPR) systems are critical tools in traffic monitoring, security enforcement, and urban mobility management. Traditional LPR systems often rely on a multi-stage pipeline involving object detection using You Only Look Once (YOLO) and Optical Character Recognition (OCR), which suffer from limitations such as high resource demands, poor performance in unstructured environments, and the need for large annotated datasets. This study explores the potential of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) as a unified, zeroshot learning solution for Nigerian license plate recognition. Using a curated dataset of 88 challenging real-world images collected in Nigeria, we evaluate five selected VLMs: Gemini 2.0 Flash Exp (Google DeepMind), Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct (Alibaba), GPT-4o (OpenAI), Claude 4 Sonnet (Anthropic), and Llama 3.2 Vision 90b (Meta). Results based on Character Error Rate (CER) reveal that Gemini and Qwen significantly outperform other models in both accuracy and robustness, on the challenging image scenarios. This work highlights the practical advantages of VLMs over YOLO+OCR, questions the claims by model providers, and compares the performances of the VLMs.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates five Vision-Language Models (VLMs) as a unified, zero-shot alternative to traditional YOLO+OCR pipelines for Nigerian license plate recognition, using a dataset of 88 challenging real-world images. Gemini 2.0 Flash Exp and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct significantly outperform other models in accuracy and robustness based on Character Error Rate.
AI.motivation: Traditional LPR systems using YOLO+OCR pipelines suffer from high resource demands, poor performance in unstructured environments, and require large annotated datasets. This study explores VLMs as a zero-shot learning solution to address these limitations, specifically for Nigerian license plate recognition where annotated data is scarce and image conditions are challenging.
AI.method: A curated dataset of 88 challenging real-world Nigerian license plate images was collected. Five VLMs (Gemini 2.0 Flash Exp, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, GPT-4o, Claude 4 Sonnet, Llama 3.2 Vision 90b) were evaluated in a zero-shot setting. Performance was measured using Character Error Rate (CER).
AI.result: Gemini 2.0 Flash Exp and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct significantly outperformed GPT-4o, Claude 4 Sonnet, and Llama 3.2 Vision 90b in both accuracy and robustness across challenging image scenarios.
AI.conclusion: VLMs demonstrate practical advantages over traditional YOLO+OCR approaches for LPR, particularly in zero-shot scenarios with challenging real-world data. The results also question the performance claims made by model providers.

title: Grounded autonomous research: a fault-tolerant LLM pipeline from corpus to manuscript in frontier computational physics
comment: 39 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at the ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop (https://openreview.net/forum?id=R5YXaPgUAx). Includes the pipeline-generated companion physics manuscript as an appendix. Data and scaffolding archive: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21126996
summary: Autonomous-research agents have demonstrated end-to-end LLM automation in machine-learning sandboxes where execution provides calibration. Frontier physical science differs categorically: physical reasoning underlies every methodology choice, toolchains are often underdocumented, and calibration must come from external literature anchors - which unscaffolded agents cite but do not confront, hallucinating plausible, unverifiable results from internal priors. We present a pipeline that runs end-to-end from a corpus of 11,083 recent condensed-matter physics arXiv papers to a publication-grade manuscript with three substantive physics findings (here on altermagnetic piezomagnetism): the agent autonomously conceives a research direction by mapping the corpus, calibrates methodology by reproducing published references, conducts novel first-principles computations, and writes the manuscript - grounded in literature throughout, across 47 fresh-context sessions in six phases sharing only on-disk state, with 2,162 literature-consultation events. Fault tolerance emerges from redundancy: fresh-context isolation, distributed grounding, and adversarial review catch what any single session misses; pre- and post-pilot stages are fully autonomous, and pilot requires bounded human intervention only at reproduction failures - operational knowledge curation, not scientific direction. Two paired failure modes - a pre-architecture baseline and a no-pilot ablation - isolate structurally enforced numerical confrontation at calibration checkpoints as the operative grounding mechanism. The primitives, characterized failure modes, and quantified intervention pattern lay a foundation for autonomous research in high-stakes scientific domains beyond computational physics.

AI.tldr: A multi-phase autonomous research pipeline that, starting from an 11,083-paper arXiv corpus, produces a publication-grade manuscript with three novel physics findings on altermagnetic piezomagnetism, using literature-anchored calibration, 47 fresh-context sessions, and adversarial review for fault tolerance, with bounded human intervention only at reproduction failures.
AI.motivation: Frontier physical science differs from ML sandboxes because physical reasoning underlies every methodology choice, toolchains are underdocumented, and calibration must come from external literature anchors rather than execution feedback. Unscaffolded agents hallucinate unverifiable results; thus a structurally enforced grounding mechanism is needed.
AI.method: A pipeline with six phases (corpus mapping, methodology calibration via reproduction of published references, novel first-principles computations, manuscript writing) across 47 fresh-context sessions with shared on-disk state and 2,162 literature-consultation events. Fault tolerance via redundancy: fresh-context isolation, distributed grounding, adversarial review. Pre- and post-pilot phases fully autonomous; pilot requires bounded human intervention only at reproduction failures for operational knowledge curation. Ablations (pre-architecture baseline, no-pilot) isolate the grounding mechanism.
AI.result: The agent autonomously conceives research direction, calibrates methodology, conducts novel computations, and writes a publication-grade manuscript with three substantive physics findings on altermagnetic piezomagnetism.
AI.conclusion: The primitives, characterized failure modes, and quantified intervention pattern lay a foundation for autonomous research in high-stakes scientific domains beyond computational physics.
