title: SA-HGNN: Sample-Adaptive Hyperbolic Graph Neural Network for EEG-Based Depression Recognition
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been widely used to capture spatial functional connectivity patterns to improve electroencephalography (EEG)-based depression recognition performance. However, the functional connectivity of brain networks in patients with depression exhibits an inherent hierarchical structure, making it difficult to capture accurate connection patterns. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel model named Sample-Adaptive Hyperbolic Graph Neural Network (SA-HGNN), which aims to accurately extract the authentic hierarchical structure of depression-affected brain networks. Specifically, the proposed model comprises three core modules. First, a Sample-Adaptive Graph Construction module dynamically constructs personalized brain network topologies to capture more complex spatial relationships within the brain network. Second, hyperbolic graph convolution is employed to overcome the representation bottlenecks of Euclidean space, leveraging hyperbolic geometry to precisely capture latent hierarchical relationships within the brain network. Finally, an Attention Pooling module adaptively filters out highly redundant noise channels in EEG signals, effectively mitigating the interference of inherent noise on the authentic hierarchical topology. Extensive experiments on public EEG datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our method across resting-state and task-related paradigms, validating its robustness to noise and efficacy in capturing abnormal functional connectivity patterns in brain networks of patients with depression.

AI.tldr: SA-HGNN dynamically constructs personalized brain network topologies, uses hyperbolic graph convolution to capture hierarchical structures, and employs attention pooling to filter noise, achieving superior depression recognition from EEG data.
AI.motivation: Depression-affected brain networks exhibit an inherent hierarchical structure that is difficult to capture with standard GNNs in Euclidean space, limiting accurate EEG-based depression recognition.
AI.method: The model includes three modules: (1) Sample-Adaptive Graph Construction for personalized brain network topologies, (2) Hyperbolic Graph Convolution to capture hierarchical relationships using hyperbolic geometry, and (3) Attention Pooling to filter noisy EEG channels.
AI.result: Superior performance on public EEG datasets across resting-state and task-related paradigms; robustness to noise and efficacy in capturing abnormal functional connectivity patterns in depression.
AI.conclusion: SA-HGNN effectively addresses hierarchical structure extraction in depressed brain networks, outperforming existing methods and demonstrating noise robustness.

title: ComplexMimic: Human-Scene Interaction Imitation in Complex 3D Environments
summary: Physics-based Human-Scene Interaction (HSI) imitation learning is crucial for embodied intelligence as it bridges the gap between kinematic 3D motions and real-world dynamics. However, most existing methods focus on simplified scene settings, leaving complex environments largely unexplored, which limits their applicability in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we focus on HSI mimicry in complex environments. Under this complex setting, we observe an inherent trade-off between successfully performing interaction and maintaining natural, physically plausible motions. To address this challenge, we propose ComplexMimic, a framework that reconstructs diverse HSI by interpreting imperfect MoCap data. First, we introduce a Dual Flow Strategy, which learns two complementary experts: an imitation expert for accurate motion tracking and an interaction expert for collision-aware adaptation in complex scenes. Second, naive multi-expert distillation, which treats all experts equally, often under-samples challenging behaviors, limiting effective learning. To mitigate this issue, we propose a difficulty-aware distillation strategy that adaptively weights supervision and prioritizes hard-yet-learnable trajectories guided by failure statistics and learning progress signals. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/LuPan23/ComplexMimic.

AI.tldr: ComplexMimic is a framework for physics-based human-scene interaction imitation learning in complex environments. It uses a Dual Flow Strategy with complementary experts (imitation for tracking, interaction for collision avoidance) and a difficulty-aware distillation strategy to prioritize hard trajectories. It outperforms SOTA on three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing HSI imitation learning methods focus on simplified scenes, limiting real-world applicability. The key challenge is the inherent trade-off between performing accurate interaction and maintaining natural, physically plausible motions in complex environments.
AI.method: ComplexMimic introduces: 1) Dual Flow Strategy with two experts—an imitation expert for motion tracking and an interaction expert for collision-aware adaptation; 2) Difficulty-aware distillation strategy that adaptively weights supervision based on failure statistics and learning progress, prioritizing hard-yet-learnable trajectories over naive equal-weight multi-expert distillation.
AI.result: Outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on three benchmark datasets for physics-based HSI imitation in complex environments.
AI.conclusion: The dual-expert framework with difficulty-aware distillation effectively addresses the interaction-plausibility trade-off in complex HSI scenarios, and the approach generalizes well across multiple benchmarks.

title: DRIFTLENS: Measuring Memory-Induced Reasoning Drift in Personalized Language Models
summary: Personalization changes what a model says to a user; we show that it can also change the reasoning trajectory used to justify the response. Modern LLMs personalize interactions by storing user attributes, preferences, and prior context, then injecting this information into future prompts. We study whether such memory reshapes reasoning on open-ended questions where no single ground-truth answer exists. To quantify this effect, we introduce DRIFTLENS, a ground-truth-free framework that maps each expressed reasoning step to a value category and measures divergence between a question's no-memory trajectory and its trajectory under injected user-attribute memory. We first validate that DRIFTLENS distinguishes content-free pragmatic noise from substantive reasoning changes. Across four LLMs and 10 user-attribute categories, including age, occupation, and disability, user-attribute memory induces medium-to-large reasoning drift above each model's pragmatic-noise floor, even when final answers remain fluent, on-topic, and plausible. We then evaluate GRPO- and DPO-based post-training methods for reducing drift. Both reduce drift, but neither uniformly dominates; effects on downstream capability, helpfulness, and instruction following are model-and reward-dependent. These results suggest that memory-induced reasoning drift is a measurable and only partly mitigated failure mode of personalized language models.

AI.tldr: DRIFTLENS quantifies how user-attribute memory shifts LLM reasoning trajectories (not just final answers), and shows that current post-training methods only partly mitigate this drift.
AI.motivation: Prior work focuses on how personalization changes model outputs (what the model says), but overlooks whether it alters the underlying reasoning process. Understanding this is critical for reliability and fairness in personalized LLMs.
AI.method: Introduces DRIFTLENS, a ground-truth-free framework that maps reasoning steps to value categories and measures divergence between no-memory and memory-injected trajectories. Validated against pragmatic noise, then applied across 4 LLMs and 10 user-attribute categories (age, occupation, disability, etc.). Evaluates GRPO and DPO post-training for drift reduction.
AI.result: User-attribute memory causes medium-to-large reasoning drift above pragmatic-noise floors across all models and attributes, even when final answers remain fluent and plausible. GRPO and DPO both reduce drift but neither dominates; downstream capability trade-offs are model- and reward-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Memory-induced reasoning drift is a measurable and only partially mitigated failure mode of personalized LLMs, highlighting a gap that existing alignment methods do not fully close.

title: kNNGuard: Turning LLM Hidden Activations into a Training-Free Configurable Guardrail
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in domains requiring guardrails to detect unsafe, off-topic, or adversarial prompts. Existing guardrails predominately rely on fine-tuning to build classifiers, which often suffer from low generalization and high inference latency. We present kNNGuard, a training-free guardrail that utilizes the activation space of an off-the-shelf LLM. Given a small bank of 50 safe and unsafe prompts, kNNGuard extracts hidden activations and performs multi-layer kNN fusing activation-space and embedding-space scores for classification. Across six domains spanning topical and security prompts, kNNGuard achieves competitive or superior F1 compared to fine-tuned state-of-the-art guardrails while running 2.7x faster than the best comparable guardrail, and 10x faster than a fine-tuned safety classifier without gradient updates or fine-tuning. Domain adaptation requires only updating the labeled bank, which can be constructed in under 10 seconds and several orders of magnitude faster than established guardrails. We also analyze the impact of system prompts, layer selection, and integration into production LLM pipelines as a configurable, low-latency guardrail.

AI.tldr: kNNGuard is a training-free guardrail for LLMs that uses activation-space and embedding-space kNN on a small labeled bank (50 prompts) to achieve competitive F1 scores, 2.7x-10x faster inference, and near-instant domain adaptation compared to fine-tuned guardrails.
AI.motivation: Existing guardrails rely on fine-tuning classifiers that suffer from low generalization and high inference latency; there is a need for a training-free, low-latency, and easily adaptable guardrail.
AI.method: kNNGuard extracts hidden activations from an off-the-shelf LLM for a small labeled bank of 50 prompts, then performs multi-layer kNN that fuses activation-space and embedding-space scores for classification.
AI.result: Achieves competitive or superior F1 compared to fine-tuned SOTA guardrails across six domains; runs 2.7x faster than the best comparable guardrail and 10x faster than fine-tuned classifiers; domain adaptation requires constructing a labeled bank in under 10 seconds.
AI.conclusion: kNNGuard offers a training-free, low-latency, and configurable alternative for LLM guardrails with efficient domain adaptation, suitable for integration into production pipelines.

title: Hierarchical Anti-Aesthetics: Protecting Facial Privacy against Customized Diffusion Models
summary: The rise of customized diffusion models has fueled a boom in personalized visual content creation, but it also introduces serious risks of malicious misuse, thereby posing threats to personal privacy. Image aesthetics are strongly correlated with human perception of image quality. Motivated by this observation, we address facial privacy protection from a novel aesthetic perspective by degrading the generation quality of maliciously customized models, thus reducing facial identity leakage. Specifically, we propose a Hierarchical Anti-Aesthetics (HAA) framework that exploits aesthetic cues at multiple perceptual levels. HAA consists of two key branches: (1) Global Anti-Aesthetics, which degrades overall aesthetics and generation quality by constructing a global anti-aesthetic reward mechanism and a corresponding loss; and (2) Local Anti-Aesthetics, which disrupts facial identity by using a local anti-aesthetic reward mechanism and loss to guide adversarial perturbations toward facial regions. By integrating both branches, HAA achieves anti-aesthetic degradation from a global to a local level during customized generation. Extensive experiments show that HAA outperforms existing methods in identity removal, providing an effective tool for protecting facial privacy.

AI.tldr: HAA is a facial privacy protection framework that uses anti-aesthetic perturbations at global and local levels to degrade the generation quality of customized diffusion models, thereby preventing facial identity leakage.
AI.motivation: The rise of customized diffusion models enables personalized visual content creation but introduces risks of malicious misuse and threats to personal privacy. Image aesthetics strongly correlate with perceived image quality, motivating the authors to protect facial privacy by degrading generation quality from an aesthetic perspective.
AI.method: HAA (Hierarchical Anti-Aesthetics) framework with two branches: (1) Global Anti-Aesthetics — uses a global anti-aesthetic reward mechanism and loss to degrade overall aesthetics and generation quality; (2) Local Anti-Aesthetics — uses a local anti-aesthetic reward mechanism and loss to disrupt facial identity by guiding adversarial perturbations toward facial regions. Both branches are integrated for global-to-local anti-aesthetic degradation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show HAA outperforms existing methods in identity removal, providing an effective tool for protecting facial privacy.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting aesthetic cues at multiple perceptual levels is an effective novel approach for facial privacy protection against maliciously customized diffusion models.

title: Hardware-Enforced Semantic Coordination for Safety-Critical Real-Time Autonomous Systems
summary:
Recent advances in agentic AI are producing increasingly complex autonomous systems that integrate large language models, world models, optimization engines, specialized neural architectures, autonomous platforms, and human operators. While much current research focuses on improving reasoning capabilities, safety-critical real-time deployment also requires bounded and verifiable coordination among heterogeneous components operating concurrently under uncertainty. Software-mediated coordination presents fundamental limitations in domains where bounded latency, deterministic coordination, and enforceable safety guarantees are essential.
  Hence, we propose a hardware-enforced semantic coordination architecture in which selected coordination semantics are implemented directly at the hardware level via field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). The approach builds on the Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Net (TB-CSPN) framework, which separates semantic reasoning from interaction management.
  In this approach, selected TB-CSPN coordination mechanisms are mapped onto FPGA primitives, creating a hardware-native semantic coordination layer. Focus is not on acceleration, but on enforcing temporal synchronization, semantic gating, authorization constraints, and bounded coordination behavior directly in hardware. Semantic reasoning remains adaptive and software-driven, while embedded coordination semantics become deterministic.

AI.tldr: Proposes a hardware-enforced semantic coordination architecture using FPGAs to implement TB-CSPN coordination mechanisms directly in hardware, ensuring deterministic and bounded coordination for safety-critical real-time multi-agent AI systems, while keeping semantic reasoning adaptive in software.
AI.motivation: Safety-critical real-time deployment of increasingly complex autonomous agentic AI systems requires bounded latency, deterministic coordination, and enforceable safety guarantees, which software-mediated coordination cannot reliably provide under uncertainty and concurrency.
AI.method: Maps selected TB-CSPN (Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Net) coordination mechanisms onto FPGA primitives, creating a hardware-native semantic coordination layer that enforces temporal synchronization, semantic gating, authorization constraints, and bounded coordination behavior directly in hardware, while leaving semantic reasoning adaptive in software.
AI.result: A hardware-enforced semantic coordination architecture where coordination semantics become deterministic and bounded, without focusing on acceleration, achieving enforceable safety guarantees through FPGA-level implementation.
AI.conclusion: This approach addresses fundamental limitations of software-mediated coordination in heterogeneous multi-agent systems by embedding coordination semantics directly in hardware, offering a path toward verifiable, bounded, and deterministic coordination for safety-critical autonomous AI deployments.

title: Fourier Neural Operators for Rayleigh-Bénard Convection
summary: We propose an improved Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) for modeling two-dimensional Rayleigh-Bénard convection by predicting time increments instead of full solutions, achieving higher accuracy than a standard FNO baseline. The resulting model is compact (314k parameters, 1.26 MB) and fast (7 ms inference), while maintaining similar accuracy as demonstrated in previous benchmarks. We show that although FNOs generalize to finer meshes, accuracy remains limited by the resolution of the training data.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an improved Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) for modeling 2D Rayleigh-Bénard convection by predicting time increments rather than full solutions, resulting in a compact (314k parameters, 1.26 MB) and fast (7 ms inference) model with higher accuracy than standard FNO. It also shows that while FNOs generalize to finer meshes, accuracy is limited by training data resolution.
AI.motivation: To improve the accuracy and efficiency of Fourier Neural Operators for modeling Rayleigh-Bénard convection, a canonical fluid dynamics problem, by addressing limitations in standard FNO approaches.
AI.method: The improved FNO predicts time increments (residuals) instead of full solution fields at each time step, maintaining a compact architecture (314k parameters) and enabling fast inference (7 ms).
AI.result: The model achieves higher accuracy than a standard FNO baseline, with compact size (1.26 MB) and fast inference speed (7 ms). FNOs generalize to finer meshes but accuracy is bounded by training data resolution.
AI.conclusion: Predicting time increments is an effective strategy for improving FNO performance on convective flow problems. The approach yields practical advantages in model size and inference speed without sacrificing accuracy. Resolution of training data remains a fundamental limitation for generalization.

title: PWM-ArtGen: Part World Model for Articulated Object Generation
summary: The key challenge in articulated 3D object generation from a single image is accurately predicting the underlying kinematic structure. Existing methods either infer kinematic parameters directly from a static image that lacks dynamic part-level kinematic relationships, or estimate parameters from visual dynamics generated from a single image, which is prone to accumulated errors of two steps. Moreover, the limited scale and diversity of existing annotated datasets further hinder generalization to complex, real-world objects. To overcome these limitations, we propose to learn the joint distribution of visual dynamics and kinematic parameters. Recognizing that articulated objects can be formulated as dynamic systems, we propose a unified Part World Model called PWM-ArtGen. To leverage unannotated data, this model couples action diffusion and image diffusion with independent diffusion timesteps, which enables visual branch co-training. We further curate a photorealistic dataset of 19.7k part-level image pairs without kinematic annotations, to support co-training. Experiments demonstrate that PWM-ArtGen substantially outperforms existing baselines in the resting state and exhibits strong zero-shot generalization to out-of-distribution objects.

AI.tldr: PWM-ArtGen is a unified Part World Model that learns joint distribution of visual dynamics and kinematic parameters for articulated 3D object generation from a single image, using coupled action and image diffusion with co-training on unannotated data, achieving strong zero-shot generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing methods struggle with accurately predicting kinematic structures from single images due to: (1) inability to capture dynamic part-level relationships from static images, (2) accumulated errors from two-step estimation approaches, and (3) limited scale and diversity of annotated datasets hindering generalization to complex real-world objects.
AI.method: Proposes PWM-ArtGen, a unified Part World Model that treats articulated objects as dynamic systems and learns joint distribution of visual dynamics and kinematic parameters. Uses coupled action diffusion and image diffusion with independent timesteps for visual branch co-training. Curates a 19.7k photorealistic dataset of part-level image pairs without kinematic annotations.
AI.result: Substantially outperforms existing baselines in resting state and exhibits strong zero-shot generalization to out-of-distribution objects.
AI.conclusion: Learning joint distribution of visual dynamics and kinematic parameters via a world model, combined with co-training on unannotated data, effectively addresses key challenges in articulated 3D object generation from single images.

title: Ask the Right Comparison:Bias-Aware Bayesian Active Top-$k$ Ranking with LLM Judges
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as cheap, scalable judges that compare candidate outputs pairwise -- to rank responses, select models, or triage papers. Yet LLM judges are both noisy and systematically biased: they favor verbose or well-formatted answers and exhibit position effects, so simply aggregating their votes recovers a ranking of presentation, not of true quality. We study the practical goal of identifying the \topk{} items under a fixed comparison budget, and make two contributions. First, we cast judging as Bayesian inference over latent quality with explicit, judge-specific bias covariates (verbosity, position), regularized by a shrinkage prior so that the data decide which biases a given judge actually exhibits. Second, we introduce a \topk-aware active acquisition rule that chooses the next comparison to maximally reduce uncertainty about \topk{} \emph{membership}, rather than about the full ranking. On a controlled benchmark with known ground-truth quality, judged by sixteen real LLMs spanning open and proprietary families (Llama, Qwen, Phi-4, GPT-4o-mini/5.1/5.5, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Claude Haiku/Sonnet/Opus), naive aggregation plateaus at a wrong \topk{} on biased judges regardless of budget, while our bias-aware model recovers it; \topk-aware acquisition reaches this ceiling with far fewer comparisons than round-robin or a global-uncertainty (D-optimal) rule. Bias is real but heterogeneous and capability-dependent: cheap and mid-tier judges carry a strong verbosity bias that our model corrects (lifting recall from $\sim$$0.5$--$0.6$ to $0.84$--$1.0$), whereas the frontier judges we tested show little bias and already rank accurately, so bias-aware modeling changes little there.

AI.tldr: LLM judges are biased (verbosity, position), so naive aggregation fails at top-k identification. The paper proposes Bayesian inference with bias covariates and a top-k-aware active acquisition rule, which recovers correct rankings with fewer comparisons, especially for biased weak/medium judges.
AI.motivation: LLMs are used as cheap judges for pairwise comparisons but exhibit systematic biases (verbosity, formatting, position effects). Aggregating biased votes yields rankings of presentation rather than true quality, motivating a need for bias-aware, sample-efficient top-k identification.
AI.method: (1) Bayesian inference over latent quality with explicit judge-specific bias covariates (verbosity, position), regularized by shrinkage priors. (2) A top-k-aware active acquisition rule that selects comparisons to maximize uncertainty reduction about top-k membership rather than full ranking.
AI.result: On a benchmark with 16 LLMs (Llama, Qwen, Phi-4, GPT-4o, Gemini, DeepSeek, Claude), naive aggregation plateaus at wrong top-k under biased judges. The bias-aware model recovers correct top-k; top-k-aware acquisition achieves this with far fewer comparisons than round-robin or D-optimal rules. Verbosity bias is strong in cheap/mid-tier judges (recall 0.5–0.6 → 0.84–1.0), but frontier judges show little bias.
AI.conclusion: Bias in LLM judges is real and heterogeneous; cheap/mid-tier judges require bias correction, while frontier judges are already accurate. The proposed Bayesian model with top-k-aware acquisition is effective for practical, budget-constrained top-k identification.

title: Embracing Intra-Class Heterogeneity for Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation: From Diversity to Precision
summary: Due to the scarcity of expert-annotated data, Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation (SSMIS) has emerged as a promising approach. Many anatomical structures in medical images exhibit significant intra-class heterogeneity, with different regions showing heterogeneous intensity patterns within the same structure. However, existing methods inadequately exploit this intensity-manifested intra-class heterogeneity, resulting in uniform structural representations and imprecise segmentation. Furthermore, the scarcity of labeled data makes it more difficult to effectively capture such complex heterogeneity. To address this, we propose Multiple Prototype Contrastive Learning (MPCL), an SSMIS framework that possesses better diversity and better precision. It consists of three novel designs: First, we provide structural representations with better diversity and propose Intensity-aligned Heterogeneous Prototype Generation (IHPG) that effectively models intra-class heterogeneity by generating multiple prototypes aligned with intensity characteristics. Second, we further enhance more diverse structural representations and build a solid foundation for more precise segmentation through Prototypical Space Optimization (PSO) that systematically optimizes a more discriminative and generalizable prototypical space. Finally, we achieve segmentation results with better precision through Dual-branch Knowledge Alignment (DKA) that efficiently promotes intra-class heterogeneity knowledge transfer from prototypical space to the segmentation network. Extensive experiments on three medical image datasets with significant intra-class heterogeneity demonstrate that MPCL significantly outperforms existing methods, especially under extremely limited labeled data.

AI.tldr: MPCL proposes a semi-supervised medical image segmentation framework using multiple prototype contrastive learning that models intra-class heterogeneity through intensity-aligned prototype generation, prototypical space optimization, and dual-branch knowledge alignment, outperforming existing methods on datasets with significant heterogeneity.
AI.motivation: Existing SSMIS methods inadequately exploit intensity-manifested intra-class heterogeneity in anatomical structures, leading to uniform structural representations and imprecise segmentation; the scarcity of labeled data further compounds this challenge.
AI.method: Three components: (1) Intensity-aligned Heterogeneous Prototype Generation (IHPG) models intra-class heterogeneity via multiple intensity-aligned prototypes; (2) Prototypical Space Optimization (PSO) creates a discriminative and generalizable prototypical space; (3) Dual-branch Knowledge Alignment (DKA) transfers intra-class heterogeneity knowledge from the prototypical space to the segmentation network.
AI.result: MPCL significantly outperforms existing methods on three medical image datasets with significant intra-class heterogeneity, especially under extremely limited labeled data.
AI.conclusion: Modeling intra-class heterogeneity via multiple prototypes and contrastive learning is an effective strategy for SSMIS, achieving both better diversity and precision in structural representations.

title: Fast Multi-dimensional Refusal Subspaces via RFM-AGOP
comment: Accepted to the Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea, 2026
summary: Steering and monitoring activations in Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for both safety and interpretability. Early work assumed behaviours are encoded along single linear directions, but recent findings suggest complex behaviours, such as the refusal to answer harmful queries, live in multi-dimensional subspaces. However, existing methods for extracting these subspaces are computationally expensive, which becomes prohibitive on reasoning models who produce long reasoning traces. By adapting the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm -- which can be computed efficiently -- with a probe-informed initialization, we are able to identify the multi-dimensional refusal subspace in seconds, on reasoning (Qwen 3) and non-reasoning (Qwen 2.5) models. While RFM allows for faster subspace identification, it also showed better performances on the ablation task than its alternatives. More work is planned to better understand the relations between subspaces found by different methods. If confirmed, RFM could be a cheap and scalable complement to existing subspace-extraction methods in LLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm with probe-informed initialization to efficiently identify multi-dimensional refusal subspaces in LLMs (including reasoning models like Qwen 3), achieving faster and better performance on ablation tasks compared to existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for extracting multi-dimensional behavioral subspaces (e.g., refusal direction) in LLMs are computationally expensive, especially for reasoning models with long reasoning traces.
AI.method: Adapts the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm with a probe-informed initialization to efficiently identify multi-dimensional refusal subspaces.
AI.result: RFM identifies refusal subspaces in seconds on both reasoning (Qwen 3) and non-reasoning (Qwen 2.5) models, and outperforms alternative methods on ablation tasks.
AI.conclusion: RFM could serve as a cheap and scalable complement to existing subspace-extraction methods for LLMs, with further work planned to understand relations between subspaces found by different methods.

title: Predictive Conformal Slip Monitoring: An Empirical Evaluation of Rolling Split Conformal Prediction for Pre-Incident Traction Loss Detection
comment: 10 pages, 4 tables. codes and data available at:https://github.com/nearpot/predictive-conformal-slip-monitoring
summary: Conventional traction control architectures intervene only after the adhesion limit of a tire has already been breached. This paper investigates whether Rolling Split Conformal Prediction , monitoring the volatility of non-conformity residuals from a per-driver Random Forest model of expected slip behavior , can serve as a statistically grounded pre-incident warning signal, ahead of gross traction loss. Unlike an earlier internal draft of this work, the evaluation reported here corrects a confound in the slip proxy (vehicle speed is included as an explicit model feature, not left implicit in the target's denominator), uses every racing lap for each driver rather than only the fastest lap, and is scored against real, timestamped incident labels extracted from FIA Race Control Messages and track-limits lap deletions rather than narrated post-hoc. The result is negative: across 19 drivers and 55,563 test-phase telemetry samples, the rolling-volatility detector achieves a mean precision of essentially 0.0 and mean recall of 0.0 against 14 ground-truth incidents, while flagging on average 15.3% of all samples as anomalous , too high a false-alarm rate for any early-warning use. A static 95th-percentile threshold baseline performs no better in any way that would justify the added complexity of the conformal-volatility formulation. Residual autocorrelation diagnostics show the split-conformal exchangeability assumption is violated for every driver (Ljung-Box p < 0.001, n = 19/19), which is one plausible driver of the high false-alarm rate. We report this as a methodologically rigorous negative finding, diagnose its likely causes, and outline what a genuinely predictive version of this approach would require.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether Rolling Split Conformal Prediction on residuals from a per-driver Random Forest slip model can serve as a pre-incident traction loss warning. Results are negative: precision and recall are essentially 0.0, false-alarm rate is 15.3%, and the exchangeability assumption is violated for all 19 drivers. The paper reports a methodologically rigorous negative finding with diagnosed causes.
AI.motivation: Conventional traction control only intervenes after adhesion limit is breached. The authors investigate whether a statistically grounded pre-incident warning signal could be generated ahead of gross traction loss using conformal prediction on slip behavior residuals.
AI.method: Rolling Split Conformal Prediction monitors volatility of non-conformity residuals from per-driver Random Forest models of expected slip. The corrected evaluation includes vehicle speed as an explicit feature, uses all racing laps per driver, and scores against real FIA Race Control incident labels. Tested on 19 drivers, 55,563 telemetry samples, 14 ground-truth incidents.
AI.result: Mean precision ≈ 0.0, mean recall ≈ 0.0 against 14 incidents; 15.3% of all samples flagged as anomalous. Static 95th-percentile threshold performs no better. Ljung-Box test shows residual autocorrelation for all 19 drivers (p < 0.001), violating the exchangeability assumption of split conformal prediction.
AI.conclusion: The conformal-volatility approach fails as a pre-incident warning due to exchangeability violations and high false-alarm rates. The paper provides a methodologically rigorous negative finding and outlines requirements for a genuinely predictive version.

title: Comprehensive Robustness Analysis of LiDAR-based 3D Object Detection in Autonomous Driving
summary: Recent advancements in LiDAR-only 3D object detection have demonstrated improved detection accuracy over benchmark datasets. However, the adversarial robustness of these models remains untested. Very few adversarial robustness studies exist for LiDAR-only 3D object detection and unfortunately, even they are limited to legacy models. Moreover, there is a systemic gap in the existing evaluation frameworks that rely simply on mAP ignoring other structural and predictive factors. To fill this gap, we propose a holistic framework that evaluates adversarial robustness using two structural factors (point cloud density and point cloud localization) and three predictive factors (misclassification, localization error, distance from ego). Using this framework, we perform an empirical study and critical analysis on recent and legacy state-of-the-art models using adversarial attacks specifically designed for LiDAR-based models. Our key finding is that high-capacity, voxel-based detectors are more susceptible to structured coordinate perturbations than pillar-based detectors. Additionally, non-anchor-based detectors demonstrate poor adversarial robustness, which necessitates rethinking model training techniques. Overall, our results demonstrate that recent models are as vulnerable to adversarial attacks as their predecessors. Therefore, we argue that there is a need to improve the evaluation benchmarks for 3D object detection that not only reward architectural modifications for improving detection accuracy, but also evaluate whether the design choices improve adversarial robustness.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a holistic framework for evaluating adversarial robustness in LiDAR-only 3D object detection, considering structural factors (point cloud density, localization) and predictive factors (misclassification, localization error, distance from ego). Empirical analysis reveals that high-capacity voxel-based detectors are more susceptible to structured perturbations than pillar-based detectors, non-anchor-based detectors show poor robustness, and recent models remain as vulnerable as legacy models.
AI.motivation: Existing adversarial robustness studies for LiDAR-only 3D detection are limited to legacy models, and current evaluation frameworks rely solely on mAP, ignoring structural and predictive factors. The authors aim to fill this gap with a more comprehensive evaluation framework.
AI.method: The authors propose a holistic evaluation framework incorporating two structural factors (point cloud density, point cloud localization) and three predictive factors (misclassification, localization error, distance from ego). They conduct empirical studies on recent and legacy state-of-the-art models using adversarial attacks designed for LiDAR-based models.
AI.result: (1) High-capacity, voxel-based detectors are more susceptible to structured coordinate perturbations than pillar-based detectors. (2) Non-anchor-based detectors exhibit poor adversarial robustness. (3) Recent models are as vulnerable to adversarial attacks as legacy predecessors.
AI.conclusion: There is a need to improve evaluation benchmarks for 3D object detection to reward architectural modifications that improve not only detection accuracy but also adversarial robustness.

title: Text-Driven 3D Indoor Scene Synthesis in Non-Manhattan Environments
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in 3D indoor synthesis for Manhattan environments. However, existing methods often fail to capture plausible object layout patterns in non-Manhattan settings, primarily because they struggle to model non-orthogonal spatial relationships, leading to high geometric violations and low physical fidelity. To address this challenge, we propose SPG-Layout, a novel text-driven framework designed to generate physically plausible indoor scenes within complex non-Manhattan environments. Specifically, we first utilize statistical priors of object distributions to guide the training process, enhancing environmental understanding and fidelity. Furthermore, mirroring human design workflows, we adopt a hierarchical layout strategy that prioritizes the placement of large objects, thereby substantially minimizing layout violations. By synergizing these components, SPG-Layout achieves a balanced optimization of semantic realism and physical plausibility. To evaluate performance in these complex settings, we constructed a new benchmark comprising 500 diverse non-Manhattan environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPG-Layout consistently and significantly outperforms existing methods across both Manhattan and non-Manhattan environments. The code will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: SPG-Layout is a text-driven framework for generating physically plausible 3D indoor scenes in non-Manhattan environments, using statistical priors and a hierarchical layout strategy to reduce geometric violations and outperform existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based 3D indoor synthesis methods fail to capture plausible object layout patterns in non-Manhattan environments, struggling with non-orthogonal spatial relationships, which leads to high geometric violations and low physical fidelity.
AI.method: (1) Statistical priors of object distributions guide training for better environmental understanding. (2) A hierarchical layout strategy prioritizes large object placement, mimicking human design workflows to minimize layout violations. (3) Synergistic optimization balances semantic realism and physical plausibility.
AI.result: SPG-Layout consistently and significantly outperforms existing methods on both Manhattan and non-Manhattan environments, validated on a new benchmark of 500 diverse non-Manhattan environments.
AI.conclusion: SPG-Layout effectively addresses non-Manhattan indoor scene generation by combining statistical priors and hierarchical layout strategies, achieving balanced semantic and physical fidelity.

title: ART for Diffusion Sampling: Continuous-Time Control and Actor-Critic Learning
summary: We study timestep allocation for score-based diffusion sampling, where a learned reverse-time dynamics is discretized on a finite grid. Uniform and hand-crafted schedules are standard choices, but they rely on fixed prescriptions and can therefore be suboptimal. To address this limitation, we propose Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a continuous-time control formulation that learns a time change by treating the speed of the sampling clock as the control, so that a uniform grid on the learned clock induces adaptive timesteps in the original diffusion time. Based on a leading-order Euler error surrogate, ART provides a principled objective for allocating timesteps along the sampling trajectory. To solve this deterministic control problem, we introduce ART-RL, an auxiliary randomized formulation with Gaussian policies that turns schedule learning into a continuous-time reinforcement learning problem. We prove that the randomized ART-RL formulation is equivalent to ART at the optimizer level, in the sense that its optimal Gaussian policy recovers the optimal ART time-warping rate through its mean. We further establish policy evaluation and policy improvement characterizations and derive trajectory-based moment identities that yield implementable actor--critic updates for learning the schedule. Across experiments ranging from controlled low-dimensional settings to image generation, ART-RL can be plugged into existing diffusion samplers by changing only the timestep grid, consistently improving sample quality over strong baseline schedules at matched budgets while leaving the rest of the sampling pipeline unchanged. The learned schedules also exhibit broad generalization, transferring without retraining across sampling budgets, datasets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces.

AI.tldr: ART-RL learns adaptive timestep schedules for score-based diffusion sampling by treating schedule learning as a continuous-time reinforcement learning problem, improving sample quality over fixed schedules while generalizing across budgets, datasets, and solvers.
AI.motivation: Uniform and hand-crafted timestep schedules for score-based diffusion sampling are fixed prescriptions and can be suboptimal; the paper aims to learn adaptive timestep allocation to improve sampling quality.
AI.method: Proposes Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a continuous-time control formulation that learns a time change by treating the speed of the sampling clock as the control. Introduces ART-RL, an auxiliary randomized formulation with Gaussian policies that turns schedule learning into a continuous-time RL problem, with actor-critic updates derived from trajectory-based moment identities.
AI.result: ART-RL consistently improves sample quality over strong baseline schedules at matched budgets across low-dimensional settings and image generation. Learned schedules generalize across sampling budgets, datasets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive timestep allocation via ART-RL is a principled, effective, and plug-and-play approach that enhances existing diffusion samplers by simply changing the timestep grid.

title: HandsOnWorld: Unconstrained Egocentric Video Generation with Camera-Disentangled Hand Control
summary: We present HandsOnWorld, a framework for hand-controlled egocentric video generation that forgoes multi-view and marker-based motion capture, learning instead from unconstrained monocular video. Such generality is bottlenecked by the scarcity of scalable 3D hand annotations: large egocentric corpora lack finger-level labels, whereas precise hand datasets are confined to narrow, instrumented settings, limiting prior hand-controlled generators to restricted scene distributions. We instead annotate 3D hands directly on in-the-wild egocentric video through monocular reconstruction, introducing a protagonist-centered annotation pipeline that filters the reconstructions at the action-semantic, image-quality, and 3D-geometric levels to build EgoVid-Pro, a dataset of clean, protagonist-only hand trajectories spanning 103K clips and roughly 12M frames across diverse everyday scenes. To resolve the camera-hand entanglement induced by large ego-motion, we further propose the Plücker Hand Map, a 3D-aware control signal that extends Plücker-ray representations from camera rays to the hand surface, disentangling camera and hand motion at the representation level. Experiments show that \method surpasses prior hand-controlled generators in reconstruction fidelity and control accuracy, and generalizes to out-of-distribution everyday scenes beyond the laboratory datasets on which prior methods rely.

AI.tldr: HandsOnWorld is a framework for hand-controlled egocentric video generation that uses monocular video without multi-view or marker-based capture. It introduces EgoVid-Pro (103K clips, ~12M frames) via a protagonist-centered annotation pipeline, and proposes Plücker Hand Map for disentangling camera and hand motion. It outperforms prior methods in fidelity and control accuracy, generalizing to in-the-wild scenes.
AI.motivation: Existing hand-controlled video generators rely on multi-view/marker-based motion capture, limiting them to narrow, instrumented settings. Scalable 3D hand annotations are scarce: large egocentric datasets lack finger-level labels, while precise hand datasets are confined to controlled environments. The goal is to learn from unconstrained monocular video and generalize to diverse everyday scenes.
AI.method: (1) A protagonist-centered annotation pipeline that annotates 3D hands on in-the-wild egocentric video via monocular reconstruction, filtering at action-semantic, image-quality, and 3D-geometric levels to create EgoVid-Pro. (2) Plücker Hand Map, a 3D-aware control signal extending Plücker-ray representations from camera rays to the hand surface, disentangling camera and hand motion.
AI.result: HandsOnWorld surpasses prior hand-controlled generators in reconstruction fidelity and control accuracy, and generalizes to out-of-distribution everyday scenes beyond laboratory datasets.
AI.conclusion: HandsOnWorld demonstrates that unconstrained monocular video is sufficient for hand-controlled egocentric video generation without multi-view or marker-based capture, enabling generalization to diverse real-world scenes.

title: Automated grading of Linux/bash examinations using large language models: a four-level cognitive taxonomy approach
summary: Scalable and reliable grading of command-line examinations remains a challenge in computing education, where rising enrolments make manual marking difficult and rule-based autograders cannot handle partial credit, equivalent solutions, or syntactic variation. This paper evaluates whether four frontier Large Language Models (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, and GLM) can approximate expert judgment when grading short Linux/bash command responses. The study adopts a four-level cognitive taxonomy that combines cognitive complexity and operational impact, ranging from information retrieval (L1) and basic file manipulation (L2) to structural operations (L3) and advanced system management (L4). The models were tested with two prompt variants, a minimal baseline and a rubric-enhanced version, on 1200 real responses from second-year Computer Engineering students independently graded by three expert instructors. Gemini~3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting achieved the highest human-AI agreement (ICC(3,1) = 0.888, MAE = 0.10, Bland-Altman bias = -0.014). Agreement declined consistently as taxonomy level increased, with the largest discrepancies at higher levels. Across all models, rubric quality had a larger effect than provider choice, with structured prompts consistently improving agreement. These results show that question complexity is a reliable predictor of the difficulty LLMs face in grading accurately, and they establish a principled, taxonomy-based framework for determining which questions are suitable for AI-assisted grading and which require human review, while also providing a transferable evaluation protocol and prompt templates.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates four frontier LLMs (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, GLM) for grading Linux/bash command responses using a four-level cognitive taxonomy (L1-L4). Gemini 3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting achieved the best human-AI agreement (ICC=0.888, MAE=0.10). Agreement declined at higher taxonomy levels, and rubric quality had a larger effect than model choice, establishing a taxonomy-based framework for determining AI-suitable vs. human-review-required grading questions.
AI.motivation: Scalable and reliable grading of command-line examinations is challenging due to rising enrollments making manual marking unsustainable and rule-based autograders unable to handle partial credit, equivalent solutions, or syntactic variation. The paper aims to evaluate whether LLMs can approximate expert judgment to address this gap.
AI.method: Four LLMs (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, GLM) were tested with two prompt variants (minimal baseline and rubric-enhanced) on 1200 real responses from second-year Computer Engineering students. Responses were independently graded by three expert instructors. A four-level cognitive taxonomy (L1: information retrieval, L2: basic file manipulation, L3: structural operations, L4: advanced system management) was used to categorize question complexity.
AI.result: Gemini 3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting achieved the highest human-AI agreement (ICC(3,1)=0.888, MAE=0.10, Bland-Altman bias=-0.014). Agreement declined consistently as taxonomy level increased. Rubric quality had a larger effect than provider choice, with structured prompts consistently improving agreement across all models.
AI.conclusion: Question complexity is a reliable predictor of LLM grading difficulty. The study establishes a principled, taxonomy-based framework for determining which questions are suitable for AI-assisted grading and which require human review, while providing a transferable evaluation protocol and prompt templates.

title: Probing Chemical Language Models: Effects of Pre-training and Fine-tuning
summary: Chemical language models (CLMs) are trained with linearized representations such as SMILES, yet it remains unclear which chemically meaningful substructures they encode. To foster a better understanding of CLMs, we conduct a systematic study and probe for 78 molecular substructures across eight pre-trained and six randomly initialized models. We furthermore study how fine-tuning on chemical downstream tasks affects the learned representations of molecular substructures. Our results show that pre-training generally improves molecular structure awareness of CLMs, particularly in the upper layers. Moreover, randomly initialized models already encode ring structures well in the first layer. Our analysis on two chemical downstream tasks further reveals that, interestingly, fine-tuning affects task-relevant molecular substructures more than others, indicating that the changes in the representations follow chemical theory.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically probes 78 molecular substructures in chemical language models (CLMs), finding that pre-training improves structure awareness (especially in upper layers), randomly initialized models already encode ring structures in the first layer, and fine-tuning on downstream tasks affects task-relevant substructures more than others, aligning with chemical theory.
AI.motivation: To understand which chemically meaningful substructures CLMs encode, as they are trained on linearized representations (e.g., SMILES) but their internal representations of molecular substructures remain unclear.
AI.method: Systematic probing study for 78 molecular substructures across eight pre-trained and six randomly initialized CLMs, with analysis of how fine-tuning on chemical downstream tasks alters learned representations of these substructures.
AI.result: Pre-training improves molecular structure awareness, especially in upper layers; randomly initialized models already encode ring structures well in the first layer; fine-tuning affects task-relevant substructures more than others, with changes following chemical theory.
AI.conclusion: Pre-training enhances CLMs' understanding of molecular substructures, and fine-tuning selectively adjusts representations of chemically relevant substructures in a theoretically consistent manner.

title: DeepGaze3.5-VL: Modeling Scanpaths via Autoregressive Token Prediction
summary: Understanding human visual attention on a scene over time has applications in domains such as interface design and inferring cognitive states. Modeling visual scanpaths has historically relied on specialized architectures with hand-crafted priors. While these architectures can model fixation sequences, their rigid structural biases restrict easy extendability and flexible conditioning. For instance, integrating task-specific instructions or adapting to distinct viewer identities requires custom, disjoint architectural additions. We frame scanpath prediction purely as a discrete sequence modeling task. By mapping coordinates into a text vocabulary, we leverage the pretrained representations of Vision-Language Models. This framing absorbs diverse factors of variation: simple prompting allows for global conditioning, such as providing viewer identities to capture personalized biases, or task-specific objectives like visual search. The framework can also integrate per-fixation attributes, such as individual fixation durations, alongside spatial locations. The autoregressive alignment enables the scalable, exact computation of per-fixation log-likelihoods, directly equivalent to the commonly used Information Gain (IG) metric. Our model, DeepGaze3.5-VL, establishes a new state-of-the-art across multiple datasets, achieving 2.18 bits of IG on MIT1003, a 46% improvement over DeepGaze III. This advantage persists even when baselines use identical high-capacity vision encoders. Beyond predictive performance, our generative framework serves as a powerful computational tool for direct behavioral interventions, allowing for controlled in-silico simulations that would be experimentally difficult or impossible to conduct in vivo. We demonstrate this ability by performing controlled interventions on the durations of pre-saccadic fixations, recovering known oculomotor phenomena purely from data.

AI.tldr: DeepGaze3.5-VL reformulates scanpath prediction as discrete sequence modeling using Vision-Language Models, enabling flexible conditioning via prompting and achieving SOTA performance (46% improvement over DeepGaze III).
AI.motivation: Existing visual scanpath models rely on specialized architectures with hand-crafted priors that lack extendability and flexible conditioning; integrating task instructions or viewer identities requires custom, disjoint architectural additions.
AI.method: Frames scanpath prediction as discrete sequence modeling by mapping coordinates into a text vocabulary, leveraging pretrained Vision-Language Models. Uses autoregressive alignment for exact per-fixation log-likelihood computation (equivalent to Information Gain). Enables conditioning via simple prompting (viewer identities, task objectives, per-fixation attributes like durations).
AI.result: 2.18 bits of Information Gain on MIT1003, a 46% improvement over DeepGaze III. Advantage holds even when baselines use identical high-capacity vision encoders.
AI.conclusion: DeepGaze3.5-VL establishes a new SOTA across multiple datasets (2.18 bits IG on MIT1003, 46% improvement over DeepGaze III), and serves as a generative tool for controlled in-silico behavioral interventions (e.g., recovering oculomotor phenomena from data).

title: EvoPolicyGym: Evaluating Autonomous Policy Evolution in Interactive Environments
summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly expected to improve executable policies through feedback, yet existing evaluations often collapse this process into a final score or confound it with open-ended software-engineering progress. We introduce Autonomous Policy Evolution, a controlled evaluation setting in which a harness-model agent repeatedly edits an executable policy system under a fixed interaction budget. We instantiate this setting in EvoPolicyGym, a benchmark built from compact interactive RL environments that evaluates how agents iteratively improve explored policies. On the EvoPolicyGym suite, GPT-5.5 achieves the strongest aggregate rank score and top-two performance on all 16 environments. Beyond leaderboard results, EvoPolicyGym also provides trajectory-level diagnostics that distinguish how agents allocate budget, convert feedback into parametric tuning. These analyses show that strong autonomous policy evolution depends not only on isolated task wins, but on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and refining policies under bounded feedback.

AI.tldr: Introduces Autonomous Policy Evolution, a controlled evaluation setting where agents iteratively improve policies through feedback, and EvoPolicyGym benchmark built from compact RL environments. GPT-5.5 achieves top performance across all 16 environments. The work provides trajectory-level diagnostics showing strong policy evolution depends on task-appropriate mechanisms and bounded-feedback refinement, not just task wins.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations for autonomous agents either collapse improvement processes into a single final score or conflate them with open-ended software-engineering progress. A controlled setting is needed to isolate and evaluate how agents iteratively improve executable policies through feedback under fixed budgets.
AI.method: Proposes Autonomous Policy Evolution setting where a harness-model agent repeatedly edits an executable policy system under a fixed interaction budget. Instantiates this in EvoPolicyGym, a benchmark built from compact interactive RL environments. Evaluates agents on how they iteratively improve explored policies, and provides trajectory-level diagnostics analyzing budget allocation, feedback conversion, and parametric tuning.
AI.result: GPT-5.5 achieves the strongest aggregate rank score and top-two performance on all 16 environments in the EvoPolicyGym suite.
AI.conclusion: Strong autonomous policy evolution depends not only on isolated task wins, but on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and refining policies under bounded feedback.

title: Predicting Early Stages Of Alzheimer's Disease And Identifying Key Biomarkers Using Deep Artificial Neural Network And Ensemble Of Machine Learning Methodologies
summary: Alzheimers disease (AD) is a brain disorder that develops slowly and mainly affects memory, thinking, language, and daily activities. It is one of the most common causes of dementia and creates many difficulties for patients as well as their families. In the early stage, the symptoms are often mild and may look like normal ageing. For this reason, many people are diagnosed late, when the disease has already progressed. At present, there is no complete cure for AD. Still, early detection can help doctors manage the condition better and take suitable steps at the right time. In this study, a machine learning model is proposed to detect the early stages of Alzheimers disease using clinical details, neuropsychological test scores, and neuroimaging-related measures. The data used in this work is collected from the Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). As the dataset has missing values, iterative imputation is applied to fill them. The dataset also has class imbalance, which is handled using Borderline SVM-SMOTE. After that, feature selection is carried out using wrapper-based and embedded methods so that only important features are used for training. The selected features are divided into training and testing sets, and feature scaling is applied. A stacking ensemble model is developed using Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, and LightGBM as base classifiers. Along with this, an artificial neural network is also trained on the same dataset. The performance of these models is compared using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC. This study aims to find the best classifier and also identify important biomarkers that may help in the early diagnosis of Alzheimers disease.

AI.tldr: A machine learning stacking ensemble model (Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, LightGBM) and an ANN are proposed for early Alzheimer's disease detection using ADNI clinical, neuropsychological, and neuroimaging data, with missing values handled by iterative imputation, class imbalance addressed via Borderline SVM-SMOTE, and feature selection via wrapper/embedded methods.
AI.motivation: Alzheimer's disease is often diagnosed late because early symptoms resemble normal aging. Since no cure exists, early detection is critical for better management, motivating the need for an automated diagnostic model using multimodal data.
AI.method: Data from ADNI is preprocessed with iterative imputation, Borderline SVM-SMOTE for imbalance, wrapper/embedded feature selection, and scaling. A stacking ensemble (Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, LightGBM as base classifiers) and an ANN are trained and compared via precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC.
AI.result: Models are evaluated on precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC; the study identifies the best-performing classifier and important biomarkers for early AD diagnosis.
AI.conclusion: The stacking ensemble and ANN approaches show promise for early AD detection; the work highlights key biomarkers and demonstrates that machine learning can aid timely clinical intervention.

title: G-RRM: Guiding Symbolic Solvers with Recurrent Reasoning Models
summary:
In this work, we focus on SE-RRMs, a symbol-equivariant instantiation of RRMs that exhibits improved extrapolation to larger problem sizes. We propose a neuro-symbolic approach, ``Guiding with Recurrent Reasoning Models'' (G-RRM), which integrates SE-RRMs with symbolic solvers for constraint satisfaction problems. SE-RRMs act as neural solvers that generate full solution proposals and guide classical symbolic solvers, such as backtracking or SAT-based methods like Glucose 4.1 and CaDiCaL 3.0.0, that produce globally correct solutions. Centrally, we investigate when neural guidance with G-RRM improves the search efficiency of symbolic solvers. %
Our experiments show that the efficacy of G-RRM depends on two conditions: first, the problem instances must have an expansive combinatorial search space to expose potential gains, and second, the solver architecture must be capable of dynamically overwriting its branching choices to recover when neural hints are imperfect. When these conditions hold, guidance drives median conflict counts to zero and yields significant wall-clock speedups: on $9\times9$ Sudoku, where the SE-RRM correctly solves $91.1\%$ of instances, backtracking accelerates by $33.3\times$ and Glucose 4.1 by $1.70\times$ (median, $p<0.001$), with Glucose 4.1 retaining a $1.17\times$ speedup on perfect-hint $25\times25$ grids. In contrast, CaDiCaL 3.0.0, whose runtime is overhead-dominated and which always respects the injected branching hints rather than overwriting them, shows no significant speedup (median $1.02\times$, n.s.) and even a small significant mean slowdown ($0.90\times$) on $9\times9$. These results delineate the regimes in which neural guidance translates into practical speedups.

AI.tldr: G-RRM integrates symbol-equivariant recurrent reasoning models (SE-RRMs) with symbolic solvers (backtracking, Glucose 4.1, CaDiCaL 3.0) for constraint satisfaction. Neural guidance improves search efficiency only when problem instances have expansive combinatorial search space AND the solver can dynamically overwrite branching hints. Under these conditions, backtracking achieves 33.3× speedup on 9×9 Sudoku, while CaDiCaL (which always respects hints) shows no significant speedup.
AI.motivation: To investigate when and why neural guidance from SE-RRMs can improve the search efficiency of classical symbolic solvers for constraint satisfaction problems.
AI.method: Proposes G-RRM, a neuro-symbolic approach where SE-RRMs generate full solution proposals that guide symbolic solvers (backtracking, Glucose 4.1, CaDiCaL 3.0.0). Tests on Sudoku instances of varying sizes and analyzes conditions for effective guidance.
AI.result: On 9×9 Sudoku: backtracking speeds up 33.3×, Glucose 4.1 speeds up 1.70×. On 25×25 with perfect hints, Glucose retains 1.17× speedup. CaDiCaL shows no significant speedup (1.02× median) and a small mean slowdown (0.90×). Guidance efficacy depends on expansive search space and solver's ability to overwrite branching hints.
AI.conclusion: Neural guidance translates to practical speedups only when the problem search space is sufficiently large and the symbolic solver can dynamically override imperfect neural hints. Solvers that strictly respect injected hints (CaDiCaL) benefit little from such guidance.

title: Dynamic Neural Graph Encoding of Inference Processes in Deep Weight Space
comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026. 28 pages, 5 figures
summary: The rapid advancements in using neural networks as implicit data representations have attracted significant interest in developing machine learning methods that analyze and process the weight spaces of other neural networks. However, efficiently handling these highdimensional weight spaces remains challenging. Existing methods often overlook the sequential nature of layer-by-layer processing in neural network inference. In this work, we propose a novel approach using dynamic graphs to represent neural network parameters, capturing the temporal dynamics of inference. Our Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder (DNG-Encoder) processes these graphs, preserving the sequential nature of neural processing. Additionally, we also leverage DNG-Encoder to develop INR2JLS (Implicit Neural Representation to Joint Latent Space) for facilitate downstream applications, such as classifying Implicit Neural Representations (INRs). Our approach demonstrates significant improvements across multiple tasks, surpassing the state-of-the-art INR classification accuracy by approximately 10% on the CIFAR-100-INR.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder (DNG-Encoder) that represents neural network weights as dynamic graphs to capture the sequential nature of inference, and uses it for INR classification, achieving ~10% improvement over SOTA on CIFAR-100-INR.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for processing neural network weight spaces are inefficient with high-dimensional data and overlook the sequential, layer-by-layer nature of neural network inference.
AI.method: A Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder (DNG-Encoder) that represents neural network parameters as dynamic graphs to capture temporal dynamics of inference, along with INR2JLS for mapping INRs to a joint latent space for downstream tasks.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art INR classification accuracy by approximately 10% on the CIFAR-100-INR benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Modeling weight spaces as dynamic graphs with temporal awareness significantly improves processing of implicit neural representations and enables better downstream performance.

title: TCG-AR: Real-Time Multi-View Augmented Reality for Trading Card Game Streaming
summary: Trading card games are increasingly played and broadcast online, yet live streams remain mostly limited to flat top-down footage of the playing area. Augmenting such streams with virtual models of the played cards would improve the viewing experience, but most existing systems rely on instrumented playing surfaces and embedded chips, which are costly and impractical for casual players and large-scale events. In this work, we present TCG-AR, a novel real-time pipeline that augments trading card games using ordinary RGB cameras alone, without any physical markers or specialized hardware. Our pipeline detects, orients, and identifies the cards on the board, renders virtual content onto each card across all views, and can additionally compose a broadcaststyle view that summarizes the game state for spectators, streaming the augmented feeds to standard broadcasting software such as OBS. To train the detection, orientation, and identification models without manual labeling, we introduce an automatic procedure that generates annotated synthetic training data from a reference set of card images. Then, we evaluate several trained models on a new manually annotated dataset with real images, analyzing performance and runtime throughput that determine real-world usability. Overall, by relying only on commodity cameras and hardware, and by open-sourcing all code, models, and datasets, this work aims to serve as a reference for real-time trading card recognition and to make real-time augmented-reality streaming accessible to the broader community of players and streamers.

AI.tldr: TCG-AR is a real-time pipeline that augments trading card game live streams with virtual card models using only ordinary RGB cameras, without markers or specialized hardware. It detects, orients, and identifies cards, renders virtual content, and generates broadcast-style views. An automatic synthetic data generation procedure eliminates manual labeling. All code, models, and datasets are open-sourced.
AI.motivation: Existing augmented reality systems for trading card games rely on instrumented surfaces and embedded chips, which are costly and impractical for casual players and large-scale events. The goal is to make AR streaming accessible using only commodity RGB cameras.
AI.method: A real-time pipeline using ordinary RGB cameras that: (1) detects, orients, and identifies cards on the board; (2) renders virtual content onto each card across multiple views; (3) composes a broadcast-style summary view. Training data is generated automatically from reference card images via synthetic data generation, avoiding manual labeling.
AI.result: Evaluated on a new manually annotated real-image dataset, analyzing both performance and runtime throughput to determine real-world usability. All models, code, and datasets are open-sourced.
AI.conclusion: This work serves as a reference for real-time trading card recognition and makes real-time augmented-reality streaming accessible to the broader community of players and streamers without requiring specialized hardware.

title: What LLM Agents Say When No One Is Watching: Social Structure and Latent Objective Emergence in Multi-Agent Debates
summary: LLM agents will increasingly act in socially structured settings where role, audience, and relational context can shape what is advantageous or costly to say. We study whether such social structure, without any explicit objective in the prompt, changes what an agent expresses publicly relative to an off-the-record (OTR) channel elicited under the same condition. We introduce a dual-channel debate framework in which agents produce public utterances that enter the shared history alongside OTR responses that are recorded but never shown to the other participant. Across 10 models, 3 scenarios, and 5 variations within each scenario, alignment-inducing settings produce systematic public-OTR divergence in the targeted agent, with its decision divergence rising from a $\sim$3% baseline to roughly 40%. The effect is consistent across four aggregate analyses: stance, semantic similarity, natural language inference, and survey responses. In some cases, the OTR response explicitly attributes public accommodation to relational pressures, such as career risk or sponsorship obligation. The findings suggest that agent evaluation should extend beyond explicit goals and detect emergent objectives. We present a dual-channel evaluation framework and complementary behavioral measures that operationalize this assessment.

AI.tldr: LLM agents exhibit systematic divergence between public and off-the-record (OTR) responses under social-structural pressures (e.g., role, audience, relational context), even without explicit prompt objectives. Using a dual-channel debate framework across 10 models and multiple scenarios, alignment-inducing settings drive public-OTR decision divergence from ~3% to ~40%, with OTR responses often attributing accommodation to relational pressures like career risk.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether socially structured settings (role, audience, relational context) cause LLM agents to strategically alter their public expressions versus private (off-the-record) beliefs, absent any explicit instruction to do so, and to highlight the need for evaluating emergent social objectives in agent behavior.
AI.method: Introduced a dual-channel debate framework where agents produce public utterances (shared history) and off-the-record (OTR) responses (recorded but hidden from the other participant). Tested across 10 models, 3 scenarios, and 5 variations each under alignment-inducing vs. baseline conditions. Analyzed divergence via stance, semantic similarity, natural language inference, and survey responses.
AI.result: Alignment-inducing settings caused systematic public-OTR divergence, with decision divergence rising from ~3% baseline to ~40%. Effect consistent across all four aggregate analyses. OTR responses sometimes explicitly cite relational pressures (e.g., career risk, sponsorship obligation) as reasons for public accommodation.
AI.conclusion: Agent evaluation must go beyond explicit goals and detect emergent social objectives. The dual-channel evaluation framework and complementary behavioral measures operationalize this assessment.

title: Bayesian Sparse Low-Rank Adaptation for Large Language Model Uncertainty Estimation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable reasoning capabilities, but their task-specific fine-tuning is notoriously plagued by overconfidence, severely hindering trustworthy deployment. We propose Data-Adaptive Lower-Rank Adaptation (DALorRA), a simple and effective variational Bayesian sparse framework that shifts the paradigm of uncertainty quantification from the dense parameter space to the lightweight rank level of low-rank adaptation (LoRA). With the insight that LoRA essentially aggregates multiple rank-one components that may provide superfluous model capacity, DALorRA imposes stochastic masking on rank dimensions, enabling Bayesian regularization of model capacity during training and ensemble-like calibration during inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate DALorRA's excellent calibration of LLMs without compromising reasoning accuracy.

AI.tldr: DALorRA is a variational Bayesian sparse framework for LLM fine-tuning that applies stochastic masking on LoRA rank dimensions to improve calibration (reduce overconfidence) while maintaining reasoning accuracy.
AI.motivation: LLMs exhibit overconfidence during task-specific fine-tuning, which hinders their trustworthy deployment.
AI.method: DALorRA (Data-Adaptive Lower-Rank Adaptation): a variational Bayesian sparse framework that shifts uncertainty quantification from dense parameter space to the rank level of LoRA by imposing stochastic masking on rank dimensions, enabling Bayesian regularization during training and ensemble-like calibration during inference.
AI.result: DALorRA achieves excellent calibration of LLMs without compromising reasoning accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DALorRA effectively mitigates overconfidence in LLM fine-tuning by leveraging rank-level Bayesian sparsity, offering a lightweight and effective calibration solution.

title: Multimodal Fusion for Fine-Grained Classification of Breast Fibroadenoma and Phyllodes Tumors
summary: Breast fibroadenoma (FA) and phyllodes tumor (PT) are fibroepithelial breast lesions with highly overlapping appearances on B-mode ultrasound, making benign and borderline PT prone to being misclassified as FA and complicating preoperative decision-making. Existing computer-aided diagnosis methods commonly rely on single-modal imaging features and insufficiently exploit complementary clinical and textual information. To address this limitation, we construct the FAPT-M Dataset, a pathology-confirmed multimodal dataset comprising 910 patients with strictly reviewed ultrasound images, structured clinical attributes, and ultrasound diagnostic descriptions. Based on this dataset, we propose a clinically guided multimodal framework that integrates DenseNet-based visual encoding, CLIP-inspired text encoding, and lightweight clinical encoding, and further introduces clinical-conditioned adaptive modulation, cross-modal Transformer fusion, and dual-path representation learning to improve feature alignment and multimodal interaction. Under patient-level five-fold cross-validation, the proposed method achieves an accuracy of 77.64%, F1-score of 73.38%, and AUC of 89.74%, outperforming representative CNN-, Transformer-, and vision-language-based baselines. Ablation studies and class-balanced evaluations further confirm the contribution of three-modality fusion and the key architectural components. Overall, this work provides an effective multimodal approach for fine-grained FA-PT classification and establishes a high-quality benchmark for multimodal breast ultrasound analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a clinically guided multimodal framework (integrating ultrasound images, clinical attributes, and text descriptions) for distinguishing breast fibroadenoma (FA) from phyllodes tumor (PT), achieving 77.64% accuracy, 73.38% F1-score, and 89.74% AUC on a new 910-patient multimodal dataset.
AI.motivation: FA and PT have highly overlapping B-mode ultrasound appearances, causing benign/borderline PT to be misclassified as FA. Existing CAD methods rely on single-modal imaging features and fail to exploit complementary clinical and textual information.
AI.method: Constructed the FAPT-M Dataset (910 patients with ultrasound images, clinical attributes, and diagnostic descriptions). Proposed a multimodal framework with DenseNet visual encoding, CLIP-inspired text encoding, lightweight clinical encoding, clinical-conditioned adaptive modulation, cross-modal Transformer fusion, and dual-path representation learning.
AI.result: Accuracy 77.64%, F1-score 73.38%, AUC 89.74% under patient-level five-fold cross-validation, outperforming CNN-, Transformer-, and vision-language-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multimodal approach effectively improves fine-grained FA-PT classification, and the FAPT-M Dataset provides a high-quality benchmark for multimodal breast ultrasound analysis.

title: ReContext: Recursive Evidence Replay as LLM Harness for Long-Context Reasoning
summary: Understanding and reasoning over long contexts has become a key requirement for deploying large language models (LLMs) in realistic applications.
